However, limitations include generic questions, limited depth, privacy concerns, and lack of human interaction. The approach is viable for short, low-risk studies but requires human oversight.
AI.motivation: Semi-structured interviews in ESE are resource-intensive and logistically complex. The authors aim to explore whether AI-conducted interviews can offer a viable, scalable alternative that reduces coordination overhead while maintaining acceptable quality.
AI.method: A customized MyGPT was deployed to conduct self-administered, short interviews via voice interaction in participants' preferred language. Two ESE studies were conducted (refactoring practices and generative AI in Scrum). The AI followed a predefined protocol and produced structured syntheses instead of verbatim transcripts. 66 submissions were analyzed for format compliance, language consistency, and protocol adherence, alongside participant questionnaires.
AI.result: 92.4% of artifacts followed the expected synthesis format; 65 were in Portuguese, 1 in English; 2 conflicted with the reported protocol. Participant feedback: 90.9% positive overall experience and comfort, 95.5% clear questions, 97.0% positive pace, 89.4% would participate again. Limitations included generic questions, insufficient depth, privacy concerns, and missed human interaction.
AI.conclusion: AI-conducted interviews are operationally viable and acceptable for short, focused, low-risk ESE studies, but they do not match human-conducted interviews in depth or fidelity. They should serve as a complementary option with protocol design, privacy guidance, artifact validation, and human oversight.

title: TEDDY: A Pediatric Foundation Model for Risk Forewarning from ICD-Coded Diagnostic Histories
summary: Pediatric electronic health records capture developmentally structured clinical trajectories, yet their potential for generative healthcare foundation models remains largely unexplored. Here we present TEDDY (Temporal Event Decoder for Disease in Youth), a 1.84-million-parameter decoder transformer trained on approximately 73 million ICD-10 diagnoses from 1.6 million children at a single pediatric institution. TEDDY models longitudinal diagnosis trajectories and visit timing. Predictions were made before visit codes were revealed, limited to first occurrences, and evaluated against sex- and age-matched controls. Across 797 disease-onset prediction tasks spanning 16 ICD-10 chapters, TEDDY achieved a median AUC of 72.0%, outperforming same-data DenseNet (50.0%), CNN (57.2%), RNN (60.1%), and LSTM (62.7%) baselines on 96-99% of tasks. Performance held across sex and age and was strongest among lower-prevalence diagnoses; 202 of the 225 rarest conditions (90%) had 95% confidence intervals above chance. Predictive signal remained detectable more than two years before first recorded diagnosis, with median AUCs of 59.7% in the unrestricted analysis and 64.4% in a fixed-cohort sensitivity analysis. In asthma and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder benchmarks, AUCs were 79.3% and 84.7%, compared with 62.7% and 71.7% for the strongest comparators, including a general-purpose language model three orders of magnitude larger. Visit-timing predictions had a 3.0-day mean absolute restricted mean survival-time error over 365 days, although median and long-tail return intervals remained miscalibrated. Together, these results establish pediatric diagnostic histories as a substrate for compact generative models supporting broad, rare-disease, and long-horizon risk forecasting without population-scale data or billion-parameter models.

AI.tldr: TEDDY is a 1.84-million-parameter decoder transformer trained on ~73M ICD-10 codes from 1.6M children, achieving median AUC of 72.0% across 797 disease-onset prediction tasks, outperforming larger models and baselines, with predictive signal detectable >2 years before diagnosis and strong performance on rare conditions.
AI.motivation: Pediatric EHR data contain structured developmental trajectories, but their potential for generative healthcare foundation models remains unexplored, motivating a compact model that can leverage longitudinal diagnosis sequences without requiring billion-parameter scale or population-wide data.
AI.method: TEDDY is a decoder-only transformer (1.84M params) trained on ~73M ICD-10 diagnoses from 1.6M pediatric patients. It models longitudinal diagnosis trajectories and visit timing via next-token prediction, masking visit codes before prediction, limiting to first occurrences, and evaluating against sex- and age-matched controls across 797 tasks spanning 16 ICD-10 chapters.
AI.result: Median AUC 72.0% across 797 tasks; outperforms DenseNet (50.0%), CNN (57.2%), RNN (60.1%), LSTM (62.7%) on 96-99% of tasks; 90% of 225 rarest conditions above chance; predictive signal >2 years before diagnosis (median AUC 59.7-64.4%); asthma AUC 79.3%, ADHD AUC 84.7% vs best comparators 62.7%/71.7%; visit-timing MAE 3.0 days over 365 days.
AI.conclusion: Pediatric diagnostic histories enable compact generative models for broad, rare-disease, and long-horizon risk forecasting without requiring population-scale data or billion-parameter models.

title: Dynamic Manipulation Hypergraphs for HAR: Beyond Pairwise Relations: Dynamic Manipulation Hypergraphs for Vision-Based Human Activity Recognition
summary: Fine-grained manipulation recognition requires modeling evolving relations among hands, objects, tools, and supporting surfaces. Conventional graph-based methods use pairwise edges that can fragment a coordinated event into disconnected binary relations. We propose a dynamic manipulation hypergraph framework that represents multi-entity configurations as higher-order relational units. At each temporal step, relevant entities are encoded using appearance, spatial, motion, and semantic-role features. Hyperedge candidates are instantiated and ranked using proximity, contact, and motion-coupling predicates. A hypergraph reasoning network performs node-to-hyperedge and hyperedge-to-node message passing, followed by temporal attention over the evolving interaction structure. The framework provides class-agnostic hyperedge-importance scores that identify entity configurations and temporal intervals emphasized by the model without treating them as causal explanations. Quantitative evaluation is conducted on EPIC-KITCHENS-100/VISOR and Assembly101 under an annotation-assisted entity-localization protocol. Video-only and entity-based methods provide contextual comparisons, while a matched pairwise graph and a static hypergraph serve as the principal controlled baselines because they use identical entity inputs and comparable relational settings. The proposed method improves HO-F1 over the matched pairwise graph by 6.9 percentage points on EPIC-KITCHENS-100/VISOR and 9.5 points on Assembly101, and exceeds the static hypergraph by 4.4 and 5.8 points, respectively. Qualitative analysis on ARCTIC further shows correspondence between highly ranked hyperedges and contact-rich manipulation intervals. These results demonstrate the value of time-varying higher-order relational modeling for fine-grained manipulation activity recognition.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dynamic manipulation hypergraph framework for fine-grained manipulation recognition that models multi-entity configurations as higher-order relational units, using hyperedge instantiation and ranking via proximity/contact/motion-coupling predicates, and message passing with temporal attention. It outperforms pairwise graphs and static hypergraphs on EPIC-KITCHENS-100/VISOR (HO-F1 +6.9 pts) and Assembly101 (+9.5 pts).
AI.motivation: Conventional graph-based methods use pairwise edges that fragment coordinated manipulation events into disconnected binary relations, failing to capture higher-order interactions among hands, objects, tools, and supporting surfaces.
AI.method: A dynamic hypergraph framework where: (1) entities are encoded with appearance, spatial, motion, and semantic-role features per timestep; (2) hyperedge candidates are instantiated and ranked using proximity, contact, and motion-coupling predicates; (3) a hypergraph reasoning network performs node-to-hyperedge and hyperedge-to-node message passing; (4) temporal attention models evolving interaction structure; (5) class-agnostic hyperedge-importance scores identify key configurations without causal explanation framing.
AI.result: Improves HO-F1 by 6.9 percentage points on EPIC-KITCHENS-100/VISOR and 9.5 points on Assembly101 over matched pairwise graphs, and 4.4 and 5.8 points over static hypergraphs. Qualitative results on ARCTIC show correspondence between high-ranked hyperedges and contact-rich manipulation intervals.
AI.conclusion: Time-varying higher-order relational modeling is valuable for fine-grained manipulation activity recognition, outperforming both pairwise graph and static hypergraph baselines across multiple benchmarks.

title: MemoHarness: Agent Harnesses That Learn from Experience
summary: An agent harness is the external control layer that turns a base LLM into an executable agent by managing context, tools, orchestration, memory, decoding, and output handling. While harness design strongly affects agent behavior, most automatic improvement methods optimize narrower artifacts such as prompts, pipelines, or workflows, and deployed agents usually reuse a single global harness for all cases. We introduce MemoHarness, an adaptive harness optimization framework that learns from its own executions. MemoHarness decomposes the harness into six editable control dimensions, stores per-case diagnoses and distilled global patterns in a dual-layer experience bank, and adapts the learned harness to each test case using retrieved experience without test-time labels, feedback, or additional search. In our evaluation across shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical-reasoning benchmarks, MemoHarness improves over the fixed harnesses we compare against and shows selective transfer to unseen suites and base models. Its additional context can also remain cost-competitive when much of the retrieved experience is cacheable. These results provide evidence that execution experience is a practical substrate for building agent harnesses that are more adaptive than a single static configuration, while leaving broader claims about statistical robustness and component attribution to future work.

AI.tldr: MemoHarness is an adaptive framework that optimizes LLM agent harnesses across six control dimensions by learning from execution experience, using a dual-layer memory bank to adapt per test case without additional feedback, showing improvements over fixed harnesses on shell-agent, code-generation, and reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing agent systems rely on fixed, global harnesses that do not adapt per case, and most automatic improvement methods focus on narrower artifacts (prompts, pipelines) rather than the harness itself, limiting agent adaptability.
AI.method: MemoHarness decomposes the agent harness into six editable control dimensions, stores per-case diagnoses and global patterns in a dual-layer experience bank, and adapts the harness for each test case via retrieved experience without needing test-time labels or search.
AI.result: MemoHarness outperforms fixed harnesses across shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical-reasoning benchmarks, demonstrates selective transfer to unseen suites and base models, and can remain cost-competitive when retrieved experience is cacheable.
AI.conclusion: Execution experience is a practical substrate for building adaptive agent harnesses that outperform static configurations, though broader claims about statistical robustness and component attribution require future work.

title: Beyond Generalist LLMs: Specialist Agentic Systems for Structured Code Workflow Execution
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have accelerated the adoption of software development agents, now widely available as Integrated Development Environment (IDE) extensions and standalone applications. While these agents are typically general-purpose, it remains unclear whether specialist agents justify their additional development effort. We investigate this question in the context of business process automation, focusing on the transformation of Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams into executable agentic workflows. Since BPMN specifies explicit control-flow semantics, we focus on deterministic workflows in which a fixed process model and inputs uniquely determine the executed path. We introduce a specialist workflow for this task and compare it against generalist agents such as Roo and Cline. Our results show that the specialist solution produces agents that outperform generalist baselines by approximately 9-20 percentage points in tool-use exactness, 2-4x in penalty-adjusted latency, and 3x fewer tool-call errors, while reducing generation token cost by over 95% and eliminating repair iterations. We also find that generalist agents generate code inconsistently in both functionality and quality, limiting their suitability for industrial settings where reliability and maintainability are essential.

AI.tldr: This paper compares specialist vs. generalist LLM agents for converting BPMN diagrams into executable workflows, finding that specialist agents outperform generalists by 9-20pp in tool-use exactness, 2-4x in latency, 3x fewer errors, and 95%+ cost reduction, while generalists produce inconsistent code unsuitable for industrial use.
AI.motivation: To determine whether specialist agents justify their additional development effort over general-purpose agents in the context of business process automation, specifically for transforming BPMN diagrams into deterministic executable workflows.
AI.method: The authors introduce a specialist workflow for converting BPMN diagrams to agentic workflows and compare it against generalist agents (Roo and Cline). The task focuses on deterministic workflows where control-flow semantics are fixed by BPMN specifications.
AI.result: Specialist agents outperform generalists by 9-20 percentage points in tool-use exactness, 2-4x in penalty-adjusted latency, 3x fewer tool-call errors, and over 95% reduction in generation token cost, while eliminating repair iterations. Generalist agents produce inconsistent code in functionality and quality.
AI.conclusion: Specialist agents are superior to generalist agents for deterministic BPMN-to-workflow transformation tasks, and generalist agents' inconsistency limits their suitability for industrial settings requiring reliability and maintainability.

title: Long-term User Engagement Optimization through Model-agnostic Downstream Rewards Learning
summary: As recommender systems mature in the past few years, their optimization objectives have evolved from a primary focusing on short-term behavioral signals to a broader emphasis on long-term user engagement and retention. However, directly optimizing retention is difficult because return signals are sparse, delayed, and only partially attributable to earlier recommendations. Prior work has addressed this challenge with sequential modeling and reinforcement learning, but these approaches typically require task specific reward engineering, substantial computational overhead, and surface specific implementations that are difficult to generalize. In this paper, we present a unified, model-agnostic downstream reward framework for optimizing long-term user value in large-scale recommendation systems. First, we formulate the downstream reward learning problem and develop an offline screening framework to identify session level behaviors that are both observable early and predictive of future retention. We then propose several model-agnostic downstream rewards signals derived from observed user action patterns across multiple sources. We further discuss the engineering effort to productionize the proposed rewards derivations and challenges we faced when adding them to our ranking models. Online A/B experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in engagement and retention-related metrics, and the framework has been deployed across multiple Pinterest surfaces, including Homefeed, Related Pins, Search, and Notifications.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified, model-agnostic downstream reward framework to optimize long-term user retention in large-scale recommendation systems, using offline screening to identify predictive session-level behaviors and deriving reward signals from observed user actions. The framework was successfully deployed across multiple Pinterest surfaces, with online A/B experiments showing consistent improvements in engagement and retention metrics.
AI.motivation: Recommender systems have shifted from optimizing short-term behavioral signals to long-term user engagement and retention, but directly optimizing retention is difficult due to sparse, delayed, and partially attributable return signals. Existing approaches like sequential modeling and reinforcement learning require task-specific reward engineering, high computational overhead, and lack generalizability.
AI.method: The authors formulate a downstream reward learning problem, develop an offline screening framework to identify session-level behaviors that are observable early and predictive of future retention, and propose model-agnostic downstream reward signals derived from observed user action patterns across multiple sources. They also detail the engineering productionization of these rewards and integration into ranking models.
AI.result: Online A/B experiments demonstrated consistent improvements in engagement and retention-related metrics. The framework has been deployed across multiple Pinterest surfaces, including Homefeed, Related Pins, Search, and Notifications.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified, model-agnostic downstream reward framework effectively addresses the challenge of optimizing long-term user retention in large-scale recommendation systems, providing a generalizable solution that outperforms prior approaches requiring task-specific engineering, and has proven successful in production across diverse surfaces at Pinterest.

title: $K$-NeAS: Scalable Multi-Material CT Reconstruction Using Neural SDFs
summary: Computed Tomography (CT) carries significant ionizing radiation risks, driving the need for sparse-view reconstruction. Implicit scene representations (ISRs) address this by recovering continuous volumetric attenuation fields directly from sparse projections, and recent geometry-aware extensions jointly model surface geometry alongside attenuation to improve fidelity and enable clean tissue segmentation without manual thresholding. However, these methods remain limited by manually tuned attenuation bounds and rigid two-material constraints. This paper proposes $K$-NeAS, a unified and scalable architecture for automated, multi-material surface reconstruction. We replace independent material networks with a shared latent backbone and introduce a fully differentiable $K$-material sequential soft selector to model an arbitrary number of overlapping tissues. To eliminate manual tuning, we automate attenuation bounding using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) and implement a scheduled auxiliary floater loss to mitigate geometric hallucinations common under extreme sparsity. Evaluated across four clinical Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) datasets, $K$-NeAS successfully scales to arbitrary material counts, achieving superior 3D volumetric fidelity at $K=3$ materials on complex multi-tissue regions such as the Abdomen ($33.28\text{ dB}$ 3D PSNR vs. $31.40\text{ dB}$ single-material NeAS baseline, a $+1.88\text{ dB}$ improvement). Furthermore, our model exhibits enhanced robustness under sparse-sampling conditions, outperforming baseline 3D PSNR by up to $1.17\text{ dB}$ under 5- and 10-view constraints.

AI.tldr: K-NeAS is a unified, scalable architecture for automated multi-material surface reconstruction from sparse CT projections, replacing manually tuned attenuation bounds and rigid two-material constraints with a shared latent backbone, a differentiable K-material sequential soft selector, GMM-based automated attenuation bounding, and a scheduled auxiliary floater loss to mitigate geometric hallucinations.
AI.motivation: CT imaging poses ionizing radiation risks, motivating sparse-view reconstruction. Existing ISR methods are limited by manually tuned attenuation bounds and rigid two-material constraints, failing to scale to arbitrary material counts.
AI.method: K-NeAS replaces independent material networks with a shared latent backbone, introduces a fully differentiable K-material sequential soft selector for arbitrary tissues, automates attenuation bounding via Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), and implements a scheduled auxiliary floater loss to reduce geometric hallucinations under extreme sparsity.
AI.result: Across four clinical CBCT datasets, K-NeAS achieves superior 3D volumetric fidelity at K=3 materials on complex multi-tissue regions (Abdomen: 33.28 dB PSNR vs. 31.40 dB baseline, +1.88 dB). Under sparse 5- and 10-view constraints, it outperforms baseline by up to 1.17 dB.
AI.conclusion: K-NeAS successfully scales to arbitrary material counts, automates attenuation bounding, and enhances robustness under sparse-sampling conditions for multi-material surface reconstruction from sparse CT projections.

title: When a Verified World Model Still Loses: Play-Adequacy vs Prediction-Accuracy in LLM-Synthesized Code World Models
comment: 41 pages, 4 figures. Code and reproduction log: https://github.com/JaviMaligno/code-world-models
summary:
Large language models can synthesize a game's rules as executable code - a Code World Model (CWM) - which a classical planner then searches over. Such models are typically accepted when they reach high transition accuracy on sampled trajectories. We argue this is the wrong notion of adequacy for planning.
  We show four things. (1) An LLM-synthesized CWM can pass a sampling gate at 100% transition accuracy and be $\geq 98\%$ state-accurate on the planner's own search distribution, yet lose systematically at play, because the $<1\%$ it gets wrong is exactly the pivotal dynamics; the play cost of the omitted rule is $0.091$ (seed-clustered 95% CI $[0.065,0.117]$, $n=4800$). We call this the verified-vs-correct gap, and confirm it end-to-end through the synthesis pipeline. (2) The harm follows a quantitative law, $\mathrm{danger}=\mathrm{play\_cost}\times(1-\mathrm{rarity})^N$, whose $(1-\mathrm{rarity})^N$ gate-miss factor is proven exact and whose play cost is empirically bounded. (3) The failure is not repaired by more data: LLM synthesis behaves as rule translation, not rule inference, and did not infer the omitted rule across models (GPT-5.x) and data regimes (including DAgger and targeted examples). (4) The same mechanism recurs on the belief-inference function of imperfect-information CWMs: we prove a coverage bound (a size-$N$ gate is identifying when $N\gtrsim b^{d_{\max}}$), explaining why shallow games such as Kuhn poker show no gap, and hand-construct Beacon, a verified-but-wrong inference function that passes the gate yet loses every game.
  These results suggest adequacy for planning-oriented world models should be measured on the search distribution or by play directly, not by prediction accuracy on sampled transitions.

AI.tldr: LLM-synthesized code world models (CWMs) can pass sampling-based accuracy tests with near-perfect scores yet fail systematically in planning/play because they miss rare but pivotal dynamics. This "verified-vs-correct gap" follows a quantitative danger law, persists across models and data regimes, extends to imperfect-information settings, and suggests planning adequacy should be measured on search distribution or by play, not by transition accuracy.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the common practice of using high transition accuracy on sampled trajectories as the measure of adequacy for LLM-synthesized world models used in planning. The authors argue that this notion is fundamentally wrong because it fails to capture rare but critically important dynamics.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate the verified-vs-correct gap empirically through end-to-end synthesis pipelines, derive a quantitative law (danger = play_cost × (1 - rarity)^N), test failure persistence across models (GPT-5.x) and data regimes (including DAgger and targeted examples), and extend analysis to imperfect-information CWMs with a coverage bound proof and a hand-constructed counterexample (Beacon).
AI.result: (1) A CWM with 100% transition accuracy and ≥98% state accuracy on the planner's search distribution can still lose systematically at play due to <1% errors on pivotal dynamics (play cost 0.091). (2) The danger follows the law danger = play_cost × (1 - rarity)^N. (3) LLM synthesis behaves as rule translation, not inference; omitted rules persist across models and data regimes. (4) For imperfect-information CWMs, a coverage bound (N ≳ b^{d_max}) explains why shallow games show no gap, and Beacon demonstrates a verified-but-wrong inference function.
AI.conclusion: Planning-oriented world model adequacy should be measured on the search distribution or by direct play, not by prediction accuracy on sampled transitions.

title: Predicting Human Visual Attention on Words in Source Code
summary: This paper presents a computational model to predict human visual attention over words in software source code. The visual attention of software engineers when reading source code has long been studied as a means to understand human cognitive processes during software engineering tasks. Predicting this visual attention is important for perfecting user interface design and understanding what information human programmers need. We propose a model of programmer visual attention in which we design a novel loss function that computes similarity between human attention measured during eye tracking experiments and the internal attention of the artificial neural network. We evaluate our model by comparing its outputs to actual eye tracking data from three separate datasets. Two are in the Java programming language and one is in the C programming language. Our model outperforms the baseline in software engineering by 64%, 16%, and 467% in each of these studies according to Pearson correlation. We used scanpath prediction as an example to demonstrate that our model is more capable of the task that requires the understanding of human thought process. Our model achieves a statistically significant improvement over the close baseline in the reading task according to normalized Levenshtein distance and outperforms both Claude and GPT-5 on both reading and writing tasks.

AI.tldr: A computational model predicts programmer visual attention on source code using a novel loss function that aligns neural network attention with human eye-tracking data, outperforming baselines by 16-467% across Java and C datasets.
AI.motivation: Understanding and predicting human visual attention in source code is crucial for optimizing UI design and comprehending programmer cognitive processes, yet accurate computational models for this task remain underdeveloped.
AI.method: The model uses a novel loss function that computes similarity between human attention (from eye-tracking experiments) and internal attention of an artificial neural network. Evaluation uses three datasets (two Java, one C) with Pearson correlation and scanpath prediction via normalized Levenshtein distance.
AI.result: Outperforms the baseline by 64%, 16%, and 467% in three studies (Pearson correlation). Achieves statistically significant improvement over close baseline in reading tasks and outperforms both Claude and GPT-5 on reading and writing tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model effectively predicts human visual attention in source code, demonstrating superior capability in tasks requiring understanding of human thought processes, with implications for improving software engineering tools and interfaces.

title: Augmentations for Robust and Efficient Imitation Learning in Streamed Video Games
comment: To be published in proceedings of IEEE Conference on Games (CoG), 2026
summary: Imitation learning is an appealing way to scale game-playing agents to complex 3D environments by training policies to map visual observations to actions from human demonstrations. However, these demonstrations are expensive to collect and modern game-playing is often done through streaming in which network delay and compression introduce spatiotemporally correlated visual artifacts that can cause a covariance shift at test time. To address these challenges, we propose streaming augmentations that mimic four types of artifacts commonly encountered during streaming with low-bandwidth network connection: pixelated blocks and scrubs, global blur, and ghosting. We instantiate our approach on top of predictive inverse dynamics models (PIDM), which combine future-state conditioning with an inverse dynamics policy in a learned latent space, and evaluate the impact of our augmentations across three tasks in modern 3D video games. Under stable streaming conditions, agents trained with spatiotemporal augmentations achieve up to 41% higher evaluation performance compared to agents trained without augmentations under an identical data budget. When network lag is introduced, agents trained with augmentations degrade by only 7.45% vs 49.82% of the original performance for agents trained only with the original data. These results clearly indicate that spatiotemporal augmentations tailored for the streaming setting are a simple yet powerful tool to train robust and efficient game-playing agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes streaming augmentations that mimic four types of network-induced visual artifacts (pixelated blocks, scrubs, global blur, ghosting) to train imitation learning agents robust to spatiotemporally correlated distortions in game streaming. Applied on top of PIDM, the method achieves up to 41% higher performance under stable streaming and degrades only 7.45% vs 49.82% under network lag, compared to agents trained without augmentations.
AI.motivation: Human demonstrations for imitation learning in 3D game environments are expensive to collect, and game-playing via streaming introduces spatiotemporally correlated visual artifacts (network delay, compression) that cause covariance shift at test time, degrading agent performance.
AI.method: Proposes streaming augmentations mimicking four artifacts: pixelated blocks, scrubs, global blur, and ghosting. Instantiated on top of predictive inverse dynamics models (PIDM), which combines future-state conditioning with inverse dynamics policy in a learned latent space.
AI.result: Under stable streaming: up to 41% higher evaluation performance vs agents without augmentations under identical data budget. Under network lag: agents degrade by only 7.45% vs 49.82% of original performance for non-augmented agents.
AI.conclusion: Spatiotemporal augmentations tailored for streaming are a simple yet powerful tool to train robust and efficient game-playing agents, significantly reducing performance degradation from network-induced visual artifacts.

title: Emergent Region-Level Facial Correspondence in Frozen Vision Foundation Models
summary: Frozen self-supervised vision models can align parts of generic objects, but it remains unclear whether this correspondence extends to human faces, where global layout is shared while identity-specific appearance varies sharply. We test whether frozen DINOv3 features define a region-level facial coordinate system: a feature space in which eyes, brows, nose, mouth, skin, and hair remain distinguishable across people and across time without face-specific training. Using DINOv3 ViT-L/16 patch embeddings and FaRL only as a face-part labeling interface, we evaluate cross-identity nearest-neighbor matching and temporal label propagation on 200 CelebDF-v2 real videos. DINOv3 achieves 83.0% region-level semantic accuracy under unconstrained cross-identity matching, compared with a 23.0% area-weighted random baseline, and 95.5% temporal tracking accuracy without a learned temporal module. A no-FaRL control collapses to 0.9%, showing that FaRL supplies semantic initialization while DINOv3 supplies dense spatial correspondence. The strongest correspondence appears at an intermediate layer: block 18 gives a 4.93x same-region versus cross-region discrimination ratio, compared with 1.48x at the final block. Against CLIP ViT-L/14, DINOv3 shows only a small aggregate advantage but a +16.8 pp gain on anatomical regions, indicating that image-level contrastive supervision captures coarse facial layout but not fine-grained anatomical identity. These results establish frozen DINOv3 as a strong zero-shot representation for region-level facial correspondence and identify intermediate self-supervised features as the most useful layer for dense face analysis.

AI.tldr: Frozen DINOv3 self-supervised vision models achieve strong zero-shot region-level facial correspondence (83.0% cross-identity accuracy, 95.5% temporal tracking) without face-specific training, with intermediate layers (block 18) providing the best fine-grained anatomical discrimination.
AI.motivation: To determine whether frozen self-supervised vision models (DINOv3) can establish a region-level facial coordinate system that distinguishes facial parts (eyes, brows, nose, mouth, skin, hair) across different identities and time without any face-specific training.
AI.method: Used frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 patch embeddings with FaRL as a face-part labeling interface (no-FaRL control collapses to 0.9%), evaluated cross-identity nearest-neighbor matching and temporal label propagation on 200 CelebDF-v2 real videos, and compared performance across DINOv3 layers and against CLIP ViT-L/14.
AI.result: DINOv3 achieved 83.0% region-level semantic accuracy under cross-identity matching (vs 23.0% random baseline) and 95.5% temporal tracking accuracy without learned temporal modules. Block 18 (intermediate layer) gave a 4.93x same-region vs cross-region discrimination ratio vs 1.48x at the final block. DINOv3 showed +16.8 pp gain over CLIP on anatomical regions.
AI.conclusion: Frozen DINOv3 serves as a strong zero-shot representation for region-level facial correspondence, with intermediate self-supervised features being the most discriminative layer for dense face analysis, outperforming CLIP on fine-grained anatomical discrimination.

title: ReasFlow: Assisting Reasoning-Centric Scientific Discovery in Applied Mathematics via a Knowledge-Based Multi-Agent System
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models have fueled autonomous AI agents capable of tackling complex scientific tasks, yet existing automated research systems remain predominantly focused on empirically driven domains with quantitative benchmarks, leaving theory-driven discovery, particularly in mathematically grounded disciplines requiring rigorous proofs and synthesis of domain knowledge, largely underexplored. Key challenges include the difficulty of verifying theoretical reasoning at scale, insufficient reasoning ability for autonomous frontier exploration, and a scarcity of procedural heuristics in the literature. We introduce ReasFlow, an end-to-end autonomous agent system for reasoning-centric scientific discovery that operationalizes a collaborative paradigm where the human expert acts as Principal Investigator while the agent executes rigorous derivations as a capable graduate student. ReasFlow incorporates (i) a robust internal verification loop that audits logical coherence and corrects fundamental errors prior to human inspection, and (ii) an automated knowledge retrieval and self-improvement mechanism that proactively surfaces both declarative facts and overlooked procedural heuristics, substantially reducing expert intervention. The system unifies literature synthesis, algorithm design, theorem proving, experimentation, and manuscript preparation in a single system. Deployed to autonomously generate five complete research papers with rigorous theoretical and empirical content from minimal prompts, ReasFlow consistently achieves the highest evaluation scores among state-of-the-art open-access baselines under a curated LLM-based review rubric. ReasFlow is publicly accessible via the ReasLab platform, providing a collaborative workspace for AI-assisted theoretical research. Github repo: https://github.com/ReasLab/ReasFlow.git.

AI.tldr: ReasFlow is an end-to-end autonomous AI agent system for reasoning-centric scientific discovery that collaborates with human experts as Principal Investigators, featuring internal verification loops and automated knowledge retrieval, capable of generating complete research papers with rigorous theoretical content.
AI.motivation: Existing automated research systems focus on empirically driven domains with quantitative benchmarks, leaving theory-driven discovery in mathematically grounded disciplines largely underexplored due to challenges in verifying theoretical reasoning, insufficient reasoning ability for frontier exploration, and scarcity of procedural heuristics.
AI.method: ReasFlow operationalizes a collaborative paradigm (human as Principal Investigator, agent as graduate student) with (i) an internal verification loop for auditing logical coherence and correcting errors before human inspection, and (ii) an automated knowledge retrieval and self-improvement mechanism for surfacing declarative facts and procedural heuristics, unifying literature synthesis, algorithm design, theorem proving, experimentation, and manuscript preparation.
AI.result: Deployed to autonomously generate five complete research papers with rigorous theoretical and empirical content from minimal prompts, achieving the highest evaluation scores among state-of-the-art open-access baselines under a curated LLM-based review rubric.
AI.conclusion: ReasFlow demonstrates that autonomous AI systems can effectively support theoretically rigorous scientific discovery. The system is publicly accessible via the ReasLab platform and open-source on GitHub.

title: A Deterministic Binary Fingerprinting Framework with Zero-Trained Feature Extraction for Sparse Count Matrices
summary: Sparse count matrices from single-cell transcriptomes to k-mer profiles and document-term frequencies are conventionally analyzed via PCA-reduced graph clustering or iterative optimization in continuous embedding spaces. We introduce MMTB, a deterministic non-learned binary representation framework that requires no label supervision, model fitting, or gradient-based optimization. Column-wise Min-Max normalization followed by fixed cutoffs maps each sample to a thermometer fingerprint whose Hamming distances show empirical correspondence with normalized L1 distances, with Pearson correlation approximately 0.92 on single-cell RNA-seq pairs. In a favorable three-cell-line mixture, the 3-threshold fingerprint achieves NMI of 0.99 at 188 bytes per cell. Under a fair Hamming nearest-neighbor graph plus Leiden readout, MMTB approaches PCA plus Leiden on this coarse task. On challenging tissue-like annotations, continuous pipelines often lead; PBMC Seurat NMI is 0.39 for MMTB versus 0.49 for Scanpy, underscoring that MMTB is suited for coarse-grained separation and resource-constrained deployments rather than fine-grained subtype discovery or as a general replacement for continuous embeddings. Relative to dense float32 representations, MMTB fingerprints reduce memory by approximately 10-fold while providing fixed-width Hamming-indexable codes. PCA30 embeddings and sparse CSR may be smaller; we do not claim universal compression. A label-free suitability score is provided as a deployment guideline, not a performance predictor.

AI.tldr: MMTB is a deterministic binary representation framework for sparse count matrices that maps samples to thermometer fingerprint codes via Min-Max normalization and fixed cutoffs, achieving ~10× memory reduction over float32 while approaching PCA+Leiden performance on coarse separation tasks, though it underperforms on fine-grained subtype discovery.
AI.motivation: To develop a non-learned, label-free, deterministic binary representation for sparse count matrices (e.g., single-cell RNA-seq, k-mer profiles) that avoids supervision, model fitting, and gradient optimization while enabling memory-efficient, Hamming-indexable analysis.
AI.method: Column-wise Min-Max normalization followed by fixed cutoffs to produce thermometer-like binary fingerprints; Hamming distance used with nearest-neighbor graph and Leiden clustering; a label-free suitability score is provided for deployment guidance.
AI.result: Pearson correlation ~0.92 between Hamming and normalized L1 distances; NMI 0.99 at 188 bytes/cell on a three-cell-line mixture; ~10× memory reduction vs float32; NMI 0.39 (MMTB) vs 0.49 (Scanpy) on PBMC Seurat annotations.
AI.conclusion: MMTB is suitable for coarse-grained separation and resource-constrained deployments but not for fine-grained subtype discovery or as a general replacement for continuous embeddings.

title: Privacy Leakage in Federated Learning in Radiology Reports: A Comparative Evaluation of Tokenizer-Driven Privacy Risks
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables multi-institutional training on clinical text without sharing raw data, but gradient inversion can reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates. The extent of this leakage for radiology reports, and the role of tokenizer design, remains unclear. We quantify gradient-based text reconstruction in FL and compare privacy risk across three tokenizers with the model architecture held fixed. Six FL clients trained a GPT-2-style transformer (sequence length 32) on public radiology corpora (368,751 diagnostic reports, 98,206 discharge summaries, 1,500 MIMIC-CXR free-text reports) using the GPT-2, RadBERT, and LLaMA-2 tokenizers at batch sizes of 64, 128, and 256. Assuming an active malicious server that modifies the shared architecture before distribution, we applied analytic gradient inversion and measured reconstruction fidelity over five runs. Exact sentence reconstruction ranged from 31% to 44% across tokenizers (30.6-43.5% across the 27 tokenizer x dataset x batch-size cells). At batch size 64 on the Discharge dataset, accuracy was 42.1% (GPT-2), 42.3% (RadBERT), and 39.4% (LLaMA-2), decreasing to 37.3%, 37.2%, and 34.3% at batch size 256. S-BLEU declined as batch size grew (GPT-2: 0.44 to 0.33; RadBERT: 0.48 to 0.35). RadBERT yielded the highest reconstruction fidelity and recovered the most clinical terms (18.1% of a 1,440-term reference vocabulary, vs 12.5% for GPT-2 and 9.4% for LLaMA-2), yet no tokenizer prevented leakage. Substantial portions of report text are therefore recoverable from FL gradients even at larger batch sizes and with domain-specific tokenizers. Tokenizer design influences leakage severity and is a privacy-relevant decision, not only a utility one; safeguards such as secure aggregation and differential privacy are likely necessary to meet HIPAA and GDPR requirements for FL in radiology NLP.

AI.tldr: Gradient inversion attacks in federated learning can reconstruct radiology report text with 31-44% exact sentence accuracy across tokenizers (GPT-2, RadBERT, LLaMA-2), and RadBERT leaks the most clinical terms (18.1%), demonstrating that tokenizer design significantly affects privacy risk and that no tokenizer alone suffices for privacy protection.
AI.motivation: Federated learning (FL) enables multi-institutional training on clinical text without sharing raw data, but gradient inversion can reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates. The extent of this leakage for radiology reports, and the role of tokenizer design, remains unclear.
AI.method: Six FL clients trained a GPT-2-style transformer (sequence length 32) on public radiology corpora (368,751 diagnostic reports, 98,206 discharge summaries, 1,500 MIMIC-CXR free-text reports) using GPT-2, RadBERT, and LLaMA-2 tokenizers at batch sizes 64, 128, and 256. An active malicious server modified the shared architecture before distribution, then applied analytic gradient inversion to measure reconstruction fidelity over five runs.
AI.result: Exact sentence reconstruction ranged from 31% to 44% across tokenizers (30.6-43.5% across the 27 cells). At batch size 64 on Discharge dataset, accuracy was 42.1% (GPT-2), 42.3% (RadBERT), and 39.4% (LLaMA-2), decreasing to 37.3%, 37.2%, and 34.3% at batch size 256. RadBERT yielded the highest reconstruction fidelity and recovered the most clinical terms (18.1% of a 1,440-term reference vocabulary, vs 12.5% for GPT-2 and 9.4% for LLaMA-2), yet no tokenizer prevented leakage.
AI.conclusion: Substantial portions of report text are recoverable from FL gradients even at larger batch sizes and with domain-specific tokenizers. Tokenizer design influences leakage severity and is a privacy-relevant decision, not only a utility one; safeguards such as secure aggregation and differential privacy are likely necessary to meet HIPAA and GDPR requirements for FL in radiology NLP.

title: Cotton-SF YOLO: Learning Structural and Frequency Cues for Early Cotton Square Detection in Complex Field Environments
summary: Cotton squares are important phenotypic indicators of the early reproductive growth of cotton, and automatic field detection of cotton squares provides an important basis for cotton growth monitoring and precision cultivation management. However, early cotton square detection in complex field environments remains insufficiently explored, as cotton squares are small, frequently occluded, easily blurred, subject to illumination variations, and exhibit low contrast against surrounding cotton leaves. To address these challenges, we propose a task-oriented framework based on YOLO26m, named Cotton-SF YOLO, for cotton square detection under natural field conditions. To improve the perception of small and irregular cotton square boundaries, we introduce Dynamic Snake Convolution into the detector, enabling adaptive extraction of deformable edge features. Furthermore, a frequency-domain feature modulation module is designed by incorporating spectral enhancement into the C2f structure, which recalibrate frequency-domain representations and strengthen discriminative edge and texture cues while reducing interference from complex cotton leaf backgrounds. Trained and evaluated on our newly constructed and annotated field dataset with manually annotated cotton squares, the proposed model achieves mAP$_{50}$, mAP$_{50:95}$, and recall values of 0.8196, 0.4942, and 0.7939, improving over the baseline YOLO26m by 1.25%, 3.45%, and 2.96%, respectively. Ablation experiments and visualization demonstrate that the best performance is achieved with the complementary effects of structural and frequency cues.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Cotton-SF YOLO, a task-oriented framework based on YOLO26m, for detecting cotton squares in complex field environments. It introduces Dynamic Snake Convolution for adaptive deformable edge feature extraction and a frequency-domain feature modulation module to enhance discriminative edge/texture cues while suppressing background interference. The model achieves improved mAP$_{50}$ (0.8196), mAP$_{50:95}$ (0.4942), and recall (0.7939), outperforming the baseline by 1.25%, 3.45%, and 2.96% respectively.
AI.motivation: Cotton squares are important phenotypic indicators of early reproductive growth, but their automatic field detection remains challenging due to small size, frequent occlusion, blur, illumination variations, and low contrast against cotton leaves. The problem is insufficiently explored under complex field environments.
AI.method: A task-oriented framework called Cotton-SF YOLO based on YOLO26m. It incorporates: (1) Dynamic Snake Convolution to improve perception of small and irregular cotton square boundaries via adaptive deformable edge feature extraction; (2) A frequency-domain feature modulation module that integrates spectral enhancement into the C2f structure to recalibrate frequency-domain representations and strengthen discriminative edge/texture cues while reducing background interference.
AI.result: On a newly constructed and annotated field dataset, the model achieves mAP$_{50}$=0.8196, mAP$_{50:95}$=0.4942, and recall=0.7939, improving over the YOLO26m baseline by 1.25%, 3.45%, and 2.96%, respectively. Ablation experiments confirm the complementary effects of structural and frequency cues yield best performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Cotton-SF YOLO effectively addresses small, occluded, and low-contrast cotton square detection in natural field conditions. The combination of structural (Dynamic Snake Convolution) and frequency-domain enhancements provides complementary benefits, advancing automated cotton growth monitoring and precision cultivation management.

title: RxBrain: Embodied Cognition Foundation Model with Joint Language-Visual Reasoning and Imagination
summary: Embodied cognition requires agents to connect high-level task reasoning with the physical states to be achieved. We introduce Hy-Embodied-RxBrain, an embodied cognition foundation model with joint language-visual reasoning and imagination. Unlike vision-language models that emphasize scene understanding and textual decision making, or generative world models that mainly predict future visual states, RxBrain represents embodied plans in a single planning sequence where language and visual imagination play complementary roles. Language provides the abstract structure of a plan, including task decomposition, planning primitives, constraints, temporal order, and decision logic, while visual imagination grounds this structure through world state prediction and joint subgoal planning, associating each planning step with intermediate and final physical states. RxBrain adopts a unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that supports language, image, and video understanding and generation within one model. To train this capability, we build an automatic pipeline that converts embodied videos into joint text-visual planning supervision by decomposing videos into planning steps and aligning them with visual state transitions. We further introduce RxBrain-Bench to evaluate whether models can represent embodied plans through joint textual and visual components rather than separate understanding or generation. Experiments show that RxBrain maintains embodied understanding and generation abilities, and produces plans with coupled textual reasoning, world state prediction, and joint subgoal planning. We also extend RxBrain to continuous robot action generation, where it shows promising real-robot performance without large-scale action-data pretraining. These results provide an initial step toward foundation models for embodied cognition.

AI.tldr: RxBrain is an embodied cognition foundation model that unifies language and visual imagination for joint planning, using a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture to understand and generate text, images, and video within a single model, demonstrating strong performance on embodied reasoning and robot action generation without large-scale action pretraining.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language models focus on scene understanding and textual decisions, while generative world models only predict future visual states; neither captures the complementary roles of language (abstract planning structure) and visual imagination (physical state grounding) needed for embodied cognition.
AI.method: A unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers architecture supporting language, image, and video understanding/generation; an automatic pipeline converting embodied videos into joint text-visual planning supervision; and RxBrain-Bench for evaluating embodied plan representation.
AI.result: RxBrain maintains both embodied understanding and generation abilities, produces plans with coupled textual reasoning, world state prediction, and joint subgoal planning, and extends to continuous robot action generation with promising real-robot performance without large-scale action-data pretraining.
AI.conclusion: This work provides an initial step toward foundation models for embodied cognition by demonstrating that joint language-visual planning representation is feasible and effective.

title: SYNAPSE: A Multi-LLM Orchestrated AI Tutor for Secure Software Development Education with Neurodivergent-First Design
comment: Accepted at the 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME 2026), Tool Demonstration and Data Showcase Track. Source code archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20480483
summary: Developers who maintain real systems must continually recognise and remediate vulnerabilities in existing code, yet this skill is rarely trained directly: secure software development is commonly taught only after programming fluency is acquired, and accessibility support is treated as a secondary concern, disadvantaging learners with ADHD and related executive-function differences. This paper presents SYNAPSE, a publicly deployed adaptive tutoring platform for Java, Python for cybersecurity, and secure software development. SYNAPSE coordinates Claude, GPT-4o, and Gemini through the Model Context Protocol, routing interactions by pedagogical intent under a three-stage Socratic hint policy. It exposes eighteen always-visible accessibility features and anchors practice in ShopSecure, a deliberately vulnerable web application mapped to six OWASP Top 10 (2021) categories, on which learners practise the detect-understand-remediate loop characteristic of software maintenance. A feasibility pilot with nineteen participants across neurodivergent and neurotypical cohorts returned a System Usability Scale score of 76.4 and engagement of 4.2/5, with comparable cognitive-load levels across cohorts. SYNAPSE is available at https://synapse-course.com; a screencast is available at https://youtu.be/9R17KC47qQI.

AI.tldr: SYNAPSE is a publicly deployed adaptive tutoring platform for Java, Python for cybersecurity, and secure software development. It coordinates multiple LLMs (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini) via the Model Context Protocol, uses a three-stage Socratic hint policy, offers 18 accessibility features, and anchors practice in ShopSecure (a vulnerable web app mapped to OWASP Top 10). A pilot study (n=19) yielded SUS score 76.4 and engagement 4.2/5 with comparable cognitive load across neurodivergent and neurotypical cohorts.
AI.motivation: Developers maintaining real systems must continuously recognize and remediate vulnerabilities, yet this skill is rarely trained directly — secure coding is taught only after programming fluency, and accessibility support for learners with ADHD/executive-function differences is treated as secondary.
AI.method: SYNAPSE coordinates Claude, GPT-4o, and Gemini through the Model Context Protocol, routing interactions by pedagogical intent under a three-stage Socratic hint policy. It exposes 18 always-visible accessibility features and uses ShopSecure, a deliberately vulnerable web app covering 6 OWASP Top 10 (2021) categories, where learners practice the detect-understand-remediate loop.
AI.result: A feasibility pilot with 19 participants (neurodivergent and neurotypical) returned a System Usability Scale score of 76.4, engagement of 4.2/5, and comparable cognitive-load levels across cohorts.
AI.conclusion: SYNAPSE demonstrates feasibility as an adaptive tutoring platform for secure software development with strong usability, high engagement, and equitable cognitive load across neurodivergent and neurotypical learners.

title: LIGO-PINN: Learned Initialization via Gated Optimization to Alleviate Convergence Failures in Physics Informed Neural Networks
comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 13 tables. Code available at https://github.com/scailab/ligo-pinn
summary:
Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have had a broad research impact in modeling domains governed by partial differential equations (PDE). However, PINNs have been shown to perform poorly, sometimes even converging to trivial solutions, in challenging PDE domains, or when generalizing to unseen but related PDE domains. Previously proposed solutions detail hyperparameter tuning to reduce loss imbalance between data-driven and physics guided losses, curriculum learning based training strategies, or dynamic re-sampling of hard collocation points. These methods face certain pitfalls: hyperparameter tuning is expensive, designing a training curriculum is ambiguous in multi-parameter PDE settings, and dynamic resampling still fails in complex PDE settings. Complementary to this line of thinking, we believe the initial PINN network weights also play a crucial role in the emergence of catastrophic failures during training, yet the effect of PINN weight initialization has been surprisingly under-investigated. To this end, we propose a framework for Learned Initialization via Gated Layerwise Optimization (LIGO-PINN) to overcome PINN convergence failures. Through rigorous evaluation on 1D and 2D PDE domains, including a challenging 2D fluid dynamics setting, we demonstrate that our methodology outperforms state-of-the-art methods designed to alleviate PINN failures, achieving a 91.5% average performance improvement across six baselines and 81% over the strongest baseline. We also verify that LIGO-PINN generalizes to 3D unstructured domains. Finally, we analyze training dynamics across all three PDE domains to explain both LIGO-PINN's improvement and the convergence failure of traditional PINNs. Code: https://github.com/scailab/ligo-pinn
  Keywords: Machine Learning, Physics-Informed Neural Networks, Deep Learning, PDE Modeling

AI.tldr: LIGO-PINN proposes a learned weight initialization framework to overcome convergence failures in Physics-Informed Neural Networks, achieving 91.5% average improvement over six baselines and demonstrating generalization to 3D domains.
AI.motivation: PINNs often fail or converge to trivial solutions in challenging PDE domains, especially when generalizing to unseen related PDEs. Existing solutions (hyperparameter tuning, curriculum learning, dynamic resampling) face pitfalls like high cost and ambiguity. The effect of weight initialization on PINN failures has been surprisingly under-investigated.
AI.method: Proposes LIGO-PINN (Learned Initialization via Gated Layerwise Optimization), a framework that learns optimal initial network weights through a gated layerwise optimization strategy to prevent catastrophic convergence failures during PINN training.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods with 91.5% average performance improvement across six baselines and 81% over the strongest baseline. Generalizes to 3D unstructured domains. Demonstrated on 1D, 2D, and challenging 2D fluid dynamics PDE domains.
AI.conclusion: Weight initialization is a critical but overlooked factor in PINN convergence failures. LIGO-PINN effectively addresses this issue and generalizes well. Analysis of training dynamics explains both the improvement and traditional PINN failures.

title: G$^2$SR: Geometric Methods for Fast and Memory-Efficient Gaussian-based Surface Reconstruction
summary: Few-view surface reconstruction recovers the visible surfaces of a scene from a few posed RGB images, providing the 3D models that robots need to explore and interact online. On mobile platforms, the reconstruction must be fast and geometrically accurate while keeping a small memory footprint to ensure safe and efficient operation. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) offers a high-fidelity scene representation, but building it from a few views is ill-posed, as many distinct surfaces reproduce the same images, making traditional photometric methods prone to "floater" artifacts. End-to-end methods resolve the ambiguity by regressing splats with large, usually Transformer-based, networks that require heavy compute and memory while generalizing poorly to new scenes. We propose G2SR, which exploits a well-posed core of the task: given cross-view 2D splat correspondences, 3D splats follow analytically from multi-view geometry. G2SR employs a lightweight neural frontend to detect and track 2D Gaussian splats on the image plane and an analytic backend to triangulate each into a metric-scale 3D splat. On ScanNet, Replica, and DTU, G2SR matches or exceeds the geometric accuracy of state-of-the-art end-to-end methods while running at 69-89 reconstructions per second within 203 MB of GPU memory (5-107x less) for 2- and 3-view inputs at 384 x 512 resolution, offering a practical path to online Gaussian-based surface reconstruction.

AI.tldr: G2SR is a fast, lightweight few-view surface reconstruction method that uses a neural frontend to detect and track 2D Gaussian splats across views and an analytic backend to triangulate them into metric-scale 3D splats, achieving state-of-the-art geometric accuracy while running at 69-89 reconstructions per second with 5-107x less GPU memory than end-to-end methods.
AI.motivation: Existing few-view surface reconstruction methods using 3D Gaussian Splatting suffer from ill-posed optimization leading to "floater" artifacts, while end-to-end regression methods require heavy compute, large memory, and generalize poorly. The goal is to achieve fast, geometrically accurate, memory-efficient online reconstruction on mobile platforms.
AI.method: G2SR decomposes the task into a well-posed core: given cross-view 2D splat correspondences, 3D splats follow analytically from multi-view geometry. It uses a lightweight neural frontend to detect and track 2D Gaussian splats on the image plane, and an analytic backend to triangulate each into a metric-scale 3D splat.
AI.result: On ScanNet, Replica, and DTU, G2SR matches or exceeds state-of-the-art end-to-end methods in geometric accuracy while running at 69-89 reconstructions per second within 203 MB of GPU memory (5-107x less) for 2- and 3-view inputs at 384x512 resolution.
AI.conclusion: G2SR offers a practical path to online Gaussian-based surface reconstruction by combining geometric accuracy with high speed and low memory footprint, suitable for mobile robotic platforms.

title: How Artificial Intelligence LLM Engines Shape the Global Conflict Information Environment
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) answer engines now field a growing share of the questions that analysts, scholars, and the public ask about issues of peace and conflict. Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to hallucinate under certain conditions, but do these errors have discernible patterns when they are asked about conflicts, and if so what can that teach us about the changing global conflict information environment? To answer, we first asked a battery of questions about 28 conflicts to five leading answer engines and scored their 5,460 answers against documented evidence. We found that the thinner the retrievable record around a given conflict, the more the engines invent, misattribute, and miscount. Thin records don't just encourage hallucination, but create structural exposure to mis- and disinformation, because they are the easiest records to warp through Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) to bias engine responses. Through an analysis of 1,048 websites that the AI LLMs pulled conflict facts from, we found that GEO source optimization is already happening, and while state-partisan digital capture remains incipient it is rapidly growing. We explain what these findings mean for scholarship with the rise of GEO information warfare, and for policy argue for a return to the deep local monitoring and translation-based research that AI tools cannot replicate, closing with a discussion of future research opportunities and challenges in this fast-moving space.

AI.tldr: AI answer engines hallucinate more on conflicts with thinner documented records, creating vulnerability to Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and disinformation; analysis of 5,460 answers across 28 conflicts and 1,048 source websites reveals incipient but growing state-partisan digital capture of conflict information.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether hallucination patterns in LLM-based answer engines exhibit systematic biases when responding to questions about peace and conflict, and what these patterns reveal about vulnerabilities in the global conflict information environment.
AI.method: Tested five leading answer engines with questions about 28 conflicts, scoring 5,460 answers against documented evidence; analyzed 1,048 source websites for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and state-partisan digital capture.
AI.result: Thinner retrievable records around a conflict lead to more hallucination (invention, misattribution, miscounting); thin records create structural exposure to mis- and disinformation via GEO; GEO source optimization is already occurring, and state-partisan digital capture, though incipient, is growing rapidly.
AI.conclusion: Findings highlight risks of GEO information warfare for scholarship; policy should prioritize deep local monitoring and translation-based research that AI tools cannot replicate.

title: Rethinking Issue Resolution for AI/ML Systems
comment: In proceedings at the 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution, ICSME 2026
summary: We advocate for AI/ML issue resolution frameworks tailored to maintenance workflows and the nature of modern AI/ML systems. Existing issue resolution frameworks largely emerged for traditional software maintenance practices and do not explicitly account for characteristics common in AI/ML systems, such as stochastic behavior, experimentation-driven workflows, and heterogeneous artifacts beyond source code. To identify the unique characteristics of issue resolution in AI/ML systems and motivate the need for tailored frameworks, we conducted a qualitative study of issue resolution workflows documented in 100 issue reports and pull requests across four widely used AI/ML systems: TensorFlow, scikit-learn, MLflow, and AutoGPT. Our findings suggest that issue resolution in AI/ML systems involves: recurring AI/ML-related activities that span multiple resolution stages; iterative experimentation and adaptive verification; and coordinated changes across artifacts such as datasets, prompts, and model configurations. We also observed challenges related to reproducibility, nondeterministic behavior, and artifact coordination. Building on these findings, we present a vision for AI/ML issue resolution frameworks and discuss research directions and tooling support needed to realize this vision.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that existing issue resolution frameworks, designed for traditional software, are inadequate for AI/ML systems due to characteristics like stochastic behavior, experimentation-driven workflows, and heterogeneous artifacts. Through a qualitative study of 100 issue reports and PRs across TensorFlow, scikit-learn, MLflow, and AutoGPT, the authors identify unique AI/ML resolution patterns and propose a vision for specialized frameworks.
AI.motivation: Existing issue resolution frameworks were developed for traditional software maintenance and fail to account for AI/ML-specific characteristics such as stochastic behavior, experimentation-driven workflows, and heterogeneous artifacts beyond source code (e.g., datasets, prompts, model configurations).
AI.method: Qualitative study of issue resolution workflows documented in 100 issue reports and pull requests across four widely used AI/ML systems: TensorFlow, scikit-learn, MLflow, and AutoGPT.
AI.result: Issue resolution in AI/ML systems involves: (1) recurring AI/ML-related activities spanning multiple resolution stages; (2) iterative experimentation and adaptive verification; (3) coordinated changes across diverse artifacts (datasets, prompts, model configurations). Challenges include reproducibility issues, nondeterministic behavior, and artifact coordination difficulties.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a vision for AI/ML-specific issue resolution frameworks and discusses future research directions and tooling support needed to realize this vision.

title: MIDiff: Tackling Sparsity and Imbalance in Mobile Usage Generation via Multivariate-Imaging Diffusion
summary: Mobile usage traces are critical for tasks such as user behavior prediction and app recommendation, yet their use is constrained by privacy restrictions and costly large-scale data collection. Although generative models perform well on general time series, their application to mobile usage data remains challenging because (i) limited user activity causes severe sparsity, (ii) heterogeneous variable types complicate joint modeling, and (iii) functional differences across apps create pronounced usage imbalance. To address these challenges, we propose Multivariate-Imaging Diffusion (MIDiff), a diffusion-based framework operating in an imaging space defined by Cross-Gramian Angular Sum Field (C-GASF). C-GASF transforms sparse multivariate sequences into correlation images, while MIDiff employs Triple Attention in a U-Net to preserve temporal consistency and variable dependencies. Experiments show that MIDiff achieves state-of-the-art performance across fidelity metrics. In particular, it obtains a Discriminative Accuracy (DA) of 0.1526, compared with 0.3476 for the strongest baseline, ZITS-VAE, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating realistic and diverse mobile usage traces. Our code is available at https://github.com/YilaiLiu-HKU/MIDiff.

AI.tldr: MIDiff is a diffusion-based framework that converts sparse, heterogeneous mobile usage traces into correlation images via C-GASF and uses Triple Attention in a U-Net to generate realistic synthetic data, achieving SOTA fidelity (DA 0.1526 vs. baseline 0.3476).
AI.motivation: Mobile usage traces are essential for tasks like behavior prediction and app recommendation, but their use is limited by privacy restrictions and costly large-scale data collection. Existing generative models struggle with severe sparsity, heterogeneous variable types, and pronounced usage imbalance across apps.
AI.method: MIDiff operates in an imaging space defined by Cross-Gramian Angular Sum Field (C-GASF), which transforms sparse multivariate sequences into correlation images. It employs Triple Attention within a U-Net architecture to preserve temporal consistency and variable dependencies during the diffusion process.
AI.result: MIDiff achieves state-of-the-art performance across fidelity metrics, notably obtaining a Discriminative Accuracy (DA) of 0.1526 compared to 0.3476 for the strongest baseline ZITS-VAE.
AI.conclusion: MIDiff effectively addresses sparsity, heterogeneity, and imbalance in mobile usage data generation, producing realistic and diverse synthetic traces with superior fidelity.

title: Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction of Unordered Input with Global Consistency
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become the method of choice for reconstructing and real-time rendering of captured scenes. To capture a scene with good visual quality, continuous image sequences are usually combined with out-of-order shots for better scene coverage. Structure from motion can reconstruct such captures, but only after they are all available and often with high computational cost. Incremental reconstruction methods -- often derived from SLAM solutions -- provide immediate feedback, but cannot handle the out-of-order capture we require. We provide the first immediate feedback solution for such radiance field capture that provides global consistency. We first introduce a method for fast matching in out-of-order sequences, by repurposing visual place recognition models and a covisibility graph, and provide an efficient way to find highly connected keyframes, improving quality even for ordered sequences. We show how these steps -- together with GPU optimization and careful Gaussian primitive placement -- provide fast local reconstruction, in our challenging radiance field reconstruction case. We then introduce a novel cluster-based method, again using the covisibility graph, to provide efficient loop closure that does not require sequential input. Finally, to handle large scenes in our context, we introduce a progressive hierarchy that allows our method to scale to large environments, without compromising efficiency. Our results show we provide immediate feedback 3DGS reconstruction with good visual quality in several datasets, with up to thousands of input images.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first immediate feedback solution for 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction that handles out-of-order image sequences, using visual place recognition, covisibility graphs, GPU optimization, cluster-based loop closure, and progressive hierarchy to achieve global consistency and scalability.
AI.motivation: Existing 3DGS reconstruction methods either require all images upfront (SfM) with high cost, or provide immediate feedback but cannot handle out-of-order captures needed for good scene coverage. The goal is to enable immediate, globally consistent feedback for radiance field capture from both ordered and out-of-order sequences.
AI.method: 1) Fast matching in out-of-order sequences using visual place recognition models and covisibility graphs; 2) Efficient keyframe selection from highly connected frames; 3) GPU optimization and careful Gaussian primitive placement for fast local reconstruction; 4) Novel cluster-based loop closure using covisibility graphs without requiring sequential input; 5) Progressive hierarchy to scale to large environments.
AI.result: The method achieves immediate feedback 3DGS reconstruction with good visual quality across multiple datasets, handling up to thousands of input images in both ordered and out-of-order capture scenarios.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first solution for real-time, globally consistent radiance field reconstruction from out-of-order captures, combining incremental feedback with scalability to large scenes.

title: Align AI to Dynamic Human-AI Workflows
summary: Current alignment approaches typically focus on emulating human behavior using static representations of human preferences, failing to capture the dynamic, context-dependent nature of real-world human-AI interactions. In this paper, we argue for a shift from static and emulative to interactive and complementary alignment, where preferences emerge through interaction and alignment is defined not by satisfying preferences alone. We first formalize this gap by contrasting existing alignment with a trajectory-level view in which human and model behavior co-evolve over time. Because these interaction dynamics have not been adequately captured within existing ML formulations, we ground this perspective in insights from an interdisciplinary workshop. We draw on lessons from social-science accounts of human-human collaboration and then argue that human-AI systems amplify these dynamics, introducing new asymmetries that make reasoning about uncertainty harder and introduce new coordination challenges. Based on these lessons and new challenges, we conclude by outlining a research agenda for developing AI systems that align with humans in interaction, requiring an interdisciplinary synthesis of machine learning and the social and decision sciences.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current AI alignment approaches are too static and emulative, and proposes a shift toward interactive, complementary alignment where human and model preferences co-evolve through dynamic interaction, drawing on interdisciplinary insights to outline a new research agenda.
AI.motivation: Current alignment methods rely on static representations of human preferences, failing to capture the dynamic, context-dependent nature of real-world human-AI interactions.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the gap between existing static alignment and a trajectory-level view of co-evolving behavior, grounds this in insights from an interdisciplinary workshop, and draws on social-science accounts of human-human collaboration to analyze emerging asymmetries and coordination challenges in human-AI systems.
AI.result: Identification that human-AI interaction dynamics amplify uncertainties and introduce new coordination challenges not adequately captured in existing ML formulations.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a research agenda for developing AI systems that align with humans interactively, requiring interdisciplinary synthesis of machine learning, social sciences, and decision sciences.

title: LLM-Driven Approach to Modeling Tool Interoperability in Automotive Domain
summary: Interoperability between heterogeneous modeling tools remains a significant challenge in Model-Driven Engineering (MDE), particularly in the automotive domain where multiple modeling languages, as well as defacto standard proprietary and open-source tools coexist. This paper presents an LLM-driven approach for automated model interoperability by considering two relevant aspects: 1) mapping model instances to a target metamodel 2) merging of metamodels. The proposed methodology is demonstrated through transformations involving Ecore and SysML v2 based metamodels and incorporates structural validation of generated model instances against user-defined target models. Automotive case studies illustrate the feasibility of the approach and show that large language models can significantly reduce manual transformation effort while generating structurally valid target models for cross-tool interoperability.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an LLM-driven approach for automated model interoperability in automotive MDE, focusing on mapping model instances to target metamodels and merging metamodels. Demonstrated with Ecore and SysML v2, the approach reduces manual transformation effort while generating structurally valid models for cross-tool interoperability.
AI.motivation: Interoperability between heterogeneous modeling tools in automotive MDE remains challenging due to multiple modeling languages and coexisting proprietary/open-source tools.
AI.method: LLM-driven approach addressing two aspects: 1) mapping model instances to a target metamodel, and 2) merging of metamodels, with structural validation against user-defined target models.
AI.result: Demonstrated through Ecore and SysML v2 based metamodel transformations; automotive case studies show LLMs can significantly reduce manual transformation effort while generating structurally valid target models.
AI.conclusion: Large language models can effectively automate model interoperability tasks in the automotive domain, reducing manual effort and ensuring structural validity of generated models for cross-tool scenarios.

title: Local Additive Feature Attribution: A Mathematical Taxonomy and Reporting Checklist
comment: 35 pages, 7 figures, and 19 tables. Ancillary files include the axiom matrix, reporting checklist, related-survey scoring, and review-corpus summary
summary: Feature-attribution methods are central to explainable artificial intelligence. Their assumptions are expressed in several mathematical languages: cooperative-game values, path integrals, gradient operators, perturbation distributions, and backpropagation rules. This survey proposes a common framework for local additive feature attribution.
