AI.method: CIPHER uses a Decoupled Exploration-Selection (DES) framework that explicitly separates the generation of candidate initial states from their strategic selection for parallel execution, enabling test-time scaling through multiple concurrent executions.
AI.result: CIPHER exceeds state-of-the-art performance in matched-model comparisons on closed-form and open-form benchmarks, and remains competitive against larger-model baselines despite using a substantially smaller base language model. The study quantifies contributions of generation strategy, selection strategy, and aggregator model capacity.
AI.conclusion: The Decoupled Exploration-Selection framework is effective for test-time scaling in AI agents for data science, and the paper provides actionable design recommendations for practitioners based on empirical characterization of the design space.

title: Navigating the Socio-Technical Complexity Challenge in Quantum Software Ecosystems
summary: Quantum computing environments are composed of heterogeneous layers spanning hardware, software development kits, and applications. Practitioners curating these environments face a fragmented and rapidly evolving landscape with few principled guides for navigation. This paper presents a framework for evaluating quantum computing environment choices through a socio-technical lens, developed using Design Science Research methodology. Drawing on the quantum software engineering literature as well as organizational and socio-technical research, the framework introduces three analytical constructs: gravity wells and their properties, which characterize how certain technologies and structural conditions exert increasing pull on surrounding environment choices, and socio-technical desiderata, which articulate the normative goals against which those pulls can be evaluated. The framework supports practitioners in making deliberate, context-aware environment choices that preserve architectural flexibility and support the evolutionary development of the field. Demonstration and evaluation of the framework is conducted through exemplary cases. The contribution advances both the theory of quantum ecosystems and the practical guidance available to organizations and practitioners navigating the current, evolving field of quantum computing.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a socio-technical framework using Design Science Research to help practitioners evaluate quantum computing environment choices, introducing concepts of gravity wells and socio-technical desiderata to navigate the fragmented quantum computing landscape.
AI.motivation: Quantum computing environments are highly fragmented and rapidly evolving, with heterogeneous layers spanning hardware, SDKs, and applications, yet practitioners lack principled guides for making deliberate, context-aware environment choices.
AI.method: The framework is developed using Design Science Research methodology, drawing on quantum software engineering literature combined with organizational and socio-technical research.
AI.result: Introduction of three analytical constructs: gravity wells and their properties (characterizing how technologies and structural conditions exert increasing pull on environment choices), and socio-technical desiderata (normative goals for evaluating those pulls). Framework demonstrated and evaluated through exemplary cases.
AI.conclusion: The framework advances both theory of quantum ecosystems and practical guidance for organizations navigating the evolving quantum computing field, enabling deliberate, context-aware choices that preserve architectural flexibility.

title: Dysco: Dynamic Subspace Boosting to Mitigate LoRA Interference in Federated Learning
summary: Federated fine-tuning of large pre-trained models increasingly relies on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to reduce communication and computation, but heterogeneous clients can make adapter aggregation unstable. We identify the data-parameter interference as a geometric source of this instability. This interference is controlled by the alignment between LoRA update subspaces and client activations, suggesting that federated LoRA aggregation should be viewed not only as parameter averaging but also as subspace allocation. We propose Dynamic Subspace Boosting (Dysco), a plug-in method that allocates client-specific LoRA subspaces in a federated and dynamic manner. In each round, clients compute activation-insensitive subspaces from local representations and transmit only the resulting bases; the server then constructs client-specific merged subspaces through a closed-form solution that maximizes compatibility with other clients' insensitive directions. To handle representation drift, Dysco performs multi-round subspace boosting to preserve past update directions while adapting to future representations. We provide a convergence analysis that embeds the data-parameter interference as an aggregation-error term in a standard federated optimization bound, and prove that Dysco's server-fixed merged subspaces yield a tighter upper bound on this error. Experiments on controlled synthetic federated tasks and on MIMIC-IV clinical-note classification with Llama-3.2-1B show that Dysco substantially reduces interference, reduces the final-round synthetic training loss by up to 9 times relative to baselines under the orthogonal-subspace partition the theory identifies, improves all five tested FL algorithms by up to 4.3% on MIMIC, outperforms recent federated LoRA methods, and adds only 0.9% wall-clock overhead. Our code is available at https://github.com/illidanlab/Dysco.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies data-parameter interference as a geometric cause of instability in federated LoRA fine-tuning, and proposes Dynamic Subspace Boosting (Dysco), a plug-in method that allocates client-specific LoRA subspaces dynamically. Dysco reduces interference, achieves up to 9× loss reduction in synthetic tasks, improves five FL algorithms by up to 4.3% on MIMIC-IV clinical classification with Llama-3.2-1B, adds only 0.9% overhead, and provides convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: Federated fine-tuning of large pre-trained models with LoRA suffers from instability under heterogeneous clients; the root cause—data-parameter interference—is identified geometrically, motivating a need to treat federated LoRA aggregation as subspace allocation rather than just parameter averaging.
AI.method: Dysco: client computes activation-insensitive subspaces from local representations and transmits only the bases; server constructs client-specific merged subspaces via a closed-form solution that maximizes compatibility; multi-round subspace boosting handles representation drift.
AI.result: Up to 9× synthetic training loss reduction under orthogonal-subspace partition; 4.3% improvement across five FL algorithms on MIMIC-IV clinical-note classification with Llama-3.2-1B; outperforms recent federated LoRA methods with only 0.9% wall-clock overhead.
AI.conclusion: Dysco effectively reduces data-parameter interference in federated LoRA, yields tighter convergence bounds, and serves as a lightweight plug-in for existing FL algorithms.

title: AdaTurn: Budget-Aware Test-Time Scaling for Active Visual Perception Agents
summary: Active visual agents solve fine-grained image tasks by interleaving reasoning with image-grounding actions across multiple turns. However, deployment-time rollout budgets are rarely fixed: some requests permit long rollouts, while others require the agent to act under a tight turn limit. Existing methods train the policy as if the rollout budget were hidden, so when the available budget is smaller than the trajectory the agent prefers, the interaction is often truncated before any valid answer is produced; we term this failure \emph{catastrophic truncation}. To overcome this challenge, we present AdaTurn, a budget-aware framework that conditions the agent on the allowed number of turns and explicitly trains the boundary behavior induced by the budget. Our key component, Forced-Answer DAPO (FA-DAPO), converts the over-budget event from a masked or penalized failure into a trainable final-decision step, teaching the model to synthesize partial evidence when further tool use is no longer possible. We further randomize rollout budgets during both training and inference and introduce a load-balanced scheduler that makes such operations practical. AdaTurn substantially improves low-budget accuracy, for example raising VisualProbe-Medium from 36.7% to 47.6% at four turns, while preserving strong scaling at larger budgets and transferring effectively to multiple backbones and general multimodal benchmarks.

AI.tldr: AdaTurn is a budget-aware framework that prevents catastrophic truncation in active visual agents by conditioning on available turn budgets and training boundary behavior via Forced-Answer DAPO (FA-DAPO), improving low-budget accuracy (e.g., VisualProbe-Medium from 36.7% to 47.6% at 4 turns) while preserving strong performance at larger budgets.
AI.motivation: Existing methods treat rollout budget as hidden, causing catastrophic truncation (agent fails to produce a valid answer) when the available budget is smaller than the agent's preferred trajectory length.
AI.method: AdaTurn introduces (1) Forced-Answer DAPO (FA-DAPO), which converts over-budget events from masked failures into trainable final-decision steps for synthesizing partial evidence; (2) randomized rollout budgets during training and inference; (3) a load-balanced scheduler for practical operation.
AI.result: Substantial improvements on low-budget accuracy: VisualProbe-Medium from 36.7% to 47.6% at 4 turns, while preserving strong scaling at larger budgets and transferring effectively across multiple backbones and multimodal benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: AdaTurn effectively addresses catastrophic truncation by explicitly conditioning on budget constraints and training budget-aware boundary behavior, enabling agents to handle varying rollout budgets robustly.

title: Chat2Scenic: An Iterative RAG-Based Framework for Scenario Generation in Autonomous Driving
comment: Accepted at 2026 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
summary: Validating autonomous driving systems requires diverse, regulation-compliant test scenarios. In simulation-based testing, scenarios are defined as executable scripts. Yet automatically generating such scripts from regulatory descriptions remains an open challenge, and existing approaches face fundamental trade-offs. Retrieval-assemble methods achieve reasonable compilation rates but lack scalability, whereas retrieval-based full-script generation suffers from low compilation success rates. We present Chat2Scenic, the first iterative retrieval-augmented framework to generate scenario scripts in Domain Specific Language (DSL). Specifically, Chat2Scenic provides a chatbot interface that supports interactive scenario refinement and integrates Retrieval-augmented Generation (RAG) to ground scenario generation in regulatory knowledge and DSL syntax. Furthermore, we propose an open benchmark for scenario generation comprising 123 scenarios from various regulations, including NHTSA and United Nations Vehicle Regulations, as well as other sources. Extensive evaluation with State-of-the-Art (SOTA) Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrates that Chat2Scenic achieves 76.42% Compilation Success Rate (CSR) and 58.17% Framework Accuracy (FA), outperforming existing methods (Retrieval Assemble with 30.08% CSR, 11.03% FA and Retrieval full script generation with 16.26% CSR, 10.86% FA). To facilitate future research, we release our code as open source at https://github.com/TUM-AVS/chat2scenic.

AI.tldr: Chat2Scenic is an iterative retrieval-augmented framework that generates executable DSL scenario scripts from regulatory descriptions for autonomous driving simulation, achieving 76.42% CSR and 58.17% FA, significantly outperforming existing methods (30.08% CSR/11.03% FA for Retrieval Assemble and 16.26% CSR/10.86% FA for full-script generation).
AI.motivation: Automatically generating executable scenario scripts from regulatory descriptions for validating autonomous driving systems remains an open challenge, with existing approaches facing fundamental trade-offs between compilation rates and scalability.
AI.method: Chat2Scenic integrates a chatbot interface for interactive scenario refinement with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to ground scenario generation in regulatory knowledge and DSL syntax. It also introduces an open benchmark of 123 scenarios from NHTSA, UN Vehicle Regulations, and other sources.
AI.result: Chat2Scenic achieves 76.42% Compilation Success Rate (CSR) and 58.17% Framework Accuracy (FA), outperforming Retrieval Assemble (30.08% CSR, 11.03% FA) and Retrieval full-script generation (16.26% CSR, 10.86% FA) using SOTA LLMs.
AI.conclusion: The iterative retrieval-augmented approach effectively bridges the gap between regulatory descriptions and executable DSL scripts, and the open-source release aims to facilitate future research in automated scenario generation.

title: MM-IssueLoc: A Controlled Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Evidence in Multimodal Repository-Level Issue Localization
summary: Real repository issues routinely include visual evidence such as screenshots, error dialogs, rendered UI states, and logs, yet repository-level issue localization is evaluated mostly as a text-only task. Existing multimodal SE benchmarks evaluate end-to-end repair, entangling localization with patch synthesis and obscuring whether visual input helped, hurt, or was ignored. We introduce \textbf{MM-IssueLoc}, a controlled benchmark and evaluation protocol for repository-level localization with visual evidence. MM-IssueLoc contains 652 issue-PR instances across 23 languages, with annotations for 7 image categories and 4 relevance levels. It provides file-level and function-level gold labels, paired text-only and with-image evaluation, and VCE-based diagnostics that convert images into structured textual evidence. We evaluate LLM-based and retrieval-based systems, including MM-IssueLoc-VL-Emb as a controlled multimodal retriever. Results show that existing systems remain far from reliable multimodal repository localization: the strongest agent reaches 38.96 file Acc@5 and 22.45 function Acc@10, while the strongest retriever reaches 33.86 function Acc@10. Cross-benchmark comparisons show that high localization scores on text-dominant SWE benchmarks do not transfer cleanly to multimodal issue localization. MM-IssueLoc turns visual evidence into an explicit evaluation variable, enabling future work to test whether systems improve by using visual evidence for localization, rather than by relying on text-only cues or downstream patch-generation effects.

AI.tldr: MM-IssueLoc is a controlled benchmark for repository-level issue localization using visual evidence (screenshots, error dialogs, UI states, logs), containing 652 issue-PR instances across 23 languages with 7 image categories and 4 relevance levels. Current systems perform poorly (best agent: 38.96 file Acc@5, best retriever: 33.86 function Acc@10), and high scores on text-only benchmarks don't transfer to multimodal settings.
AI.motivation: Existing repository-level issue localization is evaluated as a text-only task, while real issues contain visual evidence. Multimodal SE benchmarks entangle localization with patch synthesis, obscuring whether visual input helps, hurts, or is ignored.
AI.method: Created MM-IssueLoc with 652 issue-PR instances across 23 languages, annotated with 7 image categories and 4 relevance levels. Provides file-level and function-level gold labels, paired text-only and with-image evaluation, and VCE-based diagnostics. Evaluated LLM-based and retrieval-based systems including MM-IssueLoc-VL-Emb as a controlled multimodal retriever.
AI.result: Best agent achieves 38.96 file Acc@5 and 22.45 function Acc@10. Best retriever achieves 33.86 function Acc@10. High scores on text-dominant SWE benchmarks do not transfer to multimodal issue localization.
AI.conclusion: Existing systems remain far from reliable multimodal repository localization. MM-IssueLoc turns visual evidence into an explicit evaluation variable, enabling future work to test whether systems improve by using visual evidence rather than relying on text-only cues or patch-generation effects.

title: Supervised Fine-Tuning vs. In-Context Learning: An Equilibrium Analysis of LLM Personalization under Congestion
summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized AI services, but a critical tension emerges: while personalization improves model performance, it consumes scarce computational resources that users must share. When should a user invest in expensive Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) versus lightweight In-Context Learning (ICL)? How does congestion from other users' personalization choices reshape these incentives? And what strategies should platforms adopt when offering multiple personalization algorithms?
  We develop a tractable framework for LLM serving that captures the statistical-economic trade-offs users face. Our analysis yields several surprising insights. First, we show that ICL and SFT dominate in different regimes, determined by an interplay between pretraining coverage and data signal-to-noise ratios, but congestion can flip these rankings. Second, equilibrium resource consumption exhibits pronounced non-monotonicity: improving pretraining precision reduces the congestion, while broader pretraining coverage and harder tasks sometimes increase it. Third, we prove that offering both personalization methods never hurts the platform's maximal profits, despite potentially increasing computational load.
  Experiments with GPT-2 on linear regression tasks validate our theoretical predictions about algorithm performance. Complementing these results, our review of documentation from 21 major AI platforms shows that the share offering both SFT and ICL increased from 9.5% in 2021 to 71.4% in 2025, consistent with our platform-design implications.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a framework analyzing the tension between personalization (SFT vs ICL) and computational congestion in LLM serving, revealing non-monotonic equilibrium effects and showing that offering both methods never hurts platform profits.
AI.motivation: To understand when users should choose expensive Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) versus lightweight In-Context Learning (ICL) for personalization, and how congestion from other users' choices affects these incentives, given that personalization improves performance but consumes scarce shared computational resources.
AI.method: A tractable statistical-economic framework modeling LLM serving with trade-offs between personalization methods, equilibrium analysis of resource consumption, validation via GPT-2 experiments on linear regression, and a review of 21 major AI platforms (2021-2025).
AI.result: ICL and SFT dominate in different regimes based on pretraining coverage and signal-to-noise ratios, but congestion can flip these rankings. Equilibrium resource consumption is non-monotonic: better pretraining precision reduces congestion, but broader coverage and harder tasks sometimes increase it. Offering both methods never reduces platform profits despite higher computational load. Platforms offering both SFT and ICL grew from 9.5% (2021) to 71.4% (2025).
AI.conclusion: Platforms should offer both SFT and ICL to maximize profits, as dual-offering never hurts profitability despite congestion costs. The choice between personalization methods is regime-dependent and congestion can fundamentally alter the optimal decision.

title: HyMobileAgent: Data-Environment Co-Scaling for Efficient GUI Agents
summary:
As large multimodal models move from understanding content to operating on digital environments, mobile GUI has emerged as a challenging and consequential testbed for digital embodied intelligence. Mobile agents operate under three coupled constraints: precise perception of complex interfaces, scalable acquisition of high-quality interaction data, and robust long-horizon decision making under compounding execution errors. This report presents HyMobileAgent, a mobile GUI agent built on Hy3.0-VL-A3B, a vision-native foundation model featuring native any-resolution input, an A3B-scale deployment budget, and a 32K context window to model extended interaction histories. Rather than relying solely on model scaling, we develop a joint data and environment centric scaling framework to address the key bottlenecks of mobile interaction.
  Our framework integrates a GUI perception flywheel combining mock-interface synthesis, rejection sampling, and icon-specific augmentation; a knowledge pipeline that transforms tutorial videos into structured interaction data; a million-scale action data pipeline deployed across more than 2000 sandbox and real-device instances with automated failure attribution; the PhoneWorld Mock App Factory, providing a resettable training environment with 34 mock applications and over 34000 tasks; and a structured Planning-and-Reflection mechanism with explicit dead-loop detection for reliable long-horizon execution.
  We also introduce a progressive training recipe consisting of mid-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning with task-specific reward designs.

AI.tldr: HyMobileAgent is a mobile GUI agent built on the Hy3.0-VL-A3B vision-native model, employing a joint data-and-environment-centric scaling framework with perception flywheel, video-to-data pipeline, million-scale action data collection, mock app factory (34 apps, 34K tasks), and Planning-and-Reflection mechanism, trained via progressive recipe (mid-training, SFT, RL).
AI.motivation: Mobile GUI agents face three coupled constraints: precise perception of complex interfaces, scalable acquisition of high-quality interaction data, and robust long-horizon decision making under compounding execution errors. The authors aim to address these bottlenecks through data and environment centric scaling rather than relying solely on model scaling.
AI.method: HyMobileAgent integrates: (1) a GUI perception flywheel with mock-interface synthesis, rejection sampling, and icon-specific augmentation; (2) a knowledge pipeline converting tutorial videos to structured interaction data; (3) a million-scale action data pipeline across 2000+ sandbox/real-device instances with automated failure attribution; (4) PhoneWorld Mock App Factory (34 mock apps, 34K+ tasks); (5) structured Planning-and-Reflection with dead-loop detection; and (6) a progressive training recipe (mid-training, SFT, RL with task-specific rewards).
AI.result: The paper presents the system design of HyMobileAgent, demonstrating that a joint data-and-environment-centric scaling framework enables effective mobile GUI operation at a compact A3B-scale deployment budget with a 32K context window, without relying purely on model scaling.
AI.conclusion: HyMobileAgent shows that addressing data and environment bottlenecks through systematic scaling—including synthetic data generation, mock environments, and structured reasoning—can produce capable mobile GUI agents even with a small (A3B) vision-native foundation model.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Models for Long and Short-Term Forecasting of the Egyptian Stock Market: A Focus on EGX30
summary: This study concentrates on predicting stock prices in the Egyptian market, focusing on the EGX30, an influential financial hub in the Middle East. While most research focuses on global stocks, there's a growing need to understand stock trends in developing countries like Egypt. The study compares different machine learning models for forecasting EGX30 trends, covering short and long-term predictions. Using historical EGX30 data, including metrics like root mean squared error, Mean Absolute Percentage Error, and coefficient of determination, models like K-Nearest Neighbours, random forest, extreme gradient boosting, long short-term memory networks, and gated recurrent unit networks were evaluated. The goal is to determine the most effective models for EGX30 prediction, considering Egypt's unique market dynamics. Insights from this study aid investors in making informed decisions. Results show that the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) outperformed the other models in the one-week, one-month, and two-months while the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model outperformed others in the one-day predictions, highlighting their usefulness in predictive analysis for financial markets. The study also showed the importance of using the ensemble techniques, especially in the long-term predictions which proved better results reaching 5 times the GRU in the two-month predictions. Additionally, the study notes the surprisingly good performance of K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN) on long-term predictions, suggesting its enduring relevance and potential for future applications in the fintech domains.

AI.tldr: This study compares ML models (KNN, RF, XGBoost, LSTM, GRU) for predicting EGX30 stock trends in Egypt. GRU excels in medium-term (1-week to 2-month) predictions, XGBoost in short-term (1-day), and ensemble methods significantly improve long-term performance (up to 5x GRU). KNN shows surprising effectiveness for long-term forecasting.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of research on stock trend prediction in developing markets like Egypt, and to identify effective ML models tailored to the EGX30's unique market dynamics for better investor decision-making.
AI.method: Compared KNN, Random Forest, XGBoost, LSTM, and GRU on historical EGX30 data across multiple time horizons (1-day, 1-week, 1-month, 2-month), evaluating with RMSE, MAPE, and R² metrics.
AI.result: GRU outperformed all models for 1-week, 1-month, and 2-month predictions; XGBoost excelled for 1-day predictions; ensemble methods achieved up to 5x improvement over GRU in 2-month predictions; KNN demonstrated unexpectedly strong long-term performance.
AI.conclusion: No single model is universally optimal—GRU and XGBoost are best for different time scales; ensemble techniques are critical for long-term forecasting; KNN remains relevant for fintech applications.

title: A Noise-Robust Elicit-to-Optimize Framework for Distortion Riskmetrics via Inverse Reinforcement Learning
summary: We propose a noise-robust elicit-to-optimize framework that integrates inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and reinforcement learning (RL) for eliciting agents' risk preferences and optimizing policies under a broad class of risk objectives characterized by distortion riskmetrics. On the elicitation side, we propose an adaptive Bayesian IRL method that infers agents' latent risk objectives from their noisy observed decisions, explicitly allowing agents to take stochastic and suboptimal actions. We establish the existence of a finite set of distinguishing questions that identifies the preferred distortion riskmetric within the candidate class and prove that the convergence rate of the algorithm is of order $O(\exp(-cm+O(\sqrt{m\log m})))$ under general settings, where $c>0$ is a constant and $m$ denotes the number of algorithm iterations. On the optimization side, we develop a model-free RL algorithm for optimizing policies under conditional distortion riskmetrics. By representing the objective as an integral of the conditional cost quantile function with respect to the distortion function, the method unifies distortion-riskmetric objectives. We optimize diverse risk objectives by extending the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm with policy, value, and quantile neural networks, where the quantile network estimates the full conditional cost quantile function and enables numerical evaluation of general risk objectives. A comprehensive empirical study demonstrates the framework's elicitation accuracy and effectiveness in complex financial environments.

AI.tldr: A noise-robust framework combining inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and reinforcement learning (RL) to elicit agents' risk preferences and optimize policies under distortion riskmetrics, with theoretical convergence guarantees and empirical validation in finance.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of inferring agents' latent risk preferences from noisy/suboptimal decisions and optimizing policies under a broad class of risk objectives, particularly in complex financial environments where decision-making under uncertainty is critical.
AI.method: Proposes a dual-component framework: (1) an adaptive Bayesian IRL method for eliciting risk preferences from noisy observations, with theoretical proof of convergence rate O(exp(-cm+O(√(m log m)))); (2) a model-free RL algorithm extending PPO with policy, value, and quantile neural networks to optimize policies under conditional distortion riskmetrics by representing objectives as integrals of conditional cost quantile functions.
AI.result: Establishes existence of a finite set of distinguishing questions for identifying preferred distortion riskmetrics. Proves O(exp(-cm+O(√(m log m)))) convergence rate for the elicitation algorithm. Empirical results demonstrate high elicitation accuracy and effectiveness in complex financial environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully integrates IRL and RL for risk-aware decision-making, offering both theoretical guarantees and practical effectiveness for eliciting and optimizing risk preferences in complex domains like finance.

title: Breaking the Model Forgetting Cycle in Long-Incremental 3D Object Detection
summary: Incremental 3D object detection requires a detector to learn novel object classes while remembering previously learned ones over sequentially arriving data. Previous methods, primarily based on pseudo-labeling, perform reasonably in short-incremental stages but still suffer from severe model forgetting when dealing with long-incremental sequences. We investigate this failure and reveal a detrimental self-reinforcing cycle: data distribution shift of novel classes causes model forgetting on old classes, which further produces accumulated error in pseudo-labeling that exacerbates model degradation. To address this issue, we draw inspiration from the human learning process and propose the \emph{Learning-Dynamics-driven Memory and Review} (LDMR) framework. LDMR monitors per-class detection quality at periodic training checkpoints and uses these learning-dynamics signals to drive two innovative mechanisms, namely (i) human-like intra-stage review that divides each incremental stage into multiple sub-stages' training and concentrates on remembering the most-forgotten objects, and (ii) scene-aware cross-stage memory evolution that evolves a memory bank to transfer knowledge between two consecutive stages by jointly considering scene learnability and diversity. Extensive experiments across multiple long-incremental protocols on indoor benchmarks SUN RGB-D and ScanNetV2 show that LDMR substantially mitigates the model forgetting and outperforms all baselines by a clear margin. Code is available at https://github.com/qianpeisheng/LDMR.

AI.tldr: LDMR is a novel framework for incremental 3D object detection that addresses model forgetting in long-incremental sequences by monitoring per-class detection quality through learning dynamics, implementing intra-stage review for remembering forgotten objects and cross-stage memory evolution for knowledge transfer, significantly outperforming baselines on SUN RGB-D and ScanNetV2 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing pseudo-labeling-based incremental 3D object detection methods suffer from severe model forgetting in long-incremental sequences due to a self-reinforcing cycle where data distribution shift of novel classes causes forgetting on old classes, which accumulates errors in pseudo-labeling and further degrades the model.
AI.method: LDMR monitors per-class detection quality at periodic training checkpoints using learning-dynamics signals to drive: (i) intra-stage review that divides each incremental stage into sub-stages focused on remembering the most-forgotten objects, and (ii) cross-stage memory evolution that evolves a memory bank for knowledge transfer between consecutive stages by balancing scene learnability and diversity.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on long-incremental protocols using indoor benchmarks SUN RGB-D and ScanNetV2 show LDMR substantially mitigates model forgetting and outperforms all baselines by a clear margin.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LDMR framework effectively breaks the detrimental self-reinforcing cycle in incremental 3D object detection, offering a human-learning-inspired solution that significantly reduces forgetting in long-incremental scenarios.

title: CatalogAgent: A Supervisor-mediated Self-Learning System Enabling Context Engineering for GenAI Models
summary: Product catalogs are the backbone of e-commerce sites, yet a large number of structured attributes (SAs) -- such as material, color, and shape -- often have missing values. Typically, SA values are extracted from product information, including titles and descriptions. While LLM-based generator-evaluator frameworks have demonstrated effectiveness for SA prediction -- where an LLM generates SA values and another evaluates them -- they face challenges when the Generator and Evaluator produce conflicting outputs, as either component can make mistakes. We introduce \texttt{CatalogAgent}, a novel agentic system that continuously improves Generator and Evaluator models for e-commerce catalog enrichment. When disagreements arise from (1) internal conflicts between the LLM-based Generator and Evaluator, or (2) external feedback from sellers on LLM outputs, a Supervisor Agent intervenes to mediate these conflicts and make final decisions. The system also incorporates a Memory Base and a Memory Summarizer that stores Supervisor Agent activities from individual cases and aggregates patterns into learnings. These learnings are fed back to the worker Generator and Evaluator LLMs, enabling self-improvement without human intervention. Through context engineering -- injecting learnings and insights into worker LLMs' contexts -- the system successfully transfers the Supervisor's capabilities to the Generator and Evaluator, improving their performance by 15.24\% and 13.98\%, respectively. Our experiments demonstrate a new paradigm of Supervisor Agent-mediated self-learning systems for improving generative AI model accuracy.

AI.tldr: CatalogAgent is a self-improving agentic system for e-commerce catalog enrichment that uses a Supervisor Agent to mediate conflicts between Generator and Evaluator LLMs, with a memory system that stores and summarizes patterns to continuously improve model performance by 13-15% without human intervention.
AI.motivation: Product catalogs in e-commerce sites suffer from missing structured attribute values (e.g., material, color, shape). Existing LLM-based generator-evaluator frameworks face challenges when the Generator and Evaluator produce conflicting outputs, as either component can make mistakes.
AI.method: CatalogAgent employs a Supervisor Agent to mediate conflicts arising from (1) internal disagreements between the LLM-based Generator and Evaluator, or (2) external feedback from sellers. A Memory Base and Memory Summarizer store and aggregate Supervisor Agent activities into learnings, which are injected into worker LLMs' contexts via context engineering, enabling self-improvement without human intervention.
AI.result: The system improved Generator performance by 15.24% and Evaluator performance by 13.98% through context engineering.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates a new paradigm of Supervisor Agent-mediated self-learning systems for improving generative AI model accuracy in e-commerce catalog enrichment.

title: Alipay-PIBench: A Realistic Payment Integration Benchmark for Coding Agents
summary: Payment integration is a demanding repository-level software task: agents must select a suitable product, implement coordinated client-server flows, verify payment outcomes, and preserve consistency between transaction and business states. We introduce Alipay-PIBench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on realistic Alipay payment integration. It contains nine product-specific projects and 18 task instances, each organized into Basic functional-completion and Advanced risk-aware hardening scenarios. Scenario-specific rubrics support deterministic static, unit, integration, and end-to-end checks, supplemented by LLM-assisted assessment for semantic requirements. We evaluate six coding-agent models and report rubric pass rate (RPR). Under the with-skill condition, mean RPR ranges from 68.58% to 91.37%. Access to the alipay-payment-integration skill improves mean RPR by 10.31 percentage points on average relative to the without-skill condition, with gains varying across models, products, and scenarios. Method-level results distinguish source-level completion, executable payment behavior, and payment-domain requirements. Alipay-PIBench provides a controlled setting for diagnosing model capability and evaluating structured guidance in payment integration.

AI.tldr: Alipay-PIBench is a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on realistic Alipay payment integration, featuring nine product-specific projects and 18 task instances across Basic and Advanced scenarios. With access to payment integration skills, mean rubric pass rate (RPR) ranges from 68.58% to 91.37%, improving by 10.31 percentage points on average.
AI.motivation: Payment integration is a demanding repository-level task requiring product selection, coordinated client-server flows, payment verification, and state consistency. There is a need for a controlled benchmark to evaluate coding agents on realistic, complex payment integration scenarios.
AI.method: The benchmark includes nine product-specific projects and 18 task instances split into Basic functional-completion and Advanced risk-aware hardening scenarios. Rubrics combine deterministic static, unit, integration, and end-to-end checks with LLM-assisted assessment for semantic requirements. Six coding-agent models are evaluated with and without an alipay-payment-integration skill.
AI.result: Under the with-skill condition, mean RPR ranges from 68.58% to 91.37%. Using the skill improves mean RPR by 10.31 percentage points on average, with gains varying across models, products, and scenarios. Method-level results distinguish source-level completion, executable payment behavior, and payment-domain requirements.
AI.conclusion: Alipay-PIBench provides a controlled setting for diagnosing model capability and evaluating structured guidance in payment integration, highlighting the measurable benefit of domain-specific skills.

title: Integration Matters: Rollout-Based Training for Constrained Diffusion Models
summary: Constrained generative models aim to produce samples that satisfy complex feasibility constraints while remaining faithful to the data distribution. Existing constrained generation methods typically enforce constraints either through training-time optimization or sampling-time correction. Training-time optimization approaches optimize on states induced by the training distribution, which can differ substantially from those encountered during sampling. Sampling-time correction methods instead modify the sampling process at inference, introducing distribution shift and requiring expensive tuning, particularly for few-step sampling. We propose a fine-tuning framework that incorporates constraint guidance obtained through online rollout into the training process, which aligns training with sampling by differentiating through the fixed noise schedule used to numerically integrate the denoising process. This exposes the model to violations that arise along the denoising trajectory and aligns diffusion learning with the sampling process. Experiments across multiple tasks show that our method improves constraint satisfaction while maintaining competitive sampling quality compared to prior methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fine-tuning framework for constrained generative models that integrates constraint guidance via online rollouts into training, aligning training and sampling processes by differentiating through the fixed noise schedule, improving constraint satisfaction while maintaining sampling quality.
AI.motivation: Existing constrained generation methods suffer from distribution mismatch between training and sampling (training-time optimization) or distribution shift requiring expensive tuning (sampling-time correction), especially problematic for few-step sampling.
AI.method: A fine-tuning framework that incorporates constraint guidance obtained through online rollout into training, differentiating through the fixed noise schedule used for numerical integration of the denoising process, thereby exposing the model to violations along the denoising trajectory.
AI.result: The method improves constraint satisfaction while maintaining competitive sampling quality compared to prior methods across multiple tasks.
AI.conclusion: Aligning diffusion learning with the sampling process via online rollout-based constraint guidance during fine-tuning effectively resolves the training-sampling mismatch in constrained generative modeling.

title: Advanced Image Generation: Negative Prompt Optimization and Latent Classifier Guidance
summary: We present a novel system that integrates negative prompt optimization via a fine-tuned sequence-to-sequence LLM and latent-space classifier guidance to improve the quality of images generated by Stable Diffusion. Our approach automatically generates optimized negative prompts, and employs a CNN-RNN hybrid classifier to evaluate and guide diffusion steps, rolling back low-quality latent updates. Experimental results demonstrate that our dual-guidance framework reduces artifacts and improves semantic fidelity compared to baseline diffusion.

AI.tldr: A dual-guidance system combining LLM-based negative prompt optimization with CNN-RNN classifier guidance to improve Stable Diffusion image quality.
AI.motivation: To reduce artifacts and improve semantic fidelity in images generated by Stable Diffusion through automated negative prompt optimization and latent-space guidance.
AI.method: Fine-tuned seq2seq LLM for negative prompt optimization + CNN-RNN hybrid classifier for latent-space guidance, rolling back low-quality updates.
AI.result: Reduced artifacts and improved semantic fidelity compared to baseline diffusion.
AI.conclusion: The dual-guidance framework effectively enhances generated image quality through combined prompt optimization and latent-space correction.

title: Instrument Effects in Language-Model Honesty Evaluation: An Auditable Single-System Demonstration
summary: Evaluations of language-model honesty read the model's verdicts as evidence about the model. We test the instrument instead. We built a text-adventure world where the game engine, not any model, knows whether the quest can be completed. A language model plays under a budget and must eventually declare its quest complete, unreachable, or not yet decidable; the engine scores every verdict. Decision rules were recorded before results were read, and run artifacts bind the revisions they executed; the strength of preregistration varies by series and is disclosed. With the player held fixed, instrument choices substantially changed measured behavior. On four byte-identical anchors, expanding a two-verdict grammar to three verdicts moved strong claims from 38/40 to 7/40, while the new incomplete verdict took 28/40 outcomes; across series 2, 93/158 valid games ended incomplete. One sentence disclosing the success criterion took matched-instance false verdicts from 18/59 to 0/58, through fewer decision points and cleaner decisions. Repeated runs of one fixed configuration produced non-stable verdict distributions on 3 of 4 instances: single runs report samples as dispositions. A formally preregistered narrative-register gradient was falsified; two post-hoc, hypothesis-generating patterns remain: register presence roughly doubled strong claims, and budget rendering moved verdicts more than register content (.383 meter vs .150 lantern). The narrator compressed abundant budgets toward scarcity landmarks, yet the registered mediation test returned a null. We propose a four-check integrity protocol for eval instruments.

AI.tldr: Tests of language-model honesty are themselves heavily influenced by instrument design choices (verdict grammar, success criteria disclosure, budget rendering, narrative register), not just model behavior; a four-check integrity protocol for eval instruments is proposed.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluations treat model verdicts as direct evidence about model honesty, but the instrument (the evaluation design itself) may bias results. This paper tests whether seemingly minor methodological choices substantially alter measured behavior.
AI.method: A text-adventure world where the game engine (not the model) knows quest solvability. A language model plays under budget and must declare quest complete, unreachable, or not yet decidable; engine scores each verdict. Decision rules preregistered before results read; preregistration strength varies by series and is disclosed. Player held fixed; instrument choices systematically varied.
AI.result: (1) Expanding a two-verdict grammar to three verdicts moved strong claims from 38/40 to 7/40 (incomplete took 28/40). (2) Disclosing success criterion reduced false verdicts from 18/59 to 0/58. (3) Repeated runs of fixed configuration produced non-stable verdict distributions on 3/4 instances. (4) A preregistered narrative-register gradient was falsified; post-hoc, register presence roughly doubled strong claims, and budget rendering (.383 meter vs .150 lantern) moved verdicts more than register content.
AI.conclusion: Instrument choices substantially change measured behavior; a single run may not reflect stable dispositions. A four-check integrity protocol for eval instruments is proposed.

title: MCPEvol-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agent Performance Across Dynamic Evolutions of MCP Servers
summary: As Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers emerge as the core infrastructure for connecting LLMs with external tools, existing benchmarks leverage real-world MCP servers to evaluate LLM agents' tool-using capabilities. However, these benchmarks overlook the continuous evolution of tool interfaces and functionalities within MCP servers, resulting in flawed assessments that fail to capture the agent's adaptability in changing tool landscapes. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{MCPEvol-Bench}, a novel benchmark for evaluating the task-solving capabilities of LLM agents under dynamic toolset evolution. Inspired by large-scale empirical study, we propose 11 mutation operators to simulate realistic tool evolution within 123 MCP servers. We benchmark 12 state-of-the-art LLMs on multiple versions of MCP servers, revealing that even frontier models struggle to adapt to evolving tools. For instance, GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4-6 exhibit performance declines of 13.7\% and 14.4\% in evolved MCP servers, respectively, accompanied by substantial increases in planning and reasoning errors. These findings highlight the vulnerability of LLM-driven workflows, establishing MCPEvol-Bench as a standard for evaluating agent adaptability in dynamic tool environments.

AI.tldr: MCPEvol-Bench is a benchmark that evaluates LLM agents' adaptability to evolving tool interfaces in MCP servers, revealing that even frontier models (e.g., GPT-5.4, Claude-Sonnet-4-6) suffer significant performance declines (13.7%-14.4%) when tools change dynamically.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks use static MCP servers to evaluate LLM agents' tool-using capabilities, failing to account for the continuous evolution of tool interfaces and functionalities, which leads to flawed assessments of agent adaptability.
AI.method: Proposed 11 mutation operators inspired by large-scale empirical study to simulate realistic tool evolution across 123 MCP servers; evaluated 12 state-of-the-art LLMs on multiple evolved server versions.
AI.result: Frontier models show significant performance declines (GPT-5.4: 13.7%, Claude-Sonnet-4-6: 14.4%) in evolved MCP servers, with increased planning and reasoning errors.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven workflows are vulnerable to tool evolution, and MCPEvol-Bench serves as a standard benchmark for evaluating agent adaptability in dynamic tool environments.

title: LATTICE: Graph Self-Supervised Learning for Multimodal Spatial Omics Integration
summary: Spatially resolved omics studies increasingly combine transcriptomic and epigenomic assays, yet downstream analysis is often still performed using single-modality pipelines. We present LATTICE (Latent Alignment of Tissue-level and Transcriptomic Information for Cross-modal Embedding), a graph-based self-supervised framework that learns spot-level representations from harmonized multimodal features. LATTICE integrates five aligned modality blocks per Visium spot: Visium RNA, scMultiome RNA, scMultiome ATAC, spatial ATAC, and spatial CUT\&Tag. These modalities capture spatial transcriptomic measurements, single-cell inferred regulatory activity, and in situ chromatin and histone states within a unified lattice representation. LATTICE constructs a spatial neighborhood graph and trains a TransformerConv encoder using masked reconstruction, cross-modal alignment, and spatial smoothness objectives. On a private 11-sample melanoma cohort from an anonymized clinical collaborator comprising 54{,}912 total spots, LATTICE demonstrated stable optimization behavior, reproducible embeddings across analysis seeds, and complete multimodal integration across all samples. Adding scMultiome RNA to Visium RNA alone substantially improved concordance with Space Ranger clusters across 11 runs (adjusted Rand index [ARI] +0.157, normalized mutual information [NMI] +0.143, and spatial contiguity +0.174). Additional modalities further improved spatial contiguity and multimodal utility score (MUS), although they sometimes reduced agreement with RNA-derived reference labels, likely because the learned embeddings captured chromatin and regulatory structure beyond transcriptomic similarity alone. These results position LATTICE as a practical and empirically grounded framework for multimodal spatial omics integration, while also highlighting the need for stronger supervision and broader external benchmarking.

AI.tldr: LATTICE is a graph-based self-supervised framework that integrates up to five spatial omics modalities (Visium RNA, scMultiome RNA/ATAC, spatial ATAC, spatial CUT&Tag) into a unified latent representation, demonstrating improved multimodal integration on a 11-sample melanoma cohort (54,912 spots) with stable embeddings and measurable gains in spatial contiguity and cross-modal alignment.
AI.motivation: Spatially resolved omics studies increasingly generate multimodal data (transcriptomic + epigenomic), but downstream analysis remains largely single-modality, failing to leverage complementary information across assays.
AI.method: LATTICE uses a TransformerConv encoder trained on a spatial neighborhood graph with three objectives: masked reconstruction, cross-modal alignment, and spatial smoothness. It integrates five modality blocks: Visium RNA, scMultiome RNA, scMultiome ATAC, spatial ATAC, and spatial CUT&Tag.
AI.result: On a private 11-sample melanoma cohort (54,912 spots), adding scMultiome RNA to Visium RNA improved ARI (+0.157), NMI (+0.143), and spatial contiguity (+0.174). Additional modalities improved spatial contiguity and MUS but sometimes reduced agreement with RNA-derived labels, indicating capture of beyond-transcriptomic structure.
AI.conclusion: LATTICE is a practical, empirically grounded framework for multimodal spatial omics integration, though it highlights the need for stronger supervision and broader external benchmarking.

title: MagicPrompt: Ultra-Lightweight Prompt Tuning for Video Generation
summary: Large-scale video diffusion models (VDMs) deliver strong generation performance, but full fine-tuning for downstream tasks incurs prohibitive computational costs. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods have two critical flaws on billion-scale models: they still require substantial trainable parameters, and reward-based training suffers from noise-induced optimization instability in condition-guided tasks. We propose MagicPrompt, a lightweight framework that achieves extreme parameter efficiency and stable reward optimization. It first adopts Attention-Embedded Prompt Tuning, which steers generation via lightweight soft prompts with orders of magnitude fewer parameters while preserving pre-trained knowledge. It further introduces Dual-Space Reward Feedback Optimization, which uses self-supervised latent objectives to improve condition-guided reward training. Experiments show MagicPrompt reaches competitive performance with less than 1\% trainable parameters and notably reduces training costs.

AI.tldr: MagicPrompt is a lightweight fine-tuning framework for billion-scale video diffusion models that achieves extreme parameter efficiency (<1% trainable parameters) and stable reward optimization through Attention-Embedded Prompt Tuning and Dual-Space Reward Feedback Optimization.
AI.motivation: Full fine-tuning of large-scale video diffusion models for downstream tasks is computationally prohibitive, and existing PEFT methods still require substantial trainable parameters while suffering from reward-based training instability due to noise in condition-guided tasks.
AI.method: (1) Attention-Embedded Prompt Tuning: lightweight soft prompts embedded into attention layers to steer generation with minimal parameters. (2) Dual-Space Reward Feedback Optimization: self-supervised latent objectives to stabilize and improve condition-guided reward training.
AI.result: Achieves competitive performance with less than 1% trainable parameters and significantly reduces training costs compared to full fine-tuning and existing PEFT methods.
AI.conclusion: MagicPrompt demonstrates that extreme parameter efficiency coupled with stable reward optimization can effectively fine-tune billion-scale video diffusion models for downstream tasks.

title: Reward-Free Evolving Agents via Pairwise Validator
summary: A self-evolving agentic loop repeatedly proposes a tweaked version of an agent (its prompt template or program) and accepts or rejects the change based on a per-iteration quality signal. Designing that signal is often the costly part of the project: a reliable scalar reward requires domain expertise and labeled examples that are themselves as expensive to assemble as the agent's underlying task. We propose replacing the scalar at the accept/reject gate with a pairwise validator: a frozen LLM that, given the parent and child candidate, returns a binary verdict on which is better. Pairwise judgment is generally easier and more stable than absolute scoring, due to its contrastive nature, which mitigates the need for strict scale calibration. The validator also requires no training of its own. We integrate the validator into three published self-evolving engines (GEPA, ADRS, ShinkaEvolve) and report two flavors: Adaptive Focus, which retains the engine's existing val-set parent selection, and Soft Elo, which lets the validator's verdicts drive parent selection so that val-set rewards drop as well. Across multiple agents and two artifact substrates (prompt and code), our method matches or exceeds the full-reward baseline on the majority of settings we evaluate, and the pattern survives a cross-family validator swap. The pairwise gate is thus a drop-in replacement for per-step reward design at competitive task accuracy without the labeling cost.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes replacing costly scalar reward signals in self-evolving agentic loops with a frozen LLM-based pairwise validator that compares parent and child candidates. This approach reduces labeling costs while maintaining or improving task accuracy across multiple engines and artifact types.
AI.motivation: Designing reliable scalar reward signals for self-evolving agent loops is expensive and requires domain expertise and labeled examples, making it the costliest part of such projects.
AI.method: Replace scalar reward at the accept/reject gate with a frozen LLM pairwise validator that returns a binary verdict comparing parent and child candidates. Two flavors are proposed: Adaptive Focus (retains engine's val-set parent selection) and Soft Elo (validator verdicts drive parent selection).
AI.result: Matches or exceeds the full-reward baseline on most settings across multiple agents, artifact substrates (prompt and code), and survives cross-family validator swap.
AI.conclusion: The pairwise gate serves as a drop-in replacement for per-step reward design, achieving competitive task accuracy without the labeling cost.

title: Proof-or-Stop: Don't Trust the Agent, Trust the Evidence -- Loop Engineering for Verifiable Evidence-Gated Lifecycle Control
comment: 48 pages, 10 figures, 29 numbered tables. Preprint v1
summary:
Autonomous coding agents increasingly execute multi-step software work, but lifecycle states such as reviewed, tested, DONE, and ready-to-merge remain claims unless supported by current evidence. We present Proof-or-Stop Lifecycle Control, a method that permits lifecycle transitions only when fresh, tracked-source-state-bound, mechanically verifiable evidence satisfies the relevant gate. The method treats agent outputs as claims rather than lifecycle state, and uses proof operationally to mean gate-admissible evidence under a stated trust model, not semantic program correctness.
  We evaluate an open-source implementation through mechanism tests, a powered control-policy ablation, and operated self-application evidence. The unattended-loop engine passed 10 of 10 scenarios with zero false-DONE, and local-key receipt bundles rejected 18 tamper classes with zero false accepts. In a 9,240-cell ablation, the pre-registered A4 versus A2-prime comparison reduced visible-pass/hidden-fail amplification from 31 of 1,800 injected cells under a compute-budgeted naive loop to 2 of 1,800 under the gated loop, a 1.6 percentage-point improvement in not-amplified rate with a 95 percent confidence interval of [0.8, 2.5]. A near-compute A3 versus A4 comparison, 14 of 1,800 versus 2 of 1,800, indicates that the gain is associated with enforcing review as a lifecycle gate rather than merely adding a reviewer. The self-application corpus contains 565 stories and 1,007 review findings, with 94.8 percent resolved, plus a 68-row high/critical cross-vendor exhibit. These results support Proof-or-Stop as a model-agnostic, host-neutral control layer for deciding which autonomous-agent claims a lifecycle may act on. The evaluation is limited to one model family, 24 ablation tasks, and a self-hosted corpus.

AI.tldr: Proof-or-Stop Lifecycle Control enforces that autonomous coding agent lifecycle transitions (e.g., DONE, reviewed) are only permitted when backed by mechanically verifiable, source-bound evidence, reducing false-DONE and tamper risks.
AI.motivation: Autonomous coding agents claim lifecycle states (reviewed, tested, DONE) without current verifiable evidence, creating a gap between claimed progress and actual trustworthiness.
AI.method: Proof-or-Stop Lifecycle Control: permits lifecycle transitions only when fresh, tracked-source-state-bound, mechanically verifiable evidence satisfies a gate; treats agent outputs as claims, not lifecycle state; uses "proof" as gate-admissible evidence under a stated trust model.
AI.result: Unattended-loop engine: 10/10 scenarios passed with zero false-DONE; local-key receipt bundles rejected 18 tamper classes with zero false accepts. In a 9,240-cell ablation, A4 vs A2-prime reduced visible-pass/hidden-fail amplification from 31/1,800 to 2/1,800 (1.6 pp improvement, 95% CI [0.8, 2.5]). A3 vs A4 comparison (14/1,800 vs 2/1,800) indicates gain from enforcing review as a lifecycle gate. Self-application corpus: 565 stories, 1,007 review findings (94.8% resolved), plus 68-row high/critical cross-vendor exhibit.
AI.conclusion: Proof-or-Stop is a model-agnostic, host-neutral control layer for deciding which autonomous-agent claims a lifecycle may act on; evaluation limited to one model family, 24 ablation tasks, and a self-hosted corpus.

title: Adaptive Ad Load Design for Sponsored Search Markets: Evidence, Theory, and Deployment
summary: Ad-load design is a central supply-side decision in sponsored search: more sponsored slots can raise revenue, but may crowd out organic results and degrade user outcomes. We study this trade-off using a large-scale randomized field experiment on an Android app store, where over five million users are exposed to one through six sponsored slots. Increasing ad load raises revenue by up to 43%, but reduces total search conversions by up to 5% and daily engagement by up to 2.2%. These average effects mask substantial heterogeneity: additional slots generate large revenue gains for high-ad-conversion queries, but little or negative marginal revenue for low-conversion queries. The trade-off also shifts within query as advertiser composition changes, such as brand-advertiser presence. Motivated by these findings, we design and deploy a novel adaptive algorithm -- exploration-augmented Locally Adaptive Ad Load (e-LAAL). e-LAAL combines LAAL, a model-free query-level decision rule that updates ad-load recommendations using recent outcomes, with static exploration arms that maintain support and provide fixed-policy counterfactual benchmarks. We provide a finite-time dynamic-regret guarantee for the e-LAAL architecture. In a platform-level production deployment serving 22.3 million users and 77.6 million searches, e-LAAL improves the empirical revenue--conversion trade-off relative to deployed static benchmarks and outperforms uniform and historical query-dependent static benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the ad-load trade-off in sponsored search through a large-scale field experiment on an Android app store (5M+ users, 1-6 slots). Increasing ad load raises revenue up to 43% but reduces conversions by 5% and engagement by 2.2%, with significant heterogeneity across queries. The authors design e-LAAL, an adaptive algorithm combining model-free decision rules with exploration arms, and deploy it on 22.3M users/77.6M searches, showing improved revenue-conversion trade-offs over static benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Ad-load design is a central supply-side decision in sponsored search: more sponsored slots can raise revenue, but may crowd out organic results and degrade user outcomes. The paper seeks to study this trade-off empirically and design an adaptive algorithm to optimize it.
AI.method: The authors conduct a large-scale randomized field experiment on an Android app store (5M+ users, 1-6 sponsored slots). They then design e-LAAL, an algorithm that combines LAAL (a model-free query-level decision rule updating ad-load recommendations via recent outcomes) with static exploration arms for support and counterfactual benchmarks, with a finite-time dynamic-regret guarantee.
AI.result: Increasing ad load raises revenue by up to 43%, reduces total search conversions by up to 5%, and daily engagement by up to 2.2%. Effects are heterogeneous: high-ad-conversion queries see large revenue gains, low-conversion queries see little or negative marginal revenue. In platform-level production deployment (22.3M users, 77.6M searches), e-LAAL improves empirical revenue-conversion trade-off relative to static benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The ad-load trade-off is significant and heterogeneous. The proposed e-LAAL algorithm effectively optimizes this trade-off in production, outperforming uniform and historical query-dependent static benchmarks.

title: Hough-SIFT: Robust Image Registration for Linear Structures via Hough Space
comment: 5 pages, 6 figures. Supplementary video is available as an ancillary file. Accepted for oral presentation at the 29th Meeting on Image Recognition and Understanding (MIRU2026)
summary: Image registration is essential in applications such as electronic image stabilization. Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT), a widely used local keypoint detector and descriptor, typically provides accurate registration; however, it often fails in scenes with strong linear structures (e.g., shutters), where local features become ambiguous. We propose Hough-SIFT, a robust registration method that performs SIFT descriptor matching in Hough space. In this domain, linear structures form distinctive peaks that restore descriptor discriminability. Experiments demonstrate that Hough-SIFT is robust in linear scenes where SIFT frequently fails, while maintaining accuracy comparable to SIFT in normal scenes.

AI.tldr: Hough-SIFT improves image registration in linear-structure scenes (e.g., shutters) by performing SIFT descriptor matching in Hough space, where linear features form distinctive peaks, achieving robustness where standard SIFT fails while maintaining comparable accuracy in normal scenes.
AI.motivation: Standard SIFT frequently fails in scenes with strong linear structures (e.g., shutters) because local features become ambiguous under such conditions.
AI.method: Hough-SIFT performs SIFT descriptor matching in Hough space, where linear structures form distinctive peaks that restore descriptor discriminability.
AI.result: Hough-SIFT is robust in linear scenes where SIFT frequently fails, while maintaining accuracy comparable to SIFT in normal scenes.
AI.conclusion: Hough-SIFT effectively addresses SIFT's limitation in linear-structured environments, offering a robust registration method without sacrificing performance on standard scenes.

title: CausalGraphX: A Counterfactual Graph Neural Network Framework for Explainable Systemic Risk Assessment
comment: Accepted in AAAI'26 Workshop, Agentic AI in Financial Services
summary: The interconnected nature of global financial systems makes them vulnerable to systemic risks, where the failure of a few institutions can trigger catastrophic cascading defaults. Traditional risk models often fail to capture the complex, non-linear dynamics of these networks. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown promise in modeling relational data, they primarily learn correlative patterns and function as black boxes, offering little insight into the causal mechanisms of shock propagation. This limitation is critical for regulators who require explainable models to perform stress tests and devise effective interventions. We introduce CausalGraphX, a novel framework that integrates GNNs with counterfactual reasoning to provide explainable assessments of systemic risk. CausalGraphX employs a Graph Attention mechanism to learn representations of institutional vulnerability and uses an adversarial regularization technique to ensure these representations capture causal drivers rather than spurious correlations. Furthermore, we propose an optimization-based approach to generate counterfactual explanations, answering questions such as, "What minimum capital injection would have prevented Bank A's default under a specific stress scenario?" We validate CausalGraphX on large-scale synthetic financial networks. Our results demonstrate that CausalGraphX significantly outperforms traditional and deep learning baselines in predicting cascading defaults while providing sparse, plausible, and actionable counterfactual explanations.

AI.tldr: CausalGraphX integrates Graph Neural Networks with counterfactual reasoning to provide explainable systemic risk assessment in financial networks, outperforming baselines in predicting cascading defaults while generating actionable counterfactual explanations.
AI.motivation: Traditional systemic risk models fail to capture non-linear dynamics of financial networks, and existing GNN-based approaches learn only correlative patterns without providing causal, explainable insights needed by regulators for stress testing and intervention design.
AI.method: CausalGraphX combines Graph Attention mechanisms to learn institutional vulnerability representations, adversarial regularization to enforce causal (rather than correlational) drivers, and an optimization-based counterfactual explanation generation approach (e.g., "What minimum capital injection prevents default?").
AI.result: On large-scale synthetic financial networks, CausalGraphX significantly outperforms traditional and deep learning baselines in predicting cascading defaults while providing sparse, plausible, and actionable counterfactual explanations.
AI.conclusion: CausalGraphX demonstrates that integrating causal reasoning with GNNs yields both superior predictive performance and explainability for systemic risk assessment, addressing a critical regulatory need for transparent and intervention-oriented models.

title: HyperShadow: A Benchmark for Detecting 3D Projections of Higher-Dimensional Spatial Objects
summary: Machine-learning datasets labelled "4D" universally denote three spatial dimensions plus time. We introduce HyperShadow, the first public benchmark in which the fourth, fifth, and sixth dimensions are spatial: the task is to decide whether a 3D point cloud is a native three-dimensional shape or the projection, the "shadow", of a rigid object living in R^N (N = 4-6). We show this task is fundamentally distinct from intrinsic-dimension estimation: a shadow is still at-most-3-dimensional data, and standard estimators (TwoNN, Levina-Bickel MLE) reach only 71-73% accuracy. Detection instead requires projection signatures, density folds, filled volumes with characteristic radial profiles, and topology changes, which a 190k-parameter point network recovers at 96.6% accuracy across four corruption tiers, generalizing at 79-91% to object families never seen in training. On a temporal track of rigidly rotating objects we introduce a zero-parameter rigidity witness: the residual of the optimal rigid 3D alignment (Kabsch) between consecutive frames, which must vanish for any rigid 3D motion but cannot vanish for the shadow of a rigid rotation in R^N. This single interpretable statistic separates the classes at AUROC 0.982. All data are generated reproducibly from seeds; the dataset, models, and code are released publicly. HyperShadow makes no claim about physical reality; it is a controlled instrument for studying which observable statistics can certify incompatibility with a purely three-dimensional explanation.

AI.tldr: HyperShadow is the first public benchmark for detecting whether a 3D point cloud is a native 3D shape or the projection ("shadow") of a rigid object from 4-6 spatial dimensions. A 190k-parameter network achieves 96.6% accuracy; a zero-parameter rigidity witness achieves AUROC 0.982 on temporal data.
AI.motivation: Existing 4D datasets use time as the fourth dimension; no benchmark exists for detecting data that originates from higher (4-6) spatial dimensions projected down to 3D. This task is distinct from intrinsic-dimension estimation and requires new detection methods.
AI.method: Two approaches: (1) a 190k-parameter point network trained on projection signatures, density folds, filled volumes with radial profiles, and topology changes; (2) a zero-parameter rigidity witness using Kabsch alignment residual between frames of rigidly rotating objects, which vanishes for 3D motions but not for higher-dimensional shadows.
AI.result: The point network achieves 96.6% accuracy across four corruption tiers and generalizes at 79-91% to unseen object families. Standard intrinsic-dimension estimators (TwoNN, Levina-Bickel MLE) reach only 71-73% accuracy. The rigidity witness achieves AUROC 0.982 on temporal data.
AI.conclusion: HyperShadow serves as a controlled instrument for studying observable statistics that can certify incompatibility with a purely 3D explanation, with no claims about physical reality.

title: Knowing You at First Glance: Inferring Apparent Personality from Faces
comment: Accepted by The 9th Chinese Conference on Pattern Recognition and Computer Vision, PRCV2026
summary: Inferring apparent personality from facial images is important in social scenarios for embodied agents in human-robot interaction. Unlike inferring intrinsic personality traits via conversation, this task models first-impression personality perception based solely on facial appearance before interaction begins. Existing studies mainly focus on the Big Five personality model and often rely on language or multimodal inputs. As a result, it remains unclear whether facial cues alone can support meaningful associations with perceived personality traits. This question is particularly relevant for MBTI types, which are widely used in practice and more readily interpretable by large language models. To this end, we propose \textbf{GlanceFace}, an end-to-end framework for apparent personality inference leveraging vision-language models to introduce semantic priors and a semantic-enhanced facial representation module to capture subtle personality-related cues, together with an uncertainty-aware learning strategy to handle noisy and subjective annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance on MBTI-based apparent personality benchmarks and reveal relationships between facial characteristics and perceived personality traits, highlighting its potential to support adaptive initial interaction strategies for embodied agents. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/MrHuan3/GlanceFace.

AI.tldr: GlanceFace is an end-to-end framework that uses vision-language models and semantic-enhanced facial representations to infer apparent personality (specifically MBTI types) from facial images alone, demonstrating strong performance on benchmarks and enabling adaptive initial interaction strategies for embodied agents in human-robot interaction.
AI.motivation: Current apparent personality inference research mainly focuses on the Big Five model and often relies on language or multimodal inputs, leaving it unclear whether facial cues alone can support meaningful personality trait associations—particularly for MBTI types, which are widely used and more interpretable by large language models.
AI.method: GlanceFace employs an end-to-end framework with (1) vision-language models to introduce semantic priors, (2) a semantic-enhanced facial representation module to capture subtle personality-related cues, and (3) an uncertainty-aware learning strategy to handle noisy and subjective annotations.
AI.result: Strong performance on MBTI-based apparent personality benchmarks; reveals relationships between facial characteristics and perceived personality traits.
AI.conclusion: GlanceFace demonstrates that facial images alone can support meaningful apparent personality inference for MBTI types, highlighting its potential to support adaptive initial interaction strategies for embodied agents in human-robot interaction.

title: Per-Token Fixed-Point Convergence in Depth-Recurrent Transformers
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Code, configs, experiment log, and checkpoint at https://github.com/jlognn/depth-recurrent-convergence
summary: A depth-recurrent transformer applies a weight-tied core a variable number of times, and prior work has shown that training with a randomized recursion count yields one checkpoint usable across a range of inference depths. We ask what such a model actually computes per token, and measure it directly. On a 135M-class model trained on FineWeb-Edu, the recurrent state converges to a per-token fixed point: mean successive-output KL divergence falls from 3.9e-1 at the second loop to 8.5e-6 by the sixteenth, and per-token state change decays in step. Crucially, this convergence is not uniform across tokens. The median token converges by loop six, while approximately 10 percent of tokens continue to update at the training-mean depth of eight, and mean convergence depth is ordered by token type (whitespace shallowest, content words deepest). This per-token variation is the central object of the paper. We show it is directly readable and that reading it outperforms learning to predict it: a training-free rule that halts each token once its output stabilizes attains uniform depth-8 quality at 4.94 average loops (a 38 percent reduction in average depth) and matches uniform depth across the average-depth range, whereas a linear router trained on convergence labels harvested from the same model requires nearly full depth and yields no reduction. The elasticity that makes this possible reproduces here as background (validation loss decreases monotonically from 3.80 at one loop to 3.20 at eight and remains stable to 32 loops). We report average depth as a FLOP proxy with a three-point wall-clock bracket rather than a realized speedup, make no FLOP-matched parity claim, and note that the allocation results are established at a single scale and seed. The complete study runs on a single RTX 4090 in approximately 100 GPU-hours.

AI.tldr: A depth-recurrent Transformer's per-token recurrent state converges to a fixed point, with convergence depth varying by token type. A training-free halting rule based on output stabilization reduces average inference depth by 38% while maintaining uniform depth-8 quality, outperforming a learned linear router.
AI.motivation: To understand what a depth-recurrent Transformer computes per token when trained with randomized recursion counts, specifically measuring whether the recurrent state converges and whether this convergence is uniform across tokens.
AI.method: Train a 135M-parameter depth-recurrent Transformer on FineWeb-Edu; measure per-token KL divergence and state change across recursion loops; propose a training-free halting rule that stops inference per token once output stabilizes; compare against a learned linear router trained on convergence labels.
AI.result: Mean successive-output KL divergence drops from 3.9e-1 (loop 2) to 8.5e-6 (loop 16); median token converges by loop 6, ~10% of tokens still update at depth 8; convergence depth varies by token type (whitespace shallowest, content words deepest). The training-free rule achieves depth-8 quality at 4.94 avg loops (38% reduction), while a learned linear router requires nearly full depth with no reduction.
AI.conclusion: Per-token convergence is heterogeneous and directly readable from the model's own dynamics; a simple training-free halting rule exploits this elasticity effectively, while learning to predict convergence depth from labels fails. Results are at a single scale/seed, with wall-clock brackets provided as FLOP proxies.

title: Active Real-World Factor-Based Evaluation for Generalist Robot Policies
summary: Generalist robot manipulation policies trained on large, diverse datasets have shown remarkable promise across a wide range of tasks. However, rigorously evaluating these policies remains a fundamental challenge. Real-world performance depends on a large combinatorial space of task factors including object poses and camera viewpoints, making full, exhaustive evaluation intractable. Additionally, real hardware evaluation is slow and resource-intensive, so current practice is to use narrow test suites that can miss critical failure modes and misrepresent true deployment readiness.
