To introduce mechanically meaningful intermediate states, a trajectory-aware FMTO formulation is proposed, where volume-fraction-indexed BESO states are used to construct the probability path and target velocity field. This incorporates physics-guided optimisation history into generative flow learning without adding inference-time optimisation. A path--velocity mismatch analysis explains why moderate trajectory weighting can improve generation stability, whereas excessive guidance may over-constrain the learned transport. Numerical examples show that FMTO generates diverse topology candidates with improved compliance-related performance, volume-fraction satisfaction, topology fidelity, and substantially fewer sampling steps than a diffusion-based baseline. Under limited training data, trajectory-aware FMTO achieves the best overall performance with a moderate trajectory weight. Studies on trajectory-anchor density and three-dimensional topology generation further demonstrate the influence of path design and the applicability of the proposed framework beyond two-dimensional problems.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a flow matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) framework that generates diverse, physically consistent topology candidates using physics-guided trajectory information, achieving better performance and faster sampling than diffusion-based methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional topology optimisation is computationally expensive when multiple candidate designs are needed under varying conditions, and existing generative models rely on adversarial training, long sampling, or external guidance to ensure structural feasibility.
AI.method: The authors propose FMTO with two formulations: (1) Linear FMTO (endpoint-based baseline using Gaussian-to-BESO interpolation) and (2) Trajectory-aware FMTO, where volume-fraction-indexed BESO states construct the probability path and target velocity field, incorporating physics-guided optimisation history. A path-velocity mismatch analysis explains trajectory weighting effects.
AI.result: FMTO generates diverse topologies with improved compliance, volume-fraction satisfaction, topology fidelity, and fewer sampling steps than diffusion baselines. Trajectory-aware FMTO with moderate weighting achieves best overall performance under limited data. The framework also extends to 3D problems.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-aware flow matching is an effective generative approach for topology optimisation, balancing generation quality, diversity, and sampling efficiency without requiring inference-time optimisation.

title: TAMF-VTON: Texture-Aware Mask-Free Virtual Try-On via High-Fidelity Image Synthesis
summary: Recent diffusion-based virtual try-on (VTON) methods remain limited by their reliance on segmentation masks, insufficient preservation of fine-grained textures, and limited support for arbitrary multi-garment compositions. Consequently, existing approaches still face significant challenges in real-world e-commerce deployment. We present TAMF-VTON, a texture-aware, mask-free framework that enables high-fidelity image synthesis under practical unconstrained conditions. Our method requires no human parsing or inpainting masks at inference time and supports diverse garment styles, categories, and quantities, enabling the simultaneous transfer of multiple items while preserving body structure and intricate texture details. This is achieved through a unified generative pipeline with three key components: (1) a lightweight Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) adaptation scheme that enables efficient fine-tuning without compromising the base model's general editing capabilities; (2) a frequency-domain supervision mechanism that explicitly optimizes high-frequency spectral consistency to preserve high-fidelity textures; and (3) a robust data curation pipeline employing an adaptive inpainting strategy to simulate the inverse VTON process for high-quality training pair generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and perceptual quality. Optimized for efficiency, the model achieves inference in under 15 seconds per image on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with INT4 quantization. By combining mask-free operation, flexible multi-garment composition, faithful texture preservation, and efficient inference on consumer hardware, TAMF-VTON demonstrates a commercially viable solution for scalable deployment in real-world digital fashion scenarios. The project is available at https://www.style3d.ai/ai-photoshoot/virtual-clothing-try-on.

AI.tldr: TAMF-VTON is a mask-free, texture-aware virtual try-on framework that supports multi-garment composition, preserves fine-grained textures via frequency-domain supervision and MoE adaptation, and achieves fast inference (<15s on RTX 4090) without segmentation masks, outperforming state-of-the-art methods for real-world e-commerce deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based VTON methods are limited by reliance on segmentation masks, insufficient fine-grained texture preservation, and lack of support for arbitrary multi-garment compositions, hindering real-world e-commerce deployment.
AI.method: A unified generative pipeline with three components: (1) lightweight Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) adaptation for efficient fine-tuning without degrading base model editing capabilities; (2) frequency-domain supervision to optimize high-frequency spectral consistency for texture fidelity; (3) adaptive inpainting strategy for high-quality training pair generation via inverse VTON simulation.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and perceptual quality. Achieves inference under 15 seconds per image on RTX 4090 with INT4 quantization. Supports mask-free operation, flexible multi-garment composition, and faithful texture preservation.
AI.conclusion: TAMF-VTON provides a commercially viable solution for scalable real-world digital fashion deployment by combining mask-free operation, multi-garment support, texture preservation, and efficient inference on consumer hardware.

title: Scalable Training of Continuous-Time Spiking Neural Networks with Differentiable Spike-Time Discretization
summary: Continuous-time spiking neural networks (SNNs) provide an event-driven framework for temporal computation, computational neuroscience, and neuromorphic hardware. However, training deep continuous-time SNNs is severely constrained by the memory required for exact spike-time computation, which evaluates and retains candidate firing times over intervals determined by presynaptic spike ordering. Here we introduce a memory-efficient training framework based on differentiable spike-time discretization (DSTD) for leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with general membrane and synaptic time constants. DSTD maps irregular presynaptic spikes onto differentiable weighted events at fixed time points, replacing the input-dependent candidate dimension with $M$ fixed time intervals while accurately approximating continuous-time membrane-potential dynamics. This reduces candidate-related activation memory from $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}N_{\mathrm{in}})$ to $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}M)$ in the case of time-to-first-spike (TTFS) coding, where $N_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{out}}$ denote the numbers of presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons, respectively. We further introduce synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization that organizes layer-wise firing windows, mitigates dead-neuron failures, and enables pipeline-like processing. In dense LIF layers, DSTD reduced peak memory consumption by up to approximately 100-fold and training time by up to approximately 20-fold compared with exact spike-time computation. Together, these methods allowed us to train 9-layer convolutional SNNs on CIFAR-10 and 20-layer convolutional SNNs on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: DSTD is a memory-efficient training framework for continuous-time SNNs that discretizes spike times onto fixed intervals, reducing activation memory from O(N_out N_in) to O(N_out M), achieving ~100x memory savings and ~20x faster training compared to exact computation.
AI.motivation: Training deep continuous-time SNNs is severely constrained by the memory required for exact spike-time computation, which evaluates and retains candidate firing times over intervals determined by presynaptic spike ordering.
AI.method: DSTD maps irregular presynaptic spikes onto differentiable weighted events at fixed time points, replacing input-dependent candidate dimension with M fixed time intervals. Also introduces synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization for pipeline-like processing.
AI.result: DSTD reduced peak memory by ~100x and training time by ~20x compared to exact spike-time computation. Enabled training 9-layer convolutional SNNs on CIFAR-10 and 20-layer convolutional SNNs on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: DSTD provides a practical and memory-efficient solution for training deep continuous-time SNNs, overcoming the key memory bottleneck of exact spike-time computation while enabling deeper networks on limited hardware.

title: An LLM-Based Automatic Sportscast Solution for Robot Soccer Matches
summary: RoboCup has always been a scenario to develop systems that solve real-world problems. Driven by the main goal of playing against the 2050 FIFA World Cup champions, the RoboCup Soccer leagues need to constantly measure how the research community is progressing. Computing visual statistics from match videos is a crucial way to track this evolution. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a fully autonomous, real-time sports commentator for RoboCup matches. By bridging the gap between raw kinematic tracking and natural language generation, our neuro-symbolic architecture extracts precise statistics from video streams and turns them into fluent, hallucination-free narration. The proposed system is capable of generating statistics and commentary both during live match streaming and in post-game analysis, easily adapting to the new dynamism of the league where different humanoid robots of different sizes share the field. Supplemental materials are available at https://lab-rococo-sapienza.github.io/MARIO/

AI.tldr: A fully autonomous, real-time sports commentator for RoboCup matches that uses a neuro-symbolic architecture to convert raw kinematic tracking data into accurate, hallucination-free statistics and natural language narration for live and post-game analysis.
AI.motivation: RoboCup needs to track research progress toward the goal of playing against 2050 FIFA World Cup champions; computing visual statistics from match videos is crucial for measuring community advancement.
AI.method: A neuro-symbolic architecture that bridges raw kinematic tracking data with natural language generation, extracting precise statistics from video streams and producing fluent narration without hallucinations.
AI.result: The system generates statistics and commentary both during live match streaming and in post-game analysis, adapting to the dynamic RoboCup league where humanoid robots of different sizes share the field.
AI.conclusion: The proposed system enables tracking research community progress in RoboCup by providing autonomous, real-time commentary and statistical analysis that is accurate and hallucination-free.

title: TopoAgent: A Self-Evolving Topological Agent for Multimodal Scientific Reasoning
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel in general tasks, rigorous scientific reasoning remains challenging due to the limitations of monolithic, linear planning. Such sequential designs often suffer from visual-semantic misalignment, long-context hallucinations, and brittle execution under fixed task granularity. We propose TopoAgent, a self-evolving topological framework that replaces linear trajectories with dynamic, state-isolated graph evolution. TopoAgent first employs a front-end decomposer to fracture complex queries into visually-grounded atoms. These atoms are organized into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) based on their dependencies, enabling strict context isolation to shield the reasoning engine from irrelevant historical noise. Furthermore, we introduce adaptive atomic fission, which dynamically splits bottleneck nodes into finer-grained sub-atoms at runtime when tool capability boundaries are exceeded. Extensive experiments across mathematics, physics, and chemistry benchmarks demonstrate that TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agent frameworks, providing a robust, noise-resistant, and self-correcting paradigm for autonomous scientific reasoning.

AI.tldr: TopoAgent is a self-evolving topological framework that replaces linear planning trajectories with Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)-based dynamic graph evolution for multimodal scientific reasoning, featuring visual-semantic decomposition, context isolation, and adaptive atomic fission to outperform state-of-the-art linear agents on math, physics, and chemistry benchmarks.
AI.motivation: MLLMs suffer from visual-semantic misalignment, long-context hallucinations, and brittle execution under fixed task granularity due to monolithic, linear planning, which limits rigorous scientific reasoning.
AI.method: TopoAgent uses a front-end decomposer to fracture complex queries into visually-grounded atoms organized into a DAG for strict context isolation, plus adaptive atomic fission to dynamically split bottleneck nodes into finer-grained sub-atoms at runtime when tool capability boundaries are exceeded.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across mathematics, physics, and chemistry benchmarks demonstrate that TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agent frameworks.
AI.conclusion: TopoAgent provides a robust, noise-resistant, and self-correcting paradigm for autonomous scientific reasoning, replacing linear trajectories with dynamic, state-isolated graph evolution.

title: Grad2Fair: A Gradient-driven Approach for Graph Fairness without Demographics
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) frequently encounter group fairness issues, often yielding biased predictions against specific demographic groups defined by sensitive attributes such as gender or race. While this challenge has motivated extensive research, most existing solutions rely on the strong assumption that demographics are fully available. To bypass this strict requirement, a few recent studies have attempted to use predicted demographics as proxies to enforce fairness constraints. However, predicted demographics may be inaccurate, resulting in the failure to improve fairness. In this work, we investigate the problem of graph fairness without demographic information and avoid the utilization of predicted demographics. Motivated by our observation that the gradient distributions of misclassified nodes implicitly encode demographic information, we first propose GradDist, a gradient-based metric that quantifies bias by measuring the distance between local modes within these distributions. To mitigate this bias, we propose Gradient-to-Fairness (Grad2Fair), a gradient-guided approach for group fairness without demographics. Due to the potential demographics in gradients, Grad2Fair directly leverages gradients to debias and eliminates demographic prediction, thereby enabling stable fairness performance. Experiments on several real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Grad2Fair, as evidenced by superior performance over baselines in most cases. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZzoomD/Grad2Fair.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses group fairness in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) without requiring demographic information. The authors propose GradDist, a gradient-based metric to quantify bias, and Grad2Fair, a gradient-guided debiasing method that avoids using predicted demographics, achieving superior fairness performance on real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing graph fairness methods assume full demographic availability, while recent alternatives using predicted demographics are unreliable due to prediction inaccuracies. The authors aim to achieve group fairness without any demographic information or reliance on predicted demographics.
AI.method: The method first observes that gradient distributions of misclassified nodes encode demographic information. GradDist measures bias by computing distances between local modes in gradient distributions. Grad2Fair then directly leverages these gradients to debias the model, eliminating the need for demographic prediction.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world datasets show Grad2Fair outperforms baselines in most cases, demonstrating stable fairness performance without demographic information.
AI.conclusion: The proposed gradient-guided approach effectively addresses group fairness in GNNs without requiring or predicting demographic attributes, offering a more robust alternative to existing methods.

title: Blurring Modal Boundaries: A Unified Survey from Single- to Multi-Modal Person Re-ldentification
summary: Person re-identification (ReID) serves as a critical component in intelligent surveillance systems, aiming to match identities across disjoint camera networks. While traditional methods primarily rely on single-modal RGB imagery, they are often constrained by environmental challenges such as low illumination and occlusion. To overcome these limitations, the field is rapidly evolving toward cross-modal and multi-modal paradigms. This survey presents a comprehensive overview of this transition, systematically reviewing key cross-modal tasks including visible-infrared (VI-ReID), text-image (TI-ReID), sketch-based (Sketch-ReID), and the emerging Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) ReID, which extends perception beyond direct visibility. Furthermore, we examine tri-spectral and multi-modal fusion ReID, discussing how complementary information from diverse sensors enhances robustness. Beyond summarizing datasets, challenges, and methodologies, we propose a Transformer-based baseline framework for visible-infrared ReID, designed to effectively capture modality-invariant features. Finally, based on the current landscape, we outline several promising directions for future research.

AI.tldr: This survey comprehensively reviews the transition from single-modal RGB to cross-modal and multi-modal paradigms in person re-identification, covering VI-ReID, TI-ReID, Sketch-ReID, NLOS-ReID, tri-spectral and multi-modal fusion, while proposing a Transformer-based baseline for VI-ReID and outlining future research directions.
AI.motivation: Traditional single-modal RGB person re-identification methods are constrained by environmental challenges such as low illumination and occlusion, motivating the need to transition toward cross-modal and multi-modal paradigms for more robust matching across disjoint camera networks.
AI.method: The paper conducts a systematic survey of cross-modal and multi-modal ReID tasks (VI-ReID, TI-ReID, Sketch-ReID, NLOS-ReID, tri-spectral and multi-modal fusion) and proposes a Transformer-based baseline framework for visible-infrared ReID designed to capture modality-invariant features.
AI.result: Comprehensive overview of datasets, challenges, and methodologies across emerging cross-modal ReID paradigms; introduction of a Transformer-based baseline for VI-ReID that effectively models modality-invariant representations.
AI.conclusion: The field is moving from single-modality toward multi-modal fusion for greater robustness; Transformer-based architectures show promise for cross-modal feature alignment; Non-Line-of-Sight ReID opens new perception frontiers beyond direct visibility.

title: SmartRAG: Native Graph-Based RAG for Mobile Device
summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) as personal assistants on mobile devices demands privacy, low latency, and offline availability, yet the computational cost of giant models clashes with strict edge-hardware budgets. We argue that this tension cannot be resolved by model compression alone; it requires decomposing on-device intelligence into complementary functional roles. We present SmartRAG, a fully on-device framework that organizes an intelligent assistant around four coordinated modules -- Perception, Memory, Focus, and Thinking. At the core of SmartRAG is EvoNER, a continually learnable named-entity recognizer that incrementally expands its label inventory through teacher-distilled updates, enabling the system to absorb previously unseen entity types without retraining the backbone LLM. Extracted knowledge is stored in MRGraph, a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph, and retrieved at query time through a hybrid pipeline combining graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search. The on-device LLM is invoked only for high-value semantic operations -- labeling, planning, and answer synthesis -- keeping inference costs bounded. Experiments on four QA benchmarks (TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MultiHopQA) show that SmartRAG with a quantized 1.7B-parameter backbone achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with models up to 18$\times$ larger, while running entirely on commodity smartphones within practical memory and latency envelopes.

AI.tldr: SmartRAG is a fully on-device LLM framework that achieves competitive multi-hop reasoning on smartphones using a 1.7B-parameter backbone by decomposing intelligence into four modules (Perception, Memory, Focus, Thinking) with EvoNER for continual entity recognition and MRGraph for knowledge storage, performing comparably to models 18× larger.
AI.motivation: Deploying LLMs on mobile devices requires privacy, low latency, and offline availability, but the computational cost of large models conflicts with strict edge-hardware budgets, and model compression alone cannot resolve this tension.
AI.method: SmartRAG organizes an on-device assistant around four modules (Perception, Memory, Focus, Thinking), uses EvoNER (a continually learnable NER with teacher-distilled updates) for incremental entity learning, stores knowledge in MRGraph (a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph), and retrieves via a hybrid pipeline (graph traversal, lexical matching, dense semantic search). The on-device LLM is invoked only for high-value semantic operations.
AI.result: On TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, and MultiHopQA, SmartRAG with a quantized 1.7B backbone achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with models up to 18× larger, running entirely on commodity smartphones within practical memory and latency constraints.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing on-device intelligence into complementary functional roles (rather than relying solely on model compression) can overcome edge-hardware limitations, enabling competitive reasoning performance with dramatically smaller backbone models.

title: MESHA: Mechanism-Enforced Sequential Halving for Strategic Linear Bandits
summary:
We design and analyze \underline{M}echanism-\underline{E}nforced \underline{S}equential \underline{HA}lving (MESHA), an algorithm for Best Arm Identification (BAI) in strategic linear bandits. In this setting, each arm may strategically misreport its feature vector to maximize the probability of being identified as the best arm, when rewards are generated from the arms' true but unobservable features. The design of MESHA applies the naïve uniform sampling rule and an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC): the former reduces the impact of arms' strategic behaviours and the latter eliminates arms whose reported features severely deviate from the ground truth. Considering an arbitrary Nash Equilibrium, we prove that any arm would attempt to pass the GTC check to maximize its identified probability and derive an upper bound on the failure probability of MESHA within a fixed budget $T$. We also show that state-of-the-art linear BAI algorithms with $G$-optimal design would fail in such strategic environment, as the optimal design (OD)-based sampling rule based on strategically reported features may {\it starve} the optimal arm of any sampling budget. Finally, extensive numerical experiments indicate that MESHA
  outperforms baselines that rely on OD-based sampling rules as well as the feature-agnostic baselines, corroborating the efficacy of MESHA.

AI.tldr: MESHA is a Best Arm Identification algorithm for strategic linear bandits that uses uniform sampling and a Grim Trigger Condition to identify the best arm despite arms strategically misreporting their features. It outperforms optimal design-based methods and feature-agnostic baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing linear BAI algorithms fail when arms can strategically misreport their feature vectors to increase their chance of being selected as the best arm. Optimal design-based sampling rules can starve the optimal arm in such strategic environments.
AI.method: MESHA employs a naïve uniform sampling rule to reduce the impact of strategic behaviors, combined with an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC) that eliminates arms whose reported features deviate significantly from their true features.
AI.result: Any arm at Nash Equilibrium attempts to pass GTC to maximize identification probability. An upper bound on MESHA's failure probability within fixed budget T is derived. State-of-the-art linear BAI with G-optimal design fails in strategic settings due to OD-based sampling rules starving the optimal arm.
AI.conclusion: MESHA outperforms both OD-based sampling rule baselines and feature-agnostic baselines in extensive numerical experiments, demonstrating efficacy in strategic linear bandit BAI.

title: Physics-Informed Diffusion for Biomechanically Plausible 3D Sign Language Generation
summary: Sign language production, which generates continuous 3D skeletal motion from spoken language input, must simultaneously satisfy two constraints: semantic fidelity, so that a deaf viewer can recognize the intended sequence of glosses, and biomechanical plausibility, so that the generated skeleton respects anatomical constraints. Existing approaches optimize semantic reconstruction through coordinate-based objectives that treat the skeleton as an unstructured vector, thus allowing for bone length drift, joint angle violations, and temporarily locked fingers. We introduce PIDiffSign, a physics-informed diffusion model for gloss-to-pose translation that incorporates anatomical constraints into both the architecture and training objective. The model uses a Transformer encoder-decoder, where the decoder is conditioned on the diffusion time step through adaptive zero-initialized layer normalization and cross-attends to gloss representations. A differentiable geometry module enforces bone length consistency and biologically valid joint angles throughout generation. Training combines anthropomorphic, kinematic, angular, and finger-joint constraints with a contrastive gloss-pose alignment loss and classifier-free guidance for semantically conditioned sampling. Experiments on the PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily benchmarks show consistent improvements over a strong diffusion baseline in pose accuracy, joint-angle correctness, distributional realism, and back-translation quality. These results demonstrate that physics-informed diffusion improves both motion realism and semantic fidelity for sign language generation.

AI.tldr: PIDiffSign is a physics-informed diffusion model for sign language production that enforces anatomical constraints (bone length, joint angles) via a differentiable geometry module and multi-objective training, achieving improved pose accuracy and semantic fidelity on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing sign language production methods optimize semantic reconstruction through coordinate-based objectives that treat the skeleton as an unstructured vector, leading to bone length drift, joint angle violations, and temporarily locked fingers — violating biomechanical plausibility needed for realistic motion.
AI.method: A Transformer encoder-decoder conditioned on diffusion time steps via adaptive zero-initialized layer normalization, with cross-attention to gloss representations. A differentiable geometry module enforces bone length consistency and valid joint angles. Training combines anthropomorphic, kinematic, angular, and finger-joint constraints with contrastive gloss-pose alignment loss and classifier-free guidance.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over a strong diffusion baseline on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily in pose accuracy, joint-angle correctness, distributional realism, and back-translation quality.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed diffusion improves both motion realism and semantic fidelity for sign language generation.

title: Project Kaleidoscope: Contextual, Human-Aligned Evaluation for Real-World AI Applications
summary: Evaluations (Evals) are a deployment bottleneck for real-world AI applications: public benchmarks rarely match a team's users, context, or policies, and human review is often tedious to scale. Motivated by our work with AI applications in the public sector, this project addresses recurring evaluation challenges encountered when applications must satisfy local policy and governance requirements. We present Kaleidoscope, an integrated workflow for contextual functional evaluation that links persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, and human review for reliability-gated automated scoring. Generated test cases are scored against application-specific rubrics; human annotations provide reviewable labels; and LLM judges automate scoring only when their agreement with those labels meets a configured threshold. Kaleidoscope is therefore a practical, inspectable, iterative workflow for product teams. We report early evidence from a three-week pilot across four organizational use cases and custom-rubric judge experiments on 108 annotated Q\&A pairs spanning four domains and 14 evaluation dimensions. The results highlight useful features for end-to-end reliable, automated scoring.

AI.tldr: Kaleidoscope is an integrated workflow for contextual functional evaluation of AI applications, combining persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, and human review to enable reliability-gated automated scoring. Tested across four domains and 14 evaluation dimensions, it addresses deployment bottlenecks caused by mismatched benchmarks and unscalable human review.
AI.motivation: Evals (evaluations) are a deployment bottleneck for real-world AI applications because public benchmarks rarely match a team's users, context, or policies, and human review is difficult to scale. This work is motivated by recurring evaluation challenges in public sector AI applications that must satisfy local policy and governance requirements.
AI.method: Kaleidoscope links persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, and human review for reliability-gated automated scoring. Generated test cases are scored against application-specific rubrics; human annotations provide reviewable labels; LLM judges automate scoring only when their agreement with those labels meets a configured threshold.
AI.result: Early evidence from a three-week pilot across four organizational use cases and custom-rubric judge experiments on 108 annotated Q&A pairs spanning four domains and 14 evaluation dimensions. Results highlight useful features for end-to-end reliable, automated scoring.
AI.conclusion: Kaleidoscope is a practical, inspectable, iterative workflow for product teams, enabling reliable automated scoring while maintaining human oversight through reliability gating.

title: Counterfactuals for Feature-Weighted Clustering
summary: Counterfactual explanations provide local, interpretable insight by identifying changes to an input that would alter its assigned outcome. Although well established in supervised learning, their extension to clustering is less direct, since cluster assignments are unlabeled and governed by the geometry of the partition. This paper introduces VoICE, a Voronoi-Induced Counterfactual Explainability framework for feature-weighted $k$-means clustering. Rather than treating cluster change as a crossing of a single pairwise centroid boundary, VoICE formulates counterfactual generation as projection onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, incorporating feature weights directly into both the clustering geometry and the counterfactual objective to yield least-cost and parsimonious explanations under actionability constraints. Target regions are further intersected with data-derived bounds and homothetically contracted towards their centroids, limiting extrapolation and boundary sensitivity. VoICE consistently produces valid target-cluster membership, across several benchmark datasets, where the leading pairwise baseline does not.

AI.tldr: VoICE is a framework for generating counterfactual explanations in weighted k-means clustering by projecting inputs onto target Voronoi regions with actionability constraints, producing valid cluster membership where pairwise baselines fail.
AI.motivation: Counterfactual explanations are well-established for supervised learning but less straightforward for clustering due to the unlabeled nature of cluster assignments and geometric partitioning. Existing pairwise centroid-boundary approaches are insufficient.
AI.method: VoICE formulates counterfactual generation as projection onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, incorporating feature weights into clustering geometry and the counterfactual objective. Target regions are intersected with data-derived bounds and homothetically contracted toward centroids to limit extrapolation and boundary sensitivity, under actionability constraints.
AI.result: VoICE consistently produces valid target-cluster membership across multiple benchmark datasets, outperforming the leading pairwise baseline which fails to do so.
AI.conclusion: VoICE provides least-cost, parsimonious counterfactual explanations for feature-weighted k-means clustering with actionability constraints, and is more reliable than prior pairwise approaches.

title: Rotational Motion-Induced Error Compensation for Phase-Shifting Profilometry-Based Eye Reconstruction
summary: With the proliferation of immersive Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs) for Virtual and Augmented Reality (VR/AR), reliable and high-precision eye tracking has become increasingly important. Conventional 2D image-based methods offer low system complexity but remain limited in stability, accuracy, and robustness. Three-dimensional ocular surface reconstruction can provide richer geomet-ric information, and structured light profilometry is particularly attractive because it enables dense and accurate surface measurement. However, Phase-Shifting Profilometry (PSP), which estimates phase from sequentially acquired fringe images, is highly susceptible to motion-induced errors when the eye rotates between frames. This study proposes a rotational motion compensation framework for PSP-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction. Relative eye rotation is estimated from image-based motion cues using a user-specific 3D eye model in a spherical-coordinate domain. The estimated motion is then used to compensate for camera-pixel mismatch and phase-shift errors caused by inter-frame rotation. A region-wise optimization strategy is further introduced to reduce residual artifacts by inde-pendently refining the compensation strength in different ocular regions. Experiments with a rotating fake eye under non-uniform motion demonstrate that the proposed method substantially suppresses motion-induced deformation and improves reconstruction accuracy. An additional experiment with a non-spherical rigid object indicates that the compensation principle is not restricted to spherical eye geometry. These results establish a practical basis for stable PSP-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction toward future high-precision eye tracking in immersive environments.

AI.tldr: Proposes a rotational motion compensation framework for Phase-Shifting Profilometry (PSP)-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction, using a user-specific 3D eye model in spherical-coordinate domain to estimate and compensate for inter-frame eye rotation, plus a region-wise optimization to reduce residual artifacts.
AI.motivation: PSP-based 3D eye reconstruction suffers from motion-induced errors when the eye rotates between frames, limiting its applicability for high-precision eye tracking in VR/AR HMDs.
AI.method: (1) Estimate relative eye rotation from image-based motion cues using a user-specific 3D eye model in spherical-coordinate domain. (2) Compensate for camera-pixel mismatch and phase-shift errors caused by inter-frame rotation. (3) Apply region-wise optimization to independently refine compensation strength across different ocular regions.
AI.result: Substantially suppresses motion-induced deformation and improves reconstruction accuracy on a rotating fake eye under non-uniform motion. Compensation principle also generalizes to non-spherical rigid objects.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a practical basis for stable PSP-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction, enabling future high-precision eye tracking in immersive VR/AR environments.

title: Stop Thinking, Start Looking: Efficient Post-Training for Multimodal Document Question Answering via Reasoning-Free Alignment
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026, Workshop on Efficient Multimodal Question Answering (EMM-QA)
summary: Efficient multimodal document question answering with explicit visual grounding, locating the precise document region that supports each answer remains an open challenge. Current approaches bifurcate into Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), which requires large annotated datasets and reaches optimization plateaus, and reasoning-centric Reinforcement Learning (RL), which depends on verbose intermediate traces that inflate inference token cost without clear benefit. We introduce Perception-RFT, a training framework that applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to multimodal document QA, bypassing intermediate reasoning tokens to directly align visual features with structured grounding outputs. To rigorously evaluate the necessity of reasoning, we construct a reasoning variant under identical reward settings. We find that reasoning-enabled models suppress their reasoning traces during training, converging to direct perception-based policies at the 4B parameter scale, reducing per-query inference token length by more than 60%, while reasoning-enabled RL underperforms perception-only training. Through a fine-grained analysis of Qwen3-VL-4B optimization dynamics, we confirm that SFT saturation and cold-start RL instability established in text-domain post-training extend to multimodal, and identify a previously uncharacterized Grounding Divergence: a selective trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision on two out of distribution (OOD) benchmarks (4,828 samples) under joint RL optimization. We further show that an early SFT$\rightarrow$RL transition achieves comparable precision with 65% less training data.

AI.tldr: Perception-RFT applies GRPO to multimodal document QA, bypassing intermediate reasoning tokens to directly align visual features with structured grounding outputs. The method reduces inference token length by 60%+, reveals that reasoning-enabled RL underperforms perception-only training, and identifies a previously uncharacterized Grounding Divergence between semantic robustness and geometric precision under joint RL optimization.
AI.motivation: Current approaches to multimodal document QA with explicit visual grounding face two key limitations: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) requires large annotated datasets and reaches optimization plateaus; (2) reasoning-centric Reinforcement Learning (RL) depends on verbose intermediate traces that inflate inference token cost without clear benefit. The authors aim to bypass these issues by directly aligning visual features with structured grounding outputs.
AI.method: Perception-RFT applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to multimodal document QA, bypassing intermediate reasoning tokens to directly align visual features with structured grounding outputs. The authors construct a reasoning variant under identical reward settings for rigorous comparison. They analyze optimization dynamics on Qwen3-VL-4B, examining SFT saturation, cold-start RL instability, and joint RL optimization effects.
AI.result: Key results: (1) Reasoning-enabled models suppress reasoning traces during training, converging to direct perception-based policies; (2) Perception-only training reduces per-query inference token length by >60%; (3) Reasoning-enabled RL underperforms perception-only training; (4) Identification of Grounding Divergence — a selective trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision on OOD benchmarks (4,828 samples) under joint RL optimization; (5) Early SFT→RL transition achieves comparable precision with 65% less training data.
AI.conclusion: The paper confirms that SFT saturation and cold-start RL instability observed in text-domain post-training extend to multimodal settings. The proposed Perception-RFT framework demonstrates that direct perception-based RL without intermediate reasoning tokens is both more efficient and effective for multimodal document QA. The Grounding Divergence phenomenon reveals a fundamental trade-off in joint RL optimization that warrants further investigation.

title: What's in a Smoothness Constant? Tighter Rates for Local SGD with Bounded Second-order Heterogeneity
summary: Local SGD, also known as Federated Averaging, is a widely used distributed optimization algorithm. Although Local SGD often outperforms alternatives such as Mini-batch SGD in practice, theory still only partially explains when and why local updates help under realistic data heterogeneity. Recent work by [Patel et al., 2025] shows that a bounded second-order heterogeneity assumption captures the efficiency of Local SGD for strongly convex objectives, and conjectures that the same principle extends to the general convex setting. In this paper, we prove this conjecture by establishing an improved convergence guarantee for Local SGD on general convex objectives under bounded second-order heterogeneity. We also improve the best-known lower bounds for Local SGD in this setting, showing that our upper bounds are nearly tight. Together, these results provide a sharper, more fine-grained convergence theory for Local SGD. As a further application of our techniques, we provide a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement, showing how second-order heterogeneity captures the impact of rare high-curvature clients.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that Local SGD (Federated Averaging) achieves improved convergence for general convex objectives under bounded second-order heterogeneity, and nearly matches this with tighter lower bounds, extending prior results from strongly convex to convex settings.
AI.motivation: Local SGD is widely used in practice but its theoretical understanding under realistic data heterogeneity remains incomplete. Recent work showed bounded second-order heterogeneity captures its efficiency for strongly convex objectives, and this paper aims to prove the conjecture that the same extends to general convex objectives.
AI.method: The authors provide a theoretical analysis establishing improved convergence guarantees for Local SGD on general convex objectives under bounded second-order heterogeneity. They also derive improved lower bounds to demonstrate near-tightness of their upper bounds, and apply their techniques to derive a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement.
AI.result: The paper proves the conjecture that Local SGD's efficiency under bounded second-order heterogeneity extends to general convex objectives, and improves the best-known lower bounds to show near-tightness. Additionally, it provides a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement showing how second-order heterogeneity captures the impact of rare high-curvature clients.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a sharper, more fine-grained convergence theory for Local SGD, bridging the gap between theory and practice under realistic data heterogeneity in the convex setting.

title: Selectivity Drives Efficiency: Dataset Pruning for Visual Place Recognition
summary: Recent visual place recognition (VPR) studies have increasingly relied on large-scale datasets to train more robust and discriminative models. Although this trend significantly improves recognition performance, it also introduces substantial storage and training costs, especially when new architectures or training strategies need to be repeatedly developed and evaluated. Dataset pruning (DP) provides a promising way to improve data efficiency by retaining only informative training data. However, conventional DP methods mainly follow the sample-wise classification paradigm, which overlooks the relation-dependent training nature of VPR, where supervision is typically formed by image pairs rather than independent images. To address this issue, we propose a place-wise dataset pruning framework tailored for VPR. Instead of pruning individual images, our method treats each place as the basic pruning unit and introduces two complementary novel metrics, i.e., intra-place diversity (IPD) and inter-place similarity (IPS), to evaluate the training value of each place. By jointly considering these two metrics, our method ranks all places and constructs a compact yet informative coreset, thereby allowing the pruned dataset to still support the training of robust and discriminative VPR models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art DP baselines under different pruning ratios while reducing selection and training costs. Moreover, by pruning a merged dataset roughly 3.5$\times$ the size of GSV-Cities to a comparable scale, our coreset maintains highly competitive performance, achieving 94.5\% R@1 on MSLS-val and 97.0\% R@1 on Nordland with only NetVLAD. Codes will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a place-wise dataset pruning framework for visual place recognition (VPR), introducing intra-place diversity (IPD) and inter-place similarity (IPS) metrics to construct compact coresets that maintain robust VPR performance while significantly reducing storage and training costs.
AI.motivation: Existing VPR models rely on large-scale datasets for training, leading to substantial storage and training costs. Conventional dataset pruning methods follow a sample-wise classification paradigm that ignores the relation-dependent training nature of VPR, where supervision is formed by image pairs rather than independent images.
AI.method: Proposes a place-wise dataset pruning framework that treats each place as the basic pruning unit, using two complementary metrics: intra-place diversity (IPD) to measure variation within a place, and inter-place similarity (IPS) to measure distinctiveness between places. These metrics jointly rank all places to construct a compact yet informative coreset.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art DP baselines under different pruning ratios while reducing selection and training costs. Achieves 94.5% R@1 on MSLS-val and 97.0% R@1 on Nordland with NetVLAD when pruning a merged dataset ~3.5× the size of GSV-Cities to comparable scale.
AI.conclusion: The proposed place-wise pruning framework effectively addresses the limitations of conventional sample-wise DP methods for VPR, enabling compact coresets that maintain competitive recognition performance with reduced data and computational costs.

title: InCarEmo: A Multimodal Dataset for In-Cabin Emotion Recognition and Driver State Monitoring
summary: Understanding driver emotion and state is critical for the next generation of intelligent in-cabin systems that ensure safety and enhance human-vehicle interaction. However, existing public datasets for in-cabin affective computing are largely limited to visual modalities and rarely include conversational information, making it difficult to capture the linguistic and interactive cues underlying driver emotion. To address these gaps, we introduce InCarEmo, a multimodal dataset for in-cabin emotion recognition and driver state monitoring. InCarEmo integrates RGB and infrared video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text collected from scripted in-cabin scenarios designed to simulate realistic driver behaviors, covering diverse lighting conditions and driving contexts. The dataset supports three primary tasks: 1) multimodal emotion recognition, 2) fatigue detection, and 3) distraction monitoring. In addition to the original Chinese data, we construct an auxiliary English benchmark to support preliminary cross-lingual evaluation. We provide a unified benchmark with extensive baseline results across unimodal and multimodal methods, including analyses under modality-missing and noise conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of multimodal fusion and reveal remaining challenges under real-world noise and low-light conditions. By releasing InCarEmo, we aim to establish a comprehensive foundation for robust, interpretable, and human-centric in-cabin affective understanding, promoting safer and more empathetic driver-vehicle interaction.

AI.tldr: InCarEmo is a new multimodal in-cabin dataset integrating RGB/infrared video, audio, and dialogue text for emotion recognition, fatigue detection, and distraction monitoring, with baselines showing benefits of multimodal fusion but challenges under noise and low-light conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing in-cabin affective computing datasets are limited to visual modalities and lack conversational information, making it difficult to capture linguistic and interactive cues underlying driver emotion. This gap hinders the development of intelligent in-cabin systems that ensure safety and enhance human-vehicle interaction.
AI.method: InCarEmo is a multimodal dataset collecting RGB and infrared video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text from scripted scenarios simulating realistic driver behaviors across diverse lighting and driving contexts. It includes an auxiliary English benchmark for cross-lingual evaluation. Unified benchmarks with unimodal and multimodal baselines are provided, including modality-missing and noise condition analyses.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of multimodal fusion for emotion recognition, fatigue detection, and distraction monitoring. However, challenges remain under real-world noise and low-light conditions, indicating room for improvement in robustness.
AI.conclusion: By releasing InCarEmo, the authors aim to establish a comprehensive foundation for robust, interpretable, and human-centric in-cabin affective understanding, promoting safer and more empathetic driver-vehicle interaction.

title: GAttNHP: Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process for Extrapolation Reasoning in Temporal Knowledge Graphs
summary: Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs) record how facts evolve over time, but forecasting future events on a TKG remains difficult for three reasons: (i) long-range temporal dependencies are hard to encode; (ii) events on different chains mutually excite or inhibit one another in ways that snapshot-level models cannot express; and (iii) inter-arrival times are heavy-tailed and statistically sparse, so deterministic time predictors are unreliable. We address these three issues with a single framework, the \textbf{Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process (GAttNHP)}, built around three matched components. First, a self-attention encoder casts each subject--relation chain as a continuous-time point process and captures the lingering excitation of distant history. Second, a semantic soft-grouping module turns globally learnable Hawkes priors into an analytical cross-attention mask, so chains share excitation patterns through their latent group memberships rather than through exhaustive pairwise computation. Third, a Non-Crossing Quantile (NCQ) regression head replaces mean-based time prediction, providing calibrated, monotonically ordered quantile estimates that remain stable under heavy-tailed inter-arrival distributions. On six benchmark TKG datasets, GAttNHP improves over state-of-the-art baselines on both entity prediction and time prediction, and ablations confirm that its largest gains arise on the long-tail event chains where existing models fail most severely.

AI.tldr: GAttNHP unifies self-attention temporal encoding, semantic soft-grouping for cross-chain excitation sharing, and Non-Crossing Quantile regression for heavy-tailed inter-arrival times, achieving state-of-the-art entity and time prediction on six TKG benchmarks, with largest gains on long-tail event chains.
AI.motivation: TKGs face three core challenges: (i) long-range temporal dependencies are hard to encode; (ii) events on different chains mutually excite/inhibit each other beyond snapshot-level models; (iii) heavy-tailed, sparse inter-arrival times make deterministic time predictors unreliable.
AI.method: Three matched components: (1) Self-attention encoder treating each subject–relation chain as a continuous-time point process to capture long-range history; (2) Semantic soft-grouping module using globally learnable Hawkes priors as a cross-attention mask for efficient chain interaction via latent group memberships; (3) Non-Crossing Quantile (NCQ) regression head for calibrated, monotonically ordered quantile time estimates under heavy-tailed distributions.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on six TKG benchmarks for both entity prediction and time prediction; ablation studies confirm largest gains occur on long-tail event chains where existing models fail most severely.
AI.conclusion: The unified GAttNHP framework effectively addresses all three TKG forecasting challenges simultaneously, with particular strength on rare, long-tail event sequences.

title: FlashDecoder: Real-Time Latent-to-Pixel Streaming Decoder with Transformers
summary: Real-time video generation demands fast decoding as much as fast denoising, yet current latent video diffusion models rely on 3D convolutional decoders that are slow and memory-intensive at high resolutions or for long video. We introduce FlashDecoder, a fast, memory-efficient pure-Transformer video decoder that decodes latents to pixels frame by frame. At each step, the current frame attends only to a fixed-size window of past frames through a rolling KV cache. The fixed temporal window keeps decoding fast and memory bounded regardless of video length, enabling constant-latency streaming. Because frames are processed sequentially, temporal causality is enforced without explicit attention masks, enabling training at resolutions up to 1080p and matching the reconstruction quality of convolutional decoders. On the Wan2.1 and Wan2.2 latent spaces, FlashDecoder matches each convolutional decoder in reconstruction quality (e.g., 41.55dB vs. 41.49dB PSNR at 1080p) while decoding 3.6x-4.7x faster with up to 11x less memory on a single H100 GPU. With architecture-aware inference optimizations, the speedup widens to 12x.

AI.tldr: FlashDecoder is a pure-Transformer video decoder that decodes latents to pixels frame-by-frame using a rolling KV cache, achieving constant-latency streaming, faster decoding (3.6x-12x), and up to 11x less memory than 3D convolutional decoders while matching reconstruction quality up to 1080p.
AI.motivation: Real-time video generation requires fast decoding as well as fast denoising, but current latent video diffusion models use 3D convolutional decoders that are slow and memory-intensive at high resolutions or for long videos.
AI.method: FlashDecoder is a pure-Transformer video decoder that decodes latents to pixels frame by frame. Each frame attends only to a fixed-size window of past frames via a rolling KV cache, ensuring bounded memory and constant-latency streaming. Temporal causality is naturally enforced by sequential processing without explicit attention masks.
AI.result: FlashDecoder matches convolutional decoder reconstruction quality (e.g., 41.55dB vs 41.49dB PSNR at 1080p), decodes 3.6x-4.7x faster with up to 11x less memory on a single H100 GPU. With architecture-aware inference optimizations, speedup reaches 12x.
AI.conclusion: FlashDecoder demonstrates that a pure-Transformer decoder with a rolling KV cache can replace 3D convolutional decoders in latent video diffusion models, enabling efficient, memory-bounded, real-time streaming video generation at high resolutions.

title: AI vs Human Expert Reasoning: Assessing Agreements in Building Typology Predictions based on Street View Imagery
summary: This research investigates the potential of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to infer building typologies: Construction, Current Use, and Storeys from Google Street View (GSV) images. Predictions generated by VLMs are compared with inference by human experts (civil engineers and architects) as a source of manually labelled ground-truth data. We evaluate several state-of-the-art VLMs, including GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.0 Flash. By applying different scaling strategies and prompting techniques, we found that Chain-of-Thought prompts provide an overall more stable model performance. We also investigate the reasoning behind VLMs' building-typology predictions by examining the probabilities of keywords appearing in AI explanations. This enabled us to analyse patterns in these reasonings and identify key themes driving both agreements and disagreements between VLM and expert labels. We find that AI tends to focus on visual indicators, whereas human experts place greater emphasis on broader contextual cues and domain knowledge, in addition to visual cues. Overall, VLM can approximate experts' capability in building-typology classification at scale, with an average accuracy of approximately 70%. The study demonstrates the VLM's potential for AI automation in tasks that require pattern recognition and object identification in an urban context. AI have the potential to serve as complementary and collaborative tools for urban analysis, leveraging their strengths in understanding visual patterns. This study contributes to the exploration of the efficiency and scalability of AI visual prediction and provides insights into the reasoning processes that could support automation processes in urban analysis and prediction.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates Vision-Language Models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash) for inferring building typologies (Construction, Current Use, Storeys) from Google Street View images, achieving ~70% accuracy compared to human experts. Chain-of-Thought prompting improves stability, and analysis reveals AI focuses on visual cues while experts leverage broader contextual knowledge.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether VLMs can reliably infer building typologies from GSV images at scale, comparing their performance against human expert annotations and understanding the reasoning processes behind AI predictions.
AI.method: Evaluated GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.0 Flash on building typology classification (Construction, Current Use, Storeys) using GSV images. Applied various scaling strategies and prompting techniques (including Chain-of-Thought). Analyzed keyword probabilities in AI explanations to compare reasoning patterns between VLM predictions and expert labels.
AI.result: Chain-of-Thought prompts yield more stable model performance. VLMs achieve ~70% average accuracy. AI focuses on visual indicators, while human experts emphasize broader contextual cues and domain knowledge alongside visual information.
AI.conclusion: VLMs can approximate expert-level building typology classification at scale and show potential as complementary tools for urban analysis, leveraging their visual pattern recognition strengths to support automation in urban prediction tasks.

title: ChronoQG: Towards a Temporally Expressive and Hop-Bounded Benchmark for Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Generation
summary: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) aims to generate natural-language questions from structured graph evidence. Existing KGQG benchmarks, however, are mostly built on static knowledge graphs and do not encode the temporal scopes of graph facts. As a result, they cannot evaluate whether generated questions faithfully preserve temporal validity, event ordering, and answer-determining temporal constraints. In this paper, we study temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG), where a generated question must be faithful to both the support subgraph and the temporal constraints required to identify the target answer. We propose ChronoQG, the first temporally expressive and hop-bounded benchmark construction framework for TKGQG. ChronoQG integrates a comprehensive temporal-constraint taxonomy, topology-temporal subgraph sampling, and trace-grounded question generation to construct temporally faithful questions. The framework produces four benchmark datasets from heterogeneous temporal knowledge graphs, totaling 16,011 verified questions. We evaluate representative LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines across diverse TKGQG settings, including temporal-constraint counts, topological templates, and temporal-constraint types. The results show that existing methods struggle to preserve temporal constraints, especially under multi-constraint settings and harder temporal-constraint types. These findings reveal a clear gap between static KGQG and TKGQG, and establish ChronoQG as a challenging testbed for temporally faithful question generation.

AI.tldr: ChronoQG is the first framework for temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG), producing 16,011 verified questions from heterogeneous temporal KGs, revealing that existing methods fail to preserve temporal constraints like validity, ordering, and answer-determining conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing KGQG benchmarks are built on static knowledge graphs, lacking temporal scopes, so they cannot evaluate whether generated questions faithfully preserve temporal validity, event ordering, and answer-determining temporal constraints.
AI.method: ChronoQG integrates a temporal-constraint taxonomy, topology-temporal subgraph sampling, and trace-grounded question generation to construct temporally faithful benchmarks over heterogeneous temporal knowledge graphs.
AI.result: Four benchmark datasets totaling 16,011 verified questions; evaluation shows existing LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines struggle with temporal constraints, especially multi-constraint and harder temporal-constraint types.
AI.conclusion: There is a clear gap between static KGQG and TKGQG; ChronoQG serves as a challenging testbed for temporally faithful question generation.

title: TanGO: Training-Free 3D Editing via Tangent-Space Guidance and Optimization
summary: While recent flow-matching 3D generative models (e.g., VecSet) adopt structured representations, their tokens share global context, causing conventional training-free editing to suffer from semantic artifacts such as collapsed preserved regions or incomplete transformations. To address this, we propose TanGO, a training-free framework that enables adaptive per-token steering in the tangent space of generative dynamics. To realize this selective control, we formulate a one-step optimal control rule and determine the strength of each token's control signal using a von Mises-Fisher inspired directional discrepancy derived from the source and target velocity fields. Experiments show that TanGO substantially reduces structural artifacts and achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing 3D editing baselines. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/siw00-lim/TanGO.

AI.tldr: TanGO is a training-free 3D editing framework that enables adaptive per-token steering in the tangent space of generative dynamics using a one-step optimal control rule and von Mises-Fisher inspired directional discrepancy, achieving state-of-the-art performance with fewer artifacts.
AI.motivation: Existing flow-matching 3D generative models with structured representations suffer from semantic artifacts (collapsed preserved regions or incomplete transformations) during conventional training-free editing due to global context sharing among tokens.
AI.method: Proposes TanGO, a training-free framework with: (1) adaptive per-token steering in the tangent space of generative dynamics; (2) a one-step optimal control rule to realize selective control; (3) a von Mises-Fisher inspired directional discrepancy computed from source and target velocity fields to determine each token's control signal strength.
AI.result: Substantially reduces structural artifacts and achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing 3D editing baselines.
AI.conclusion: TanGO effectively solves the semantic artifact problem in training-free 3D editing by introducing per-token adaptive steering, and the code is publicly available.

title: Global Index on Responsible AI: 2026 Report
summary: Grounded in human rights-based frameworks such as the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the Global Index on Responsible AI (GIRAI) examines how countries translate responsible AI commitments into enforceable protections, institutional capacity, and redress mechanisms. GIRAI 2026 assesses these across five dimensions: Inclusion and Diversity, Ethics and Sustainability, Labour and Skills, Trust and Safety, and AI Use in Public Service. A global network of 135 country-level researchers collected and assessed 68,138 data points on 38 indicators organised across three pillars: government AI policy and implementation (17 indicators), civil society engagement (5), enabling conditions (15), and documented cases of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems. The data covers November 2023 to September 2025. A score of 100 is derived from the indicators to rank all countries. Findings show that while responsible AI governance is expanding, with 126 of 135 countries having at least one government policy or initiative across the 17 AI Policy indicators, this does not often translate into meaningful protection. For instance, Global South countries account for 203 of 306 new cases of indicators with frameworks since the first edition, yet 78% of their frameworks remain non-binding compared with 42% in the Global North. Government commitment to AI governance also does not extend to their own algorithms: whereas Transparency and Explainability is the strongest performing indicator, with 58% of countries having some framework, only 18% require Public Disclosure of Government Algorithms. Credible evidence of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems was also found in 35 countries. These findings show that responsible AI governance must move beyond framework adoption toward enforceable rights-based protections, resourced oversight institutions, and accessible redress.

AI.tldr: The Global Index on Responsible AI (GIRAI) 2026 evaluates 135 countries across five dimensions, finding that while 126 countries have some AI governance policies, these rarely translate into enforceable protections—particularly in the Global South where 78% of frameworks are non-binding. Only 18% of countries require disclosure of government algorithms, and 35 countries show evidence of deploying unacceptable-risk AI systems.
AI.motivation: To assess how countries translate responsible AI commitments into enforceable protections, institutional capacity, and redress mechanisms, grounded in human rights-based frameworks like the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI.
AI.method: A global network of 135 country-level researchers collected and assessed 68,138 data points on 38 indicators across three pillars (government AI policy, civil society engagement, enabling conditions), plus documented cases of unacceptable-risk AI deployment. Data covers November 2023 to September 2025. A composite score of 100 is derived to rank countries.
AI.result: 126 of 135 countries have at least one AI governance policy, but Global South countries account for 203 of 306 new framework indicators yet 78% are non-binding (vs. 42% in Global North). Only 18% require Public Disclosure of Government Algorithms despite Transparency being the strongest indicator (58%). Credible evidence of unacceptable-risk AI deployment found in 35 countries.
AI.conclusion: Responsible AI governance must move beyond framework adoption toward enforceable rights-based protections, resourced oversight institutions, and accessible redress mechanisms.

title: Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty: Beyond OOD Detection and Active Learning
summary: Current evaluation of epistemic uncertainty relies on tasks such as out-ofdistribution detection and active learning. However, the Bayes-optimal decision strategies for these tasks do not coincide with the scores commonly used to quantify epistemic uncertainty. Building on the epistemic reject-option framework, we evaluate epistemic uncertainty using its ability to identify regret, the reducible error. Formulating selective prediction as a constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret, we prove the optimal selector is a thresholded convex combination of the ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. This theoretical unification exposes a weakness in recent uncertainty disentanglement literature: we demonstrate that standard correlation metrics between learned components do not necessarily predict their actual operational utility. We instead propose to evaluate the achievable risk, regret, coverage surface of the decomposition as a diagnostic for joint disentanglement and utility. Benchmarking standard methods on datasets with dense human annotations reveals that decision-theoretic rankings can disagree substantially with proxy-task rankings, including pairwise rank inversions between methods that are top-ranked on one criterion and bottom-ranked on other.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes evaluating epistemic uncertainty via the epistemic reject-option framework using regret (reducible error) rather than proxy tasks like OOD detection. It proves the optimal selective predictor is a thresholded convex combination of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, shows that standard correlation metrics for disentanglement do not predict operational utility, and proposes evaluating the risk-regret-coverage surface. Benchmarks reveal decision-theoretic rankings disagree substantially with proxy-task rankings.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of epistemic uncertainty relies on proxy tasks (OOD detection, active learning) whose Bayes-optimal strategies do not match commonly used epistemic uncertainty scores. The authors aim to provide a principled evaluation framework grounded in decision theory.
AI.method: Formulates selective prediction as constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret; proves the optimal selector thresholds a convex combination of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties; proposes evaluating the achievable risk-regret-coverage surface as a diagnostic for disentanglement and utility.
AI.result: Standard correlation metrics for disentanglement do not predict operational utility. Decision-theoretic rankings disagree substantially with proxy-task rankings, including pairwise rank inversions between methods top-ranked on one criterion and bottom-ranked on another.
AI.conclusion: Epistemic uncertainty should be evaluated by its ability to identify regret within a decision-theoretic framework rather than through proxy tasks. The proposed risk-regret-coverage surface provides a better diagnostic for joint disentanglement and utility.

title: Benchmarking Face Recognition without Real Faces
summary: Synthetic face datasets have become effective enough to train face recognition models with accuracy rivaling that of models trained on real photographs. This progress sidesteps the ethical and legal burdens of collecting real biometric data, yet evaluation has not kept pace. Even studies that train entirely on synthetic images still rely on real-face benchmarks to measure performance, leaving the privacy problem only half solved. We ask whether synthetic datasets can replace real benchmarks for face recognition evaluation. We test 12 synthetic datasets against 7 established real benchmarks using 24 pre-trained models that span both convolutional and transformer architectures. Our evaluation covers biometric verification metrics, similarity score distributions, cross-model ranking consistency, and the underlying distributional properties of each dataset. Benchmarking fidelity varies widely across the synthetic candidates, but the two strongest, MorphFace and Vec2Face, reproduce the relative behavior of real benchmarks and reach agreement levels that fall within the natural disagreement already observed among the real benchmarks themselves. These results establish that well-constructed synthetic datasets can support reliable comparative evaluation for face recognition, moving the field closer to a fully synthetic and privacy-preserving pipeline for both training and benchmarking.

AI.tldr: This study shows that well-constructed synthetic face datasets (MorphFace, Vec2Face) can replace real benchmarks for evaluating face recognition models, achieving agreement levels within the natural variance of real benchmarks, thereby enabling a fully synthetic, privacy-preserving pipeline.
AI.motivation: Current face recognition research still relies on real-face benchmarks for evaluation even when training on synthetic data, leaving privacy concerns unresolved. The authors aim to determine whether synthetic datasets can fully replace real benchmarks for evaluation.
AI.method: Tested 12 synthetic datasets against 7 real benchmarks using 24 pre-trained models (convolutional and transformer). Evaluated biometric verification metrics, similarity score distributions, cross-model ranking consistency, and distributional properties.
AI.result: Benchmarking fidelity varies widely across synthetic datasets, but MorphFace and Vec2Face reproduce relative behavior of real benchmarks and reach agreement levels within the natural disagreement observed among real benchmarks themselves.
AI.conclusion: Well-constructed synthetic datasets can support reliable comparative evaluation for face recognition, moving toward a fully synthetic, privacy-preserving pipeline for both training and benchmarking.

title: Transcoders for Investigating Deception in Language Models
summary: Transcoders have recently emerged as a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability (MI), enabling circuit-level analysis of model behaviour. In this paper, we investigate the use of transcoders to analyse deceptive behaviour in language models, a behaviour that poses a safety and security risk. Using a Qwen3-4B model with pre-trained transcoders, specifically per-layer transcoders (PLTs), we construct attribution graphs that capture feature activations and inter-feature dependencies, allowing circuit-level analysis of deception. Through feature steering and circuit analysis, we identified a dictionary of deception-related features and show that these features exert a stronger influence on deceptive outputs, as they produce predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses. These findings suggest that deception emerges from internal model mechanisms and highlight the potential of transcoders for behavioural monitoring and early detection of security vulnerabilities related to malicious behaviours in language models.

AI.tldr: This paper uses transcoders (specifically per-layer transcoders) to analyze deceptive behavior in a Qwen3-4B language model, constructing attribution graphs for circuit-level analysis of deception. Through feature steering and circuit analysis, the authors identify deception-related features that produce predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses, demonstrating that deception emerges from internal model mechanisms.
AI.motivation: To address safety and security risks posed by deceptive behavior in language models by using transcoders for mechanistic interpretability to understand how deception arises from internal model mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors use pre-trained per-layer transcoders (PLTs) on a Qwen3-4B model to construct attribution graphs capturing feature activations and inter-feature dependencies, combined with feature steering and circuit analysis to identify and validate deception-related features.
AI.result: Identified a dictionary of deception-related features that exert stronger influence on deceptive outputs and produce predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses.
AI.conclusion: Deception emerges from internal model mechanisms, and transcoders show potential for behavioral monitoring and early detection of security vulnerabilities related to malicious behaviors in language models.

title: Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss for Peak-Critical Time Series Forecasting
summary: In many operational time-series forecasting applications, such as crowd demand forecasting, the risk related to under-prediction is substantially higher than that of over-prediction. Accurate prediction of rare demand spikes plays a critical role in downstream tasks. Yet most time-series forecasters are trained with symmetric objectives (e.g., MSE, MAE) and evaluated primarily on aggregate error, which can mask failures in extreme-values and peak-timing predictions. We introduce Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL), a simple, model-agnostic objective that (i) penalizes under-predictions more heavily and (ii) increases the training weight of peak regions within each forecast window. We further propose a peak-critical evaluation protocol that complements MAE/MSE with channel-wise tail error (Top-10% and Top-1%) and peak metrics (precision, recall, F1 under timing tolerance, and peak timing error). We evaluate APAL on long-horizon multivariate forecasting across five state-of-the-art backbones, with a focus on pedestrian demand forecasting using (i) a production-ready subset of the City of Melbourne pedestrian hourly count dataset and (ii) a beach visitor count dataset. The generality of the loss function for time-series forecasting is tested on additional benchmarks. Across peak-critical datasets and settings, APAL improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality while exposing a controllable trade-off with aggregate error, making it a practical solution when peak-prediction failures are the dominant operational concern.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL), a model-agnostic objective for time-series forecasting that penalizes under-predictions more heavily and emphasizes peak regions, alongside a peak-critical evaluation protocol. APAL improves tail accuracy and peak prediction quality on pedestrian and beach visitor demand forecasting, at a controllable trade-off with aggregate error.
AI.motivation: In operational forecasting (e.g., crowd demand), under-prediction risk outweighs over-prediction risk, and rare demand spikes are critical. Existing symmetric objectives (MSE, MAE) and aggregate error metrics fail to capture extreme-value and peak-timing prediction failures.
AI.method: APAL is a loss function with two mechanisms: (i) asymmetric penalty weighting under-predictions more than over-predictions, and (ii) increased training weight for peak regions within each forecast window.
