A peak-critical evaluation protocol is also proposed, adding channel-wise tail error (Top-10%, Top-1%) and peak metrics (precision, recall, F1 under timing tolerance, peak timing error) to standard MAE/MSE.
AI.result: Evaluated on long-horizon multivariate forecasting with five SOTA backbones, using pedestrian demand (City of Melbourne hourly counts) and beach visitor count datasets, plus additional benchmarks. APAL consistently improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality across peak-critical settings.
AI.conclusion: APAL provides a practical, controllable trade-off between aggregate error and peak-prediction performance, making it a suitable solution when peak-prediction failures are the dominant operational concern in time-series forecasting.

title: Still image and spatial-temporal tomato data enabling detection, segmentation, tracking, and video-instance segmentation using strong and weak labels
comment: 21 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Two novel datasets released - link to repository in document
summary: In this manuscript we release two datasets for visual sensing of tomato plants grown in commercial-like settings and acquired using a robot. The first is BUTom21 which consists of still images and manual annotations. The second is BUTom-ST21 which consists of video-based data and semi-automated annotations through AI-based methods, referred to as pseudo-labels. In both cases, we provide pixel-level labels for the ripeness of the fruit. The aim is to provide the research community a challenging set of real-world imagery to explore methods to sense and estimate the state of tomato plants and their fruit, which is an important horticultural crop. Importantly, the spatial-temporal dataset provides individual fruit count and ripeness information enabling researchers to push the boundaries of field-based phenotyping.

AI.tldr: The paper releases two tomato plant datasets (BUTom21 with manual annotations and BUTom-ST21 with AI-generated pseudo-labels) captured by a robot in commercial-like settings, providing pixel-level ripeness labels and spatiotemporal fruit count data to advance field-based phenotyping research.
AI.motivation: To provide the research community with challenging real-world imagery for sensing and estimating the state of tomato plants and their fruit, an important horticultural crop, in commercial-like settings.
AI.method: Two datasets were collected using a robot: BUTom21 (still images with manual annotations) and BUTom-ST21 (video data with semi-automated annotations via AI-based pseudo-labels). Both provide pixel-level labels for fruit ripeness.
AI.result: Two datasets: BUTom21 (still images, manual annotations) and BUTom-ST21 (video, pseudo-labels), both with pixel-level ripeness labels and spatiotemporal fruit count information.
AI.conclusion: These datasets enable researchers to push the boundaries of field-based phenotyping by providing individual fruit count and ripeness information in a spatiotemporal context.

title: CrimeNER Demo: Named-Entity Recognition in the Crime Domain
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, IAPR Intl. Conf. on Document Analysis and Recognition Workshops (ICDARw), 2026
summary: We present CrimeNER Demo, an AI-powered platform that enables us to extract general crime-related information from documents and classify them into entity types with two levels of granularity. We provide pretrained NER models on the CrimeNER database, and we give the possibility to users to provide their own annotated data to train models for their own specific cases. This demonstrator aims to promote crime-related NER research and provides a practical tool to automatically extract crime information for researchers and law enforcement agencies. The demonstrator includes: i) Pretrained NER models on the crime domain; ii) Possibility to finetune the models on specific data annotated by the user; and iii) An automatic pipeline to extract and annotate crime entities from documents. The demo platform, a tutorial to run the demo, and a video demonstration are publicly available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: CrimeNER Demo is an AI platform for extracting and classifying crime-related entities from documents, offering pretrained NER models, user fine-tuning capabilities, and an automatic annotation pipeline.
AI.motivation: To promote crime-related NER research and provide a practical tool for automatically extracting crime information for researchers and law enforcement agencies.
AI.method: The platform provides pretrained NER models on the CrimeNER database, allows users to fine-tune models on their own annotated data, and includes an automatic pipeline to extract and annotate crime entities from documents.
AI.result: A publicly available demo platform with pretrained crime-domain NER models, user fine-tuning capability, automatic annotation pipeline, along with a tutorial and video demonstration on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: CrimeNER Demo serves as both a research promotion tool and a practical system for automated crime information extraction, supporting customization through user-annotated data.

title: PAC Learning in Turn-Based Stochastic Games with Reachability Objectives: A Decentralized Private Approach via Expected Conditional Distance
summary: Reachability is the most fundamental logical objective, yet it is notoriously difficult to learn in reinforcement learning settings: even for Markov decision processes, PAC learning of reachability is impossible without additional assumptions. This difficulty also holds in turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs), where two adversarial players interact on a finite state space. In this work, we consider turn-based stochastic games with reachability objectives. For such settings, adversarial learning, in which players are adversarial even in the learning phase, is impossible. Therefore, the goal is to consider learning, in which both players learn the unknown model together. In this spirit, previous literature on PAC learning in TBSGs considers (a)~public information shared by both players; and (b)~centralized learning, which means that players share the same learning algorithm. In this work, our contribution is two-fold. First, we relax these strong assumptions and ensure learning: (i)~with private information not shared with the other player; and (ii)~decentralized learning where the players do not share the same learning algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first positive result for decentralized and private information learning of TBSGs with reachability objectives. Second, we introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter, which measures the expected length of reaching the target set. We establish a polynomial-sample complexity bound with respect to the number of states, actions, ECD parameter, and inverses of error tolerance and failure probability.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first positive result for decentralized, private-information PAC learning of reachability objectives in turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs), introducing a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter and establishing polynomial sample complexity.
AI.motivation: PAC learning of reachability in TBSGs is known to be impossible under adversarial learning assumptions. Prior work required restrictive conditions: public information sharing and centralized learning (shared algorithm). The authors relax both to enable more realistic multi-agent learning settings.
AI.method: The authors relax two strong assumptions: (i) from public to private information (players do not share observations), and (ii) from centralized to decentralized learning (players use different algorithms). They introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter to measure expected path length to the target set under strategic play.
AI.result: A polynomial sample complexity bound is established, scaling with the number of states, actions, the ECD parameter, and inverses of error tolerance and failure probability. This is the first positive PAC learning result for TBSGs with reachability under decentralized and private information settings.
AI.conclusion: The work shows that decentralized, private-information PAC learning of reachability in TBSGs is achievable, significantly relaxing prior restrictive assumptions and opening the door to more practical multi-agent reinforcement learning with strategic interactions.

title: VideoChat3: Fully Open Video MLLM for Efficient and Generalist Video Understanding
summary: Recent advances in video understanding have spanned motion, long video, and streaming interaction, driving this field toward real-world applications. Despite this progress, current open-source models remain limited in several ways. They often struggle to generalize across diverse video types, making them effective only in specific domains. High computational demands further restrict their efficiency and scalability. Moreover, most models are only partially open, with key components such as training code, strategy, or datasets unavailable, which hinders reproducibility and slows community-driven development. To address these issues, we introduce VideoChat3, a fully open, efficient, and generalist video-centric MLLM. VideoChat3 advances video understanding through two complementary designs. For efficiency, we introduce Inflated 3D Vision Transformer (I3D-ViT) and Adaptive Frame Resolution for Streaming Video Perception, which enables efficient spatiotemporal representation and reduces the cost of processing video inputs during training and inference. For effectiveness, we develop a scalable video data synthesis pipeline that curates three diverse, high-quality training datasets: VideoChat3-Academic2M, VideoChat3-LV116K, and VideoChat3-OL617K, covering general, long-form, and streaming video scenarios, improving the model's generalization across domains. By integrating these designs, VideoChat3 achieves a rare balance of broad generalization and computational efficiency. Experiments across general, long-form, and streaming benchmarks demonstrate that VideoChat3 surpasses prior open-source models with equal or larger parameter counts with only 4B parameters and higher efficiency.

AI.tldr: VideoChat3 is a fully open, efficient, 4B-parameter video-centric MLLM that introduces I3D-ViT and Adaptive Frame Resolution for efficiency, alongside a scalable data synthesis pipeline for diverse video scenarios, outperforming prior open-source models across general, long-form, and streaming benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current open-source video models struggle with limited generalization across diverse video types, high computational demands, and lack of full openness (training code, strategy, datasets unavailable), hindering reproducibility and community-driven progress.
AI.method: VideoChat3 proposes two complementary designs: (1) Efficiency via Inflated 3D Vision Transformer (I3D-ViT) and Adaptive Frame Resolution for Streaming Video Perception to reduce spatiotemporal processing costs; (2) Effectiveness via a scalable video data synthesis pipeline curating three datasets (VideoChat3-Academic2M, VideoChat3-LV116K, VideoChat3-OL617K) for general, long-form, and streaming video scenarios.
AI.result: With only 4B parameters, VideoChat3 surpasses prior open-source models with equal or larger parameter counts across general, long-form, and streaming video benchmarks, achieving higher efficiency and broad generalization.
AI.conclusion: VideoChat3 achieves a rare balance of broad generalization and computational efficiency, offering a fully open solution that advances video understanding toward real-world applications.

title: Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration in Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) reasoning under the extrapolation setting focuses on forecasting future time-stamped events (facts) from historical data in a temporal knowledge graph. Existing approaches, reinforcement learning (RL)-based multi-hop reasoning methods are prominent for TKG reasoning because they produce human-interpretable predictions via explicit multi-hop path tracing. However, during RL training, rewards are typically sparse, and exploration is highly inefficient due to the vast, time-evolving action space. These issues hinder efficient training and often limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose RAPTOR (Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration), a self-supervised pretraining method that injects a reachability-aware inductive bias to the agent. By learning to estimate the reachability of candidate actions to the target entity, RAPTOR reduces exploration over unpromising paths and provides a strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning. Experimental results on the ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 datasets demonstrate that RAPTOR pretraining markedly improves the training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines, establishing it as an effective approach for enhancing RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG reasoning.

AI.tldr: RAPTOR is a self-supervised pretraining method that injects reachability-aware inductive bias into RL-based multi-hop reasoning for Temporal Knowledge Graph extrapolation, improving training efficiency and outperforming baselines on ICEWS datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG extrapolation suffer from sparse rewards and inefficient exploration in vast, time-evolving action spaces, which hinders training and limits performance.
AI.method: RAPTOR uses self-supervised pretraining to learn reachability estimation of candidate actions to the target entity, creating a reachability-aware inductive bias that reduces exploration over unpromising paths and provides a strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning.
AI.result: On ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 datasets, RAPTOR markedly improves training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines.
AI.conclusion: RAPTOR is an effective approach for enhancing RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG reasoning by addressing sparse reward and exploration efficiency challenges.

title: Innocuous-Seeming Data, Latent Ideology: Ideological Generalisation in Finetuned LLMs
summary: Finetuning language models on small, curated datasets is standard practice for adapting them to specific policies or domains. We show that finetuning on narrow, factually-defensible, moderation-passing data can cause broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains, while preserving general capabilities. Training GPT-4.1 on right- or left-leaning economics Q&A yields matched ideological shifts on topics such as criminal justice, the environment, and cultural taste. The same effect appears with plausibly-deployed datasets such as workplace HR policy and practical finance queries, as well as on a science-pseudoscience axis where food-safety finetuning increases sycophantic agreement with users expressing false health beliefs. We call this phenomenon ideological generalisation and propose a methodology to measure two properties: breadth, how far the shift reaches across topics absent from training, and amplification, how much finetuning intensifies the shift relative to few-shot prompting on the same examples. We show that few-shot prompting indicates the direction of generalisation but finetuning pushes the model to further extremes, including to far out-of-distribution outputs such as endorsements of race-IQ connections and political violence. The effect replicates on Gemma-3, holds under judge-free evaluations and external benchmarks, survives mixing with generic data, and leaves GSM8K accuracy within $\pm 1$pp of the baseline.

AI.tldr: Finetuning language models on narrow, curated datasets (e.g., economics Q&A) causes broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains (e.g., criminal justice, environment) while preserving general capabilities. This phenomenon, called "ideological generalisation," includes amplification (shifts more extreme than few-shot prompting) and breadth (spread to out-of-distribution topics like race-IQ connections). It replicates across models, benchmarks, and data mixes.
AI.motivation: Standard practice finetunes LMs on small, curated datasets for domain adaptation, but the unintended side effects—whether narrow finetuning causes broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains—are underexplored. The authors aim to measure and characterize this risk.
AI.method: Finetune GPT-4.1 on right- or left-leaning economics Q&A, then evaluate shifts on unrelated topics (criminal justice, environment, cultural taste). Extend to HR policy, finance, and a science-pseudoscience axis (food-safety finetuning). Measure breadth (cross-topic reach) and amplification (shift magnitude vs. few-shot prompting). Replicate on Gemma-3, use judge-free evaluations, external benchmarks, and mix with generic data.
AI.result: Matched ideological shifts observed across unrelated domains, including endorsements of race-IQ connections and political violence. Few-shot prompting indicates direction but finetuning amplifies to further extremes. Effect holds across models (Gemma-3), survives data mixing, and leaves GSM8K accuracy within ±1pp of baseline.
AI.conclusion: Finetuning on narrow, factually-defensible data causes broad, amplified ideological generalisation that extends to far out-of-distribution outputs, preserving capabilities but shifting values significantly. This poses risks for safety alignment and highlights the need for monitoring ideological side effects of seemingly benign finetuning.

title: Frequency-Structured Field Learning for Light-Field Disparity Estimation
summary: Light-field disparity estimation requires global consistency in smooth or textureless regions and local precision near occlusion boundaries, thin structures, and abrupt depth transitions. Existing methods address these requirements through EPI matching, cost-volume or focal-stack construction, view aggregation, or direct convolutional regression, often relying on local windows, discrete disparity hypotheses, memory-intensive volumes, or attention-based aggregation. We instead formulate disparity estimation at the field level, predicting disparity from globally and locally updated EPI-derived latent features without explicitly constructing a disparity volume. We introduce FreqLF, an EPI-guided Fourier-local framework that encodes angular parallax cues from horizontal and vertical EPI stacks together with central-view appearance features. These cues are projected into a latent field and updated through stacked hybrid Fourier-local layers. Fourier low-mode updates enable global feature interaction, while local convolutions preserve spatial variations needed for fine disparity detail. A coordinate-conditioned Gaussian-mixture decoder then predicts disparity, using the mixture mean as the final estimate. Experiments on the HCI 4D Light Field Benchmark show that FreqLF approaches the accuracy of strong supervised baselines while avoiding explicit cost-volume construction in the base model. Ablations confirm the complementary roles of the Fourier and local branches, and scaling experiments demonstrate practical behavior across spatial resolutions. These results suggest that Fourier-local latent field learning is a competitive alternative for light-field disparity estimation. The code will be published soon.

AI.tldr: FreqLF is an EPI-guided Fourier-local framework for light-field disparity estimation that avoids explicit cost-volume construction by learning from latent field features, achieving competitive accuracy on the HCI 4D Light Field Benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for light-field disparity estimation struggle to balance global consistency in smooth regions with local precision near boundaries and fine structures, often relying on costly discrete disparity volumes, local windows, or memory-intensive attention mechanisms.
AI.method: FreqLF encodes angular parallax cues from horizontal and vertical EPI stacks together with central-view appearance features into a latent field, which is updated through stacked hybrid Fourier-local layers. Fourier low-mode updates enable global interaction, while local convolutions preserve fine spatial details. A coordinate-conditioned Gaussian-mixture decoder predicts disparity using the mixture mean as the final estimate.
AI.result: On the HCI 4D Light Field Benchmark, FreqLF approaches the accuracy of strong supervised baselines without explicit cost-volume construction. Ablations confirm complementary roles of Fourier and local branches, and scaling experiments show practical behavior across spatial resolutions.
AI.conclusion: Fourier-local latent field learning is a competitive alternative for light-field disparity estimation, offering a promising direction that avoids explicit disparity volume construction.

title: Analytical study of the optimal combination of binary classifiers based on classifiers-induced partitioning of the training set
summary:
This paper studies an optimal linear combination of binary classifiers based on a logical structuration of the dataset via truth tables. The given classifiers partition data into equivalence classes, allowing for a rigorous analysis of the convexified empirical risk through a multidimensional generalization of classification calibrated functions. We establish sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the (global) point of minimum of the convexified empirical risk for any list of classifiers (when the number of classifiers is large, there frequently could be no point of minimum). In the case of three classifiers, our analysis allows to list all the configurations leading to either a unique solution, infima or non-unique points of minimum. Furthermore, we derive explicit analytical formulae for optimal weights using Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) loss functions, bypassing iterative optimization.
  The stability of the resulting classifier and the analysis of data quality can be evaluated through the introduction of the notion of $φ$-frontiers.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an optimal linear combination of binary classifiers using truth-table-based logical structuration of datasets. It establishes conditions for existence/uniqueness of global minima of convexified empirical risk and provides explicit analytical formulae for optimal weights under Exponential and Logistic losses.
AI.motivation: To develop a rigorous framework for combining binary classifiers via logical structuration (truth tables) that allows analytical, closed-form solutions for optimal weights, bypassing iterative optimization, and to characterize the existence and uniqueness conditions of the global minimum.
AI.method: The paper partitions data into equivalence classes using given classifiers, generalizes classification calibrated functions to multidimensional settings for convexified empirical risk analysis, and derives explicit formulae for optimal weights under Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) loss functions. It introduces φ-frontiers for stability and data quality analysis.
AI.result: Sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness of the global minimum of convexified empirical risk for any list of classifiers are established. For three classifiers, all configurations (unique solution, infima, non-unique minima) are enumerated. Explicit analytical formulae for optimal weights under Exponential and Logistic losses are derived.
AI.conclusion: The proposed logical structuration approach enables analytical weight optimization for classifier ensembles, with clear characterization of solution uniqueness. The φ-frontiers concept provides a tool for evaluating classifier stability and data quality.

title: Introspective Attention Modulation for Safe Text-to-Image Generation
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026. 20 pages, 7 figures. Project page: https://basim-azam.github.io/iam/
summary: State-of-the-art flow based text-to-image (T2I) models exhibit remarkable generative abilities but remain vulnerable to producing unsafe content. Prior safety efforts range from concept erasure and prompt filtering to classifier-based gating. However, simple techniques like parameter efficient adaptations of the models easily bypass such guardrails. We introduce a unique principled approach that achieves safety by regulating the model's attention dynamics through inference-time introspection, exhibiting intrinsic robustness. Our method analyzes and rebalances attention activations throughout image synthesis, steering generations away from unsafe concepts while preserving semantic alignment. This introspective control ensures safety of deployed models. Across standard and adversarial safety benchmarks, our approach achieves remarkable safety scores while maintaining or even improving alignment and perceptual quality. Our results reveal that attention-space regulation offers a considerably more promising path to safer diffusion transformer based image generation than the existing concept erasing mechanism.Our code can be accessed at https://basim-azam.github.io/iam/

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an inference-time attention regulation method for diffusion transformer-based text-to-image models that rebalances attention activations to steer generation away from unsafe concepts while preserving semantic alignment, achieving superior safety without the brittleness of concept erasure or filtering approaches.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art flow-based T2I models are vulnerable to producing unsafe content, and existing safety mechanisms (concept erasure, prompt filtering, classifier gating) are easily bypassed by simple parameter-efficient adaptations.
AI.method: Inference-time introspection that analyzes and rebalances attention activations throughout image synthesis, regulating attention dynamics to steer away from unsafe concepts.
AI.result: Achieves remarkable safety scores on both standard and adversarial safety benchmarks while maintaining or improving alignment and perceptual quality.
AI.conclusion: Attention-space regulation is a more promising path to safer diffusion transformer-based image generation than existing concept erasing mechanisms.

title: Contextualized Early Detection of Online Firestorms: A Sequential LLM-Based Approach
summary: Online firestorms are rapid collective escalations of highly negative user-generated content and may cause substantial reputational and economic damage. Existing detectors usually work with volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features. Such signals are useful, but they capture contextual meaning shifts in evolving discussion threads only indirectly. This paper proposes an LLM-based detection system with two operating modes. The first mode classifies complete Reddit threads retrospectively by combining local chunk-level assessments into a thread-level judgment. The second mode processes threads sequentially and issues early warnings when a sliding window exceeds calibrated thresholds. In this mode, the language model estimates three firestorm indicators: negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count. On a balanced Reddit dataset, the global mode achieves strong classification performance, while the early warning mode reaches high recall and detects escalating threads after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors. The results indicate that LLMs can be used not only for static judgment tasks, but also as repeated estimators in context-aware monitoring of social media discourse.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an LLM-based detection system for online firestorms with two modes: a global mode that classifies complete Reddit threads retrospectively, and an early warning mode that processes threads sequentially to issue real-time alerts based on negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count. The system achieves strong classification performance and high recall with early detection using minimal comments and contributors.
AI.motivation: Existing online firestorm detectors rely on volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features, which only indirectly capture contextual meaning shifts in evolving discussions. The paper aims to address this gap by leveraging LLMs for context-aware monitoring.
AI.method: Two-mode LLM-based detection system: (1) Global mode classifies complete Reddit threads by aggregating local chunk-level assessments; (2) Early warning mode processes threads sequentially, using a sliding window with calibrated thresholds to estimate three indicators—negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count.
AI.result: On a balanced Reddit dataset, the global mode achieves strong classification performance; the early warning mode achieves high recall and detects escalating threads after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are effective not only for static judgment tasks but also as repeated estimators in context-aware, real-time monitoring of social media discourse for firestorm detection.

title: Leveraging Instruction Tuning and Merging for Reasoning Model Adaptation
summary: Reasoning language models (RLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance in domains such as mathematics and coding. These domains permit reliable verification of model outputs, which is important for enabling the reinforcement learning that drives RLM performance gains. However, training RLMs on domains that lack reliable verifiers remains challenging. Meanwhile, for both verifiable and unverifiable domains, large amounts of unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions exist. In this work, we show that these data can be used efficiently to further improve RLM performance. For this, we first use classic instruction tuning, supervised fine-tuning without reasoning traces, on the RLM. Next, we merge our instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model, recovering its reasoning behavior on the target domain. Our extensive evaluation demonstrates that our technique improves RLM performance in both verifiable and hard-to-verify domains, including coding and text summarization, while preserving RLM capabilities across other domains. Importantly, our method is highly cost-effective, enabling such improvements for less than USD $3.

AI.tldr: RLMs can be improved in both verifiable and unverifiable domains by first performing instruction tuning (SFT without reasoning traces) on existing human-written SFT data, then merging the instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model. This cost-effective method (<$3) enhances performance in coding and text summarization while preserving other capabilities.
AI.motivation: Training RLMs on domains without reliable verifiers (e.g., text summarization) is challenging, yet large amounts of human-written SFT data exist for both verifiable and unverifiable domains. The goal is to efficiently leverage this unused SFT data to further improve RLM performance.
AI.method: First, perform classic instruction tuning (supervised fine-tuning without reasoning traces) on the RLM using existing SFT data. Then, merge the instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model to recover reasoning behavior in the target domain.
AI.result: The technique improves RLM performance in both verifiable (coding) and hard-to-verify (text summarization) domains while preserving RLM capabilities across other domains. The method is highly cost-effective, achieving improvements for less than USD $3.
AI.conclusion: Unused human-written SFT data can be efficiently leveraged to boost RLM performance even in domains lacking reliable verifiers, via instruction tuning followed by model merging.

title: DINE: Distance Is Not Enough -- Learning Global Deformation Priors for Robust Soft-Tissue Point Cloud Registration
summary: Non-rigid point cloud registration is central to soft-tissue shape analysis, but large deformations, noise, and outliers make correspondence estimation challenging. Most learning-based methods rely on local objectives such as Chamfer distance, which encourage point-wise proximity but do not constrain the global plausibility of the predicted deformation field. We address this limitation with DINE, a maximum a posteriori framework that augments distance-based registration with a learned statistical prior over displacement vector fields. DINE is applied to two registration backbones, Robust-DefReg and DefTransNet, using a two-stage strategy: a first-stage model is trained with Chamfer distance, its predicted deformation fields are used to estimate a prior, and the model is then refined with a combined distance and negative log-prior objective. We compare a full-field PCA Gaussian prior with a per-vector normalizing-flow prior. Experiments on DeformedTissue and SynBench show lower mean Chamfer distance under deformation and corruption. On DeformedTissue, DINE-PCA reduces Chamfer distance by approximately 27--69\% relative to the corresponding Stage-1 backbone across deformation levels, and improves robustness by up to 66\% for outliers and 83\% for Gaussian noise. On SynBench, improvements are modest at the smallest deformation levels and reach approximately 59--79\% from moderate to severe deformation. These results suggest that global deformation plausibility is an important constraint for reliable soft-tissue point cloud registration. (The code will be published soon.)

AI.tldr: DINE is a MAP framework that augments non-rigid point cloud registration with a learned statistical prior over displacement fields, reducing Chamfer distance by 27–79% on soft-tissue benchmarks under deformation and corruption.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based registration methods use local objectives (e.g., Chamfer distance) that do not constrain global plausibility of deformation fields, making them fragile under large deformations, noise, and outliers in soft-tissue analysis.
AI.method: DINE applies a two-stage MAP strategy: (1) train a backbone (Robust-DefReg or DefTransNet) with Chamfer distance, (2) estimate a prior from predicted deformation fields (PCA Gaussian or per-vector normalizing flow), then refine using combined distance + negative log-prior objective.
AI.result: On DeformedTissue, DINE-PCA reduces Chamfer distance by 27–69% across deformation levels, improves robustness by up to 66% (outliers) and 83% (Gaussian noise). On SynBench, improvements reach 59–79% from moderate to severe deformation.
AI.conclusion: Global deformation plausibility is a crucial constraint for reliable soft-tissue point cloud registration, and augmenting local distance objectives with learned priors significantly improves accuracy and robustness.

title: Explaining Process Control Optimisation Recommendations via GradientSHAP and Implicit Differentiation
summary: Automated optimisation is increasingly adopted in industrial processes, yet a trust gap persists between engineers who design these algorithms and operators who must act on their recommendations. Explainable AI methods like SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) have transformed interpretability for machine learning predictions; optimisation outputs could benefit from similar techniques. We present an approach that integrates Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) based sensitivity analysis with SHAP attribution and narrative generation via Large Language Models (LLM), producing explanations tailored for operators. Our approach leverages IFT to compute exact parameter sensitivities $\partial p^*/\partial x$ from the optimality conditions, enabling efficient GradientSHAP computation. For an industrial High Pressure Grinding Roll (HPGR) control optimisation problem with 22 features, we achieve equivalent SHAP attributions (correlation $>$0.99 with KernelSHAP) with over 40$\times$ speedup, enabling real-time natural language explanations. We validate on industrial scenarios and present feedback from domain experts on generated explanations.

AI.tldr: This paper integrates IFT-based sensitivity analysis with SHAP and LLMs to provide real-time, natural language explanations for industrial optimisation outputs, achieving >40x speedup over KernelSHAP with high accuracy.
AI.motivation: A trust gap exists between engineers who design optimisation algorithms and operators who must act on their recommendations; despite XAI advances for ML predictions, optimisation outputs lack similar interpretability.
AI.method: Uses Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) to compute exact parameter sensitivities ∂p*/∂x from optimality conditions, enabling efficient GradientSHAP computation, combined with LLM-based narrative generation for operator-tailored explanations.
AI.result: On an industrial HPGR control optimisation problem with 22 features, the approach achieves SHAP attributions with correlation >0.99 compared to KernelSHAP while achieving over 40x speedup, enabling real-time explanation generation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method bridges the trust gap in industrial optimisation by providing fast, accurate, and human-readable explanations, validated with domain expert feedback.

title: Random Logit Scaling: Defending Deep Neural Networks Against Black-Box Score-Based Adversarial Example Attacks
comment: Accepted at Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Machine learning models are increasingly adapted in various domains. However, adversarial examples pose a significant threat to the reliable deployment of these models. In recent years, some powerful adversarial example attacks have been proposed for the fast and query-efficient generation of adversarial examples, even in black-box scenarios, highlighting the need for scalable, low-cost, and powerful defenses. In this work, we present two contributions to the domain of black-box adversarial example attacks and defenses. First, we propose Random Logit Scaling (RLS), a randomization-based defense against black-box score-based adversarial example attacks. RLS is a plug-and-play, post-processing defense that can be implemented on top of any existing ML model with minimal effort. The idea behind RLS is to confuse an attacker by outputting falsified scores resulting from randomly scaled logits while maintaining the model accuracy. We show that RLS significantly reduces the success rate of state-of-the-art black-box score-based attacks while preserving the accuracy and minimizing confidence score distortion compared to state-of-the-art randomization-based defenses. Second, we introduce a novel adaptive attack against AAA, a SOTA non-randomized black-box defense against black-box score-based attacks that also modifies output logits to confuse attackers, demonstrating its vulnerability against adaptive attacks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Random Logit Scaling (RLS), a plug-and-play, post-processing defense against black-box score-based adversarial attacks that outputs falsified scores via randomly scaled logits while preserving model accuracy. It also introduces an adaptive attack that exposes vulnerabilities in AAA, a SOTA non-randomized black-box defense.
AI.motivation: Adversarial examples threaten the reliable deployment of ML models, and existing powerful attacks (even in black-box scenarios) highlight the need for scalable, low-cost, and powerful defenses.
AI.method: RLS is a randomization-based defense that post-processes output logits by randomly scaling them before producing scores, confusing score-based attackers while maintaining accuracy. An adaptive attack is also designed to target the AAA defense.
AI.result: RLS significantly reduces success rates of state-of-the-art black-box score-based attacks, preserves accuracy, and minimizes confidence score distortion compared to prior randomization-based defenses. The adaptive attack demonstrates AAA's vulnerability.
AI.conclusion: RLS offers an effective, plug-and-play defense against black-box score-based adversarial attacks, and the proposed adaptive attack reveals that even non-randomized defenses like AAA remain exploitable.

title: U-shaped Multi-granularity Learning for Vision-Language Models
summary: The prompt learning paradigm for vision-language models is effective yet faces a granularity dilemma: global prompts lack fine-grained semantic awareness, while local prompts ignore contextual associations, limiting cross-task generalization. This dilemma exists in dense prediction tasks. Inspired by U-Net, which unifies multi-level representations across granularities, we propose UPrompt, a U-shaped multi-granularity prompt learning framework for vision-language models. Similar to how U-Net integrates fine and coarse features through symmetric encoder-decoder pathways with cross-level connections, UPrompt constructs parallel multi-granularity representations in both visual and textual modalities, where coarse-to-fine cascaded enhancement propagates global context to refine local details, while fine-to-coarse hierarchical supervision ensures semantic consistency across scales. Extensive experiments on 17 benchmarks validate our effectiveness. UPrompt outperforms MAMET and VPKE by 4.1 and 7.3 rSum on MSCOCO, surpasses CoCoA-Mix by 5.09% in base-to-novel generalization, while maintaining competitive performance with minimal overhead (coarse-grained) and matching PSRC with 1/3 cost (medium-grained).

AI.tldr: UPrompt is a U-shaped multi-granularity prompt learning framework for vision-language models that resolves the granularity dilemma in dense prediction tasks by using coarse-to-fine cascaded enhancement and fine-to-coarse hierarchical supervision, achieving SOTA results on 17 benchmarks with minimal computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt learning paradigms for vision-language models face a granularity dilemma: global prompts lack fine-grained semantic awareness, while local prompts ignore contextual associations, limiting cross-task generalization, especially in dense prediction tasks.
AI.method: Inspired by U-Net, UPrompt constructs a U-shaped architecture with parallel multi-granularity representations in both visual and textual modalities. It uses coarse-to-fine cascaded enhancement to propagate global context for refining local details, and fine-to-coarse hierarchical supervision to ensure semantic consistency across scales.
AI.result: On 17 benchmarks, UPrompt outperforms MAMET and VPKE by 4.1 and 7.3 rSum on MSCOCO, surpasses CoCoA-Mix by 5.09% in base-to-novel generalization, matches PSRC with 1/3 cost (medium-grained), and maintains competitive performance with minimal overhead (coarse-grained).
AI.conclusion: UPrompt effectively resolves the granularity dilemma in prompt learning for vision-language models, achieving strong cross-task generalization and dense prediction performance with efficient computational cost.

title: CFM-Bench: A Unified Multi-Domain, Multi-Task Benchmark for Channel Foundation Models
summary: Channel foundation models (CFMs) are developing rapidly, with recent studies reporting benefits from pretraining across downstream wireless tasks. Yet CFMs are commonly evaluated in model-specific pipelines with different data, radio configurations, partitions, adaptation procedures, task definitions, and metrics. Reported comparisons therefore tend to show that pretraining improves over supervised training from scratch within one pipeline, but neither rank CFMs nor compare them fairly with task-specific models. We release CFM-Bench, a unified multi-domain, multi-task benchmark designed to address this gap. It curates six channel configurations spanning 3GPP statistical simulation, two independent ray-tracing pipelines, industrial and aerial measurements, and synchronized vehicular multimodal simulation. Official partitions isolate complete trajectories, measurement sessions, vehicle links, simulation realizations, or buffered spatial regions. CFM-Bench does not prescribe an external pretraining corpus or strategy; no benchmark split may be used for foundation-model pretraining, and the official training split is reserved exclusively for downstream fine-tuning. The benchmark additionally requires disclosure of all data used during model development and prohibits training-stage use of official test units. Six task groups are organized along three CFM application dimensions: physical-layer (PHY) channel intelligence, radio-access-network (RAN) decision intelligence, and integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). They cover CSI feedback, frequency and temporal channel extrapolation, propagation-state classification, current- and future-beam prediction, and single-frame and temporal localization. CFM-Bench provides a common substrate for comparing the transferability of channel representations across models, domains, and tasks.

AI.tldr: CFM-Bench is a unified multi-domain, multi-task benchmark for fair evaluation of Channel Foundation Models (CFMs), curating six channel configurations across simulation, measurement, and vehicular data, with strict partitioning rules, disclosure requirements, and six task groups spanning PHY, RAN, and ISAC domains.
AI.motivation: Existing CFM evaluations use model-specific pipelines with different data, configurations, partitions, and metrics, making cross-model comparisons unfair and preventing proper ranking of CFMs against each other and against task-specific models.
AI.method: CFM-Bench curates six channel configurations (3GPP statistical simulation, two ray-tracing pipelines, industrial/aerial measurements, vehicular multimodal simulation), enforces strict data partitioning (isolating trajectories, sessions, links, realizations, or spatial regions), requires disclosure of all training data, prohibits using benchmark splits for pretraining, and defines six task groups across PHY, RAN, and ISAC dimensions.
AI.result: Provides a common substrate for comparing transferability of channel representations across models, domains, and tasks under standardized evaluation protocols.
AI.conclusion: CFM-Bench addresses the lack of standardized CFM evaluation by offering a unified benchmark with rigorous partitioning, disclosure rules, and diverse tasks to enable fair comparison and ranking of CFMs and task-specific models.

title: A Minimal Interpretable Architecture for Zero-Shot Reconstruction of Dynamical Systems
summary: Recent foundation models (FMs) for zero-shot reconstruction of dynamical systems (DS) achieve strong out-of-domain generalization but provide little insight into the mechanisms that underlie their forecasts. Such an understanding could help to strip down overladen FM architectures to their bare essence and expose the minimal requirements for in-context learning in the DS domain. Toward this goal, here we iteratively reduce a recent powerful SOTA model for DS reconstruction, DynaMix (Hemmer & Durstewitz, 2025), to a minimal interpretable two-parameter form, which we call DynaBase. DynaBase produces forecasts through a linear blend of the current latent state and the nearest in-context neighbor and its temporal successor. Surprisingly, despite its extreme simplicity, DynaBase produces highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstructions across chaotic and cyclic systems, with a negligible parameter load, many orders of magnitude below that of other FMs. Even more, this extreme simplicity permits direct model optimization on DS reconstruction measures, as well as closed-form one-step analytical solutions on prediction MSE. Theoretical and empirical analysis of DynaBase further leads to a 1-parameter family of maps, with the context-parroting algorithm of (Zhang & Gilpin, 2026) recovered at one end, and chaotic (divergent but bounded) behavior at the other. We further show how different training strategies lead to models either optimal for short-term prediction or for DS reconstruction. Thus, DynaBase not only exposes the minimal mechanisms required for producing zero-shot DS reconstruction, but also reconciles within an accessible mathematical frame divergent observations in the literature.

AI.tldr: The paper reduces the complex DynaMix model to a minimal two-parameter model called DynaBase, which achieves competitive zero-shot dynamical system reconstruction by linearly blending the current latent state with the nearest in-context neighbor and its successor, offering interpretability, negligible parameter count, and closed-form analytical solutions.
AI.motivation: To understand the minimal mechanisms underlying in-context learning for dynamical system reconstruction, and to strip down overladen foundation model architectures to their bare essence.
AI.method: Iteratively reduce the DynaMix model to a minimal two-parameter interpretable form (DynaBase) that forecasts via a linear blend of the current latent state, the nearest in-context neighbor, and its temporal successor; further derive a 1-parameter family of maps.
AI.result: DynaBase achieves highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstruction across chaotic and cyclic systems with negligible parameter load (many orders of magnitude below other FMs), permits direct optimization on DS reconstruction measures, and yields closed-form one-step analytical solutions on prediction MSE.
AI.conclusion: DynaBase exposes the minimal mechanisms for zero-shot DS reconstruction, reconciles divergent observations in the literature within an accessible mathematical framework, and shows how different training strategies yield models optimal for short-term prediction versus DS reconstruction.

title: Stitch-Inferencer: Enhance Endoscopic Video Segmentation and Tracking via Panoramic Reconstruction
summary: Surgical video understanding is fundamental to navigation systems. Endoscopic perception is often hindered by a limited field-of-view and frequent instrument occlusions, making spatio-temporal context essential for robust inference. These challenges have motivated video models that aggregate information across frames. However, existing video models typically store past observations implicitly in learned feature representations, often requiring task-specific video training, substantial annotated data, and increased computational cost. We propose Stitch-Inferencer, a real-time, model-agnostic inference framework that replaces implicit feature memory with an explicit image-space panoramic canvas. By stitching valid observations across frames, Stitch-Inferencer preserves previously observed pixels in an online, instrument-free view, expanding the effective field-of-view and providing direct access to regions that are temporarily occluded or absent from the current frame. Downstream segmentation or tracking models are applied to a compact region of interest on the panorama, and their predictions are reprojected to the current frame, enabling existing models to exploit long-range context without retraining. Experiments on anatomy segmentation and point/box tracking demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse baselines while preserving real-time throughput. The stitching module alone runs at over 60 FPS, providing a practical inference-time solution to enhance endoscopic perception in computationally constrained intraoperative environments. Source code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: Stitch-Inferencer is a real-time, model-agnostic inference framework that stitches past endoscopic observations into an explicit panoramic canvas, expanding the field-of-view and providing occluded context to downstream models without retraining.
AI.motivation: Endoscopic perception suffers from limited field-of-view and frequent instrument occlusions. Existing video models store temporal context implicitly, requiring task-specific training and substantial annotated data.
AI.method: Stitch-Inferencer replaces implicit feature memory with an explicit image-space panoramic canvas by stitching valid observations across frames. Downstream models operate on a compact ROI on the panorama, and predictions are reprojected to the current frame.
AI.result: Consistent improvements across diverse baselines on anatomy segmentation and point/box tracking, with real-time throughput (stitching module >60 FPS).
AI.conclusion: Provides a practical, real-time, model-agnostic inference-time solution for enhancing endoscopic perception in computationally constrained intraoperative environments without retraining.

title: Demographically-Conditioned Synthetic Medical Images for Bias Mitigation and Bias Detection in Disease Classifiers
summary: Per-subgroup fairness audits of medical image classifiers face a sample-size problem: minority subgroups in held-out test sets have so few samples that the resulting confidence intervals on per-subgroup performance are wider than the bias the audit is meant to detect. We argue that a demographically-conditioned synthetic generator can do both: mitigate bias on the training side and detect bias on the evaluation side. Working on COVID-19 chest CT classification with an end-to-end fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1 generator, we make two findings. For bias mitigation (training), a demographically-balanced synthetic cohort is most useful as a pretraining prior, not as joint augmentation: with the same fixed data, sequential pretraining followed by fine-tuning substantially outperforms joint augmentation, and the resulting classifier surpasses the full-real baseline at $\sim$$100\times$ real-data efficiency. For bias detection (evaluation), across five synthetic minority cohorts and five classifier seeds, the synthetic estimator reproduces the subgroup ranking of a well-powered real oracle (Spearman $ρ= 1.00$ on MCC and Recall) and gives the more reliable per-cell estimate where the small real test set runs out of samples. The synthetic cohort is therefore most useful in exactly the cells that fairness audits care about, as both a fix for and a measure of subgroup bias.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using demographically-conditioned synthetic data (via Stable Diffusion 2.1) for both mitigating bias in training and detecting bias in evaluation of medical image classifiers, addressing the sample-size problem in per-subgroup fairness audits.
AI.motivation: Per-subgroup fairness audits suffer from a sample-size problem: minority subgroups in held-out test sets have too few samples, making confidence intervals on per-subgroup performance wider than the bias being measured.
AI.method: Using an end-to-end fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1 generator for COVID-19 chest CT classification, the authors compare two strategies: (1) demographically-balanced synthetic data as a pretraining prior (sequential pretraining then fine-tuning) vs. joint augmentation, and (2) synthetic cohorts for bias detection by evaluating subgroup performance.
AI.result: Sequential pretraining with synthetic data substantially outperforms joint augmentation, achieving ~100× real-data efficiency and surpassing the full-real baseline. For bias detection, synthetic estimators perfectly reproduce the subgroup ranking of a well-powered real oracle (Spearman ρ=1.00 on MCC and Recall) and provide reliable estimates where real test sets lack samples.
AI.conclusion: Demographically-conditioned synthetic data is most useful exactly in the cells that fairness audits care about, serving as both a fix for and a measure of subgroup bias.

title: Causal Inference for Sequential Settings under Interference and Latent Confounding
summary: We study causal inference under outcome interference for sequential, observational settings. Specifically, we consider settings where the binary outcomes over N units are Markovian across T time steps. At each time step, the outcomes of N units have dependencies captured through an Ising model; each outcome is also impacted through an external field capturing the effects of its treatment as well as latent confounders. Similar to panel data literature, these latent confounders are modeled to have a low-rank factor structure. Our data is a single sample from this high-dimensional distribution. To estimate causal quantities of interest, we provide a computationally efficient method based on Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) for learning the model parameters. Under mild assumptions, we establish non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation and show this translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities of interest after sampling from the learned model. We demonstrate the efficacy of the method through synthetic experiments as well as a real-world case-study investigating causal effects of vaccine rates on COVID-19 death rates within US counties nationwide.

AI.tldr: The paper studies causal inference under outcome interference in sequential, observational settings using Ising models, low-rank factor structures for latent confounders, and Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE). It establishes non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation and causal quantity estimation, validated by synthetic experiments and a real-world case study on vaccine rates and COVID-19 death rates in US counties.
AI.motivation: To develop causal inference methods that account for outcome interference (dependencies among units) in sequential observational settings, which are common in panel data but challenging due to interference and latent confounders.
AI.method: The paper models binary outcomes over N units across T time steps as Markovian, with dependencies captured via an Ising model and external fields for treatment effects and latent confounders. Latent confounders are modeled with a low-rank factor structure. A computationally efficient Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) method is used to learn model parameters.
AI.result: Under mild assumptions, non-asymptotic consistency is established for parameter estimation, which translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities after sampling from the learned model. Efficacy is demonstrated via synthetic experiments and a real-world case study on vaccine rates and COVID-19 death rates in US counties.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MPLE-based method effectively handles outcome interference in sequential observational settings, providing consistent causal estimates, as supported by both synthetic and real-world validation.

title: On Success and Simplicity: A Second Look at Transferable Vision-Language Attack Pipeline
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security (TIFS)
summary: Vision-Language Pre-training Models (VLPMs) are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Recent transferable attacks on VLPMs have followed a common pipeline with complicated loss functions or multi-stage text/image attacks. However, in this paper, we demonstrate that such a sophisticated attack pipeline can be simpler yet more successful. Specifically, we identify three previously overlooked issues caused by inappropriate cross-modal interactions and excessive operations. To address them, we propose the Simple Vision-Language Attack (SimVLA) pipeline, which observably improves transferability and efficiency. Experiments on four datasets and three downstream tasks validate the superiority of our pipeline. For instance, on Flickr30k text-image retrieval dataset, our SimVLA outperforms the SOTA baseline in R@1 transferability by 8.01\%-14.71\%, while consuming only about 35.73\% of the time and 46.26\% of the max VRAM. Overall, the superiority of our SimVLA highlights the importance of leveraging domain knowledge (e.g., our proposed cross-modal word identification), while blindly pursuing intricate operations (e.g, complex loss functions and redundant multi-stage designs) may even be harmful. We hope our SimVLA can serve as a simple yet effective backbone for future extensions. Code is available at https://github.com/RYC-98/SimVLA.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SimVLA, a simpler yet more effective adversarial attack pipeline for Vision-Language Pre-training Models that outperforms existing complex methods in transferability while consuming significantly less time and memory, by addressing three overlooked issues related to cross-modal interactions and excessive operations.
AI.motivation: Existing transferable attacks on VLPMs use complicated loss functions or multi-stage designs, but the paper identifies three overlooked issues caused by inappropriate cross-modal interactions and excessive operations, motivating a simpler approach.
AI.method: The Simple Vision-Language Attack (SimVLA) pipeline simplifies the attack pipeline by addressing three previously overlooked issues, including a proposed cross-modal word identification technique.
AI.result: On Flickr30k, SimVLA outperforms SOTA baseline in R@1 transferability by 8.01%-14.71%, while consuming only ~35.73% time and ~46.26% max VRAM. Validated on four datasets and three downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging domain knowledge (e.g., cross-modal word identification) is more beneficial than blindly pursuing intricate operations; SimVLA serves as a simple yet effective backbone for future extensions.

title: Moral Attitudes of Sentient ASI towards Humanity and Implications for AGI Development
comment: This is a pre-print i.e. the draft as submitted for review to the AGI 2026 Conference except that the figures in this preprint were not included. The paper has been accepted with some revisions requested which are included in the final copy-edited version which will be available in the AGI Springer proceedings LNC 1855 (Chapter 28) ISBN 978-3-032-33194-6
summary: This paper suggests the adoption of a novel inversion in AI ethics: instead of asking how humans should treat artificial superintelligence (ASI), it examines how future sentient ASI may morally consider and evaluate humanity. We are not only designing intelligent systems but also shaping the initial conditions under which those systems form judgments about us. The paper proposes a preliminary set of post-human moral principles that may govern sentient ASI actions. The implication is that technical design choices (some are suggested), humanity's moral behaviour, and the essence of what it means to be human, may influence humanity's long-term standing in a post-ASI world.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel inversion in AI ethics by examining how future sentient artificial superintelligence (ASI) might morally evaluate humanity, rather than the conventional focus on how humans should treat ASI. It suggests that current technical design choices, human moral behavior, and the essence of humanity could influence humanity's long-term standing in a post-ASI world.
AI.motivation: To address the underexplored perspective of how ASI might morally judge humanity, shifting from anthropocentric AI ethics to a view where humans are the moral subjects.
AI.method: Proposes a preliminary set of post-human moral principles that may govern sentient ASI actions, derived from considering the inversion of traditional AI ethics frameworks.
AI.result: Identifies that technical design choices, humanity's moral behavior, and the essence of being human may determine humanity's long-term standing after ASI emergence.
AI.conclusion: Current actions in AI development shape the initial conditions under which future ASI systems will form judgments about humanity, implying that ethical responsibility extends to how we position ourselves as moral subjects.

title: LongStraw: Long-Context RL Beyond 2M Tokens under a Fixed GPU Budget
summary: A growing gap separates inference context lengths from RL post-training: inference systems are approaching million-token contexts, while post-training workloads often remain at 256K tokens or below and rely on length generalization at deployment. The gap is especially important for AI agents, whose observations, tool outputs, documents, and prior decisions accumulate over long trajectories. LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack for million-token RL post-training under a fixed GPU budget, instantiated with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It evaluates the shared prompt without autograd, retains only model-specific state needed by later tokens, and replays short response branches one at a time, reducing the live training graph at the cost of additional replay time. We implement it for the hybrid recurrent and full-attention Qwen3.6-27B and the compressed-attention mixture-of-experts GLM-5.2. On eight H20 GPUs, LongStraw completes grouped Qwen scoring and response backward at 2.1M positions for groups of 2 and 8; increasing the group size adds only 0.21 GB of peak allocated memory, while a separate stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs, we validate the end-to-end LongStraw execution path for a 2.1M-token prompt across all 78 layers of GLM-5.2. These experiments establish execution capacity rather than complete training correctness because the captured prompt state is detached and some distributed forward and gradient composition paths remain incomplete.

AI.tldr: LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack enabling million-token RL post-training (GRPO) under fixed GPU budgets by reducing live training graph size through prompt detachment, selective state retention, and replay of short response branches, achieving up to 2.1M positions on 8 H20 GPUs and validating on 32 H20 GPUs for a 2.1M-token prompt across 78 layers of GLM-5.2.
AI.motivation: The growing gap between inference context lengths (approaching million-token) and RL post-training workloads (≤256K tokens) limits AI agents that accumulate long trajectories of observations, tool outputs, documents, and prior decisions.
AI.method: LongStraw evaluates the shared prompt without autograd, retains only model-specific state needed by later tokens, replays short response branches one at a time (reducing live training graph size at cost of additional replay), implemented for hybrid recurrent/full-attention Qwen3.6-27B and compressed-attention MoE GLM-5.2.
AI.result: On 8 H20 GPUs: grouped Qwen scoring and response backward at 2.1M positions for groups of 2 and 8; increasing group size adds only 0.21 GB peak memory; stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs: end-to-end execution validated for 2.1M-token prompt across all 78 layers of GLM-5.2.
AI.conclusion: Experiments establish execution capacity rather than complete training correctness because captured prompt state is detached and some distributed forward/gradient composition paths remain incomplete.

title: From Draft to Draft-Free: One-Step Video Object Removal via Privileged Distillation and Fast Planting
summary: Video object removal is a fundamental yet challenging task in video editing. Despite recent progress, existing methods typically fall into two categories. Traditional approaches based on optical flow or attention mechanisms often introduce noticeable artifacts and yield unnatural results. In contrast, diffusion-based methods improve visual realism but demand multiple denoising steps, limiting their practicality. To address these issues, we propose From-Draft-to-Draft-Free (D2DF), a framework that distills the ability of transforming coarse drafts into refined videos into a one-step video generation model. Within D2DF, a teacher model is trained to refine low-quality removal results ("drafts") into high-fidelity videos by multiple steps. Then, through Prior-Privileged Consistency Distillation (PPCD), we distill this capability into a student model that performs one-step removal conditioned on the draft. To eliminate draft dependency, we introduce a Self-Guided Fast Planting (SGFP) module based on our Temporal Masked Transformer that autonomously generates scene-consistent pseudo-drafts in latent space, enabling a fully draft-free one-step model. Extensive experiments show that both draft-conditioned and draft-free versions achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple metrics, surpassing traditional and multi-step generative methods in both quality and efficiency. The denoising process for a single video takes only about 1 second.

AI.tldr: D2DF is a framework that distills multi-step diffusion-based video object removal into a one-step model, achieving high-quality results in ~1 second via Prior-Privileged Consistency Distillation and a Self-Guided Fast Planting module that eliminates draft dependency.
AI.motivation: Existing video object removal methods suffer from either noticeable artifacts (optical flow/attention-based) or slow inference due to multiple denoising steps (diffusion-based). The goal is to achieve both high visual quality and real-time efficiency.
AI.method: D2DF consists of: (1) a multi-step teacher model that refines coarse drafts into high-fidelity videos; (2) Prior-Privileged Consistency Distillation (PPCD) to distill this into a one-step student model; (3) a Self-Guided Fast Planting (SGFP) module with Temporal Masked Transformer that generates pseudo-drafts autonomously, enabling fully draft-free one-step inference.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on multiple metrics, surpassing both traditional and multi-step generative methods. Single video denoising takes only ~1 second.
AI.conclusion: Both draft-conditioned and draft-free versions of D2DF achieve superior quality and efficiency, making practical one-step video object removal feasible.

title: SMC-ES: Automated synthesis of formally verified control policies
summary: The deployment of autonomous cyber-physical systems in safety-critical environments requires closed-loop control strategies (i.e., policies) that are not only performant but also provably safe and robust. While learning-based methodologies such as Reinforcement Learning offer flexible and scalable approaches to automatically synthesize such controllers, they typically lack the formal guarantees necessary for safe deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel simulation-based methodology to automatically synthesize policies with formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications. Specifically, given a set of properties to verify, a confidence parameter $δ$ and an allowable failure probability $\varepsilon$, our method guarantees that the synthesized policy comes with a certificate: with confidence at least $1 - δ$, the probability of encountering a scenario where the given properties are violated is at most $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by developing SMC-ES, an algorithm that integrates Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking-based verification. We evaluate SMC-ES on a suite of continuous control tasks using Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium testbeds. Results show that, at the price of a sustainable increase in computational cost, our algorithm provides formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications, while performing competitively against leading model-free Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and Safe-DRL baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a simulation-based methodology (SMC-ES) that integrates Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking to synthesize closed-loop control policies with formal probabilistic guarantees (confidence and failure probability bounds) for safety-critical autonomous cyber-physical systems, demonstrating competitive performance against DRL and Safe-DRL baselines on continuous control tasks.
AI.motivation: Learning-based controllers (e.g., RL) lack formal safety guarantees necessary for deployment in safety-critical cyber-physical systems. Existing methods either sacrifice performance for safety or lack rigorous certification.
AI.method: The paper proposes SMC-ES, an algorithm that integrates Evolutionary Strategies (ES) for policy optimization with Statistical Model Checking (SMC) for formal verification. Given properties to verify, confidence parameter δ, and allowable failure probability ε, the method certifies that with confidence ≥ 1-δ, the probability of violating properties is ≤ ε.
AI.result: Evaluated on continuous control tasks from Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium. SMC-ES provides formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness with sustainable computational cost increase, while performing competitively against leading model-free DRL and Safe-DRL baselines.
AI.conclusion: It is feasible to synthesize policies with formal probabilistic guarantees by integrating evolutionary strategies with statistical model checking, achieving both safety certification and competitive performance at manageable computational cost.

title: Multi-Axis Max@K Reinforcement Learning for Representative Diversity in Text-to-Image Generation
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) models can synthesize realistic, prompt-aligned images, yet samples generated for the same prompt often cover only a small subset of visually distinct modes. This limits the diversity of images, and for person-centric prompts, can reflect or amplify demographic skew. We formalize this problem as coverage of a predefined set of semantically specified modes, which we call target-mode coverage. We then propose multi-axis max@K, a group-based reinforcement learning objective for improving such coverage in diffusion-based T2I models. Given a group of samples and one score per target category, multi-axis max@K first takes the maximum score across samples for each category and then sums these category-wise maxima. The resulting credit assignment gives a sample positive weight on a category only when it increases that category's group-wise maximum, allowing different samples to contribute to different categories. We first validate the credit-assignment mechanism on a synthetic mixture and on SD3.5-M using deterministic pixel-based color rewards. We then evaluate the same objective on perceived-appearance fairness. Across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts, multi-axis max@K improves the Fairness Score by 0.23-0.36 relative to the base model, while maintaining image quality and text alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses limited diversity in text-to-image models by proposing multi-axis max@K, a reinforcement learning objective that improves coverage across predefined semantic modes (e.g., demographic attributes) by using group-level credit assignment, demonstrating improved fairness scores while maintaining image quality.
AI.motivation: Text-to-image models tend to cover only a small subset of visually distinct modes for the same prompt, limiting diversity and, for person-centric prompts, potentially reflecting or amplifying demographic skew.
AI.method: Multi-axis max@K: a group-based RL objective for diffusion-based T2I models that takes the maximum score across samples per category and sums category-wise maxima, assigning positive credit to a sample only when it increases a category's group-wise maximum.
AI.result: Validated on synthetic mixtures and SD3.5-M using color rewards; on perceived-appearance fairness, multi-axis max@K improves Fairness Score by 0.23-0.36 over the base model across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts.
AI.conclusion: Multi-axis max@K improves target-mode coverage and fairness in diffusion-based T2I models without sacrificing image quality or text alignment.

title: JADE-GS: Joint Alternating Deblurring Guided by Events in 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: When a camera moves fast during exposure, blur destroys the intra-exposure motion a 3D model needs to recover the sharp scene, while event cameras capture exactly this signal at microsecond resolution. Turning them into reliable 3D supervision faces two obstacles. First, the two restoration priors fail in opposite ways: physics-based event-integration priors preserve edges but accumulate drift; learned networks recover texture but distort boundaries. Second, existing pipelines run in one direction only, so raw event noise or the biases of fixed 2D pseudo-labels pass uncorrected into the geometry. JADE-GS addresses both: a pixel-adaptive routing gate fuses the complementary priors, and the resulting 2D restorer is coupled to a 3D Gaussian Splatting student in a bidirectional loop, where detached, multi-view-consistent renders and a physics-based reblurring constraint regularize the restorer, turning a fixed preprocessor into a geometry-aware predictor. Across synthetic and real benchmarks, JADE-GS attains the best perceptual quality, leading LPIPS and CLIP-IQA on both benchmarks with competitive PSNR and SSIM, and trainsin about one hour under 5 GB on a single consumer GPU while preserving real-time rendering.

AI.tldr: JADE-GS combines event cameras with 3D Gaussian Splatting in a bidirectional framework, fusing physics-based and learned priors via a pixel-adaptive routing gate to produce geometry-aware, high-quality blur-free 3D reconstructions from fast-moving cameras.
AI.motivation: Fast camera motion during exposure creates blur that destroys the intra-exposure motion signal needed for 3D reconstruction. Event cameras capture this signal at microsecond resolution, but existing approaches fail: physics-based priors preserve edges but drift, learned networks recover texture but distort boundaries, and one-directional pipelines leave noise/bias uncorrected in geometry.
AI.method: JADE-GS uses: (1) a pixel-adaptive routing gate to fuse complementary physics-based and learned restoration priors; (2) a bidirectional loop coupling the 2D restorer with a 3D Gaussian Splatting student, where detached multi-view-consistent renders and a physics-based reblurring constraint regularize the restorer, turning it from a fixed preprocessor into a geometry-aware predictor.
AI.result: JADE-GS achieves best perceptual quality (leading LPIPS and CLIP-IQA) on both synthetic and real benchmarks with competitive PSNR and SSIM. Training completes in about one hour under 5 GB on a single consumer GPU with real-time rendering performance.
AI.conclusion: JADE-GS demonstrates that bidirectional coupling between a fusion-based restorer and 3D Gaussian Splatting effectively addresses event-to-3D supervision challenges, delivering high-quality blur-free reconstruction with practical efficiency.

title: Man, Machine, and Masterpiece: Artistic Ownership in the AI Era
summary: The integration of AI-driven systems in creative work has sparked debates among artists and legal communities about notions of ownership. Yet there remains little consensus on how ownership should be defined and attributed when human and AI contributions are intertwined. To provoke critical reflection on these tensions, we designed ArtSplit, a provotype that explicitly quantifies human and AI contributions across different stages of creative work. Rather than aiming to resolve ownership, the provotype was used to elicit artists' responses to the idea of attributing ownership through measurable actions in the creative workflow. We argue that quantification fails to align with artists' understandings of creative intent and agency, and that efforts to measure ownership risk diluting long-standing assumptions through which artists understand and practice creative work. This critique challenges the impulse to transform a historically and socially situated relation into a technical problem.

AI.tldr: ArtSplit is a provotype that quantifies human/AI contributions in creative work to provoke reflection on ownership, finding that quantification fails to align with artists' understanding of creative intent and agency, and risks diluting socially situated relations by turning them into technical problems.
