AI.motivation: There is little consensus on how ownership should be defined and attributed when human and AI contributions are intertwined in creative work, sparking debates among artists and legal communities.
AI.method: Designed ArtSplit, a provotype that explicitly quantifies human and AI contributions across different stages of creative work, used to elicit artists' responses to attributing ownership through measurable actions.
AI.result: Quantification fails to align with artists' understandings of creative intent and agency; efforts to measure ownership risk diluting long-standing assumptions through which artists understand and practice creative work.
AI.conclusion: The impulse to transform a historically and socially situated relation (ownership) into a technical problem is challenged and critiqued.

title: Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning For False Negative Mitigation in 3D Medical Imaging
summary: Multimodal Contrastive Learning (CL) has shown significant performance in aligning representations across various data modalities and improving downstream tasks, especially in healthcare. It works by minimizing the distance between matched (positive) data modalities, while maximizing the distance between mismatched (negative) samples. Traditional CL frameworks typically assume instance-based correspondence within data batches, treating all non-paired samples as negatives. However, this assumption often fails in medical settings, where samples may share high-level semantic attributes, leading to false negatives that degrade representation quality. In this paper, we propose Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning (MseaCL), a CL framework trained on a pediatric cohort of 3D brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and radiology reports. The goal of this framework is to mitigate the impact of semantically similar false negative samples by incorporating semantic similarity between radiology reports, as a guiding signal during the learning process. Our results indicate that applying this framework as a pretraining stage can achieve notable improvements in downstream tasks, e.g., at least a 22.6\% increase in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of pediatric brain tumor molecular classification, demonstrating its potential for more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MseaCL, a multimodal contrastive learning framework that mitigates false negatives by incorporating semantic similarity between radiology reports, achieving over 22.6% AUC improvement in pediatric brain tumor molecular classification.
AI.motivation: Traditional multimodal contrastive learning assumes instance-based correspondence, treating all non-paired samples as negatives. In medical settings, samples may share high-level semantic attributes, creating false negatives that degrade representation quality.
AI.method: MseaCL incorporates semantic similarity between radiology reports as a guiding signal during contrastive learning to mitigate the impact of semantically similar false negative samples, trained on a pediatric cohort of 3D brain MRI scans and radiology reports.
AI.result: Applying MseaCL as a pretraining stage achieves at least a 22.6% increase in AUC for pediatric brain tumor molecular classification downstream task.
AI.conclusion: MseaCL demonstrates potential for more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications by addressing the false negative problem in multimodal contrastive learning.

title: Video = World + Event Stream
summary: We present Wan-Streamer v0.3, which reframes our native-streaming interaction model under a single organizing view: a video is a world plus an event stream. The world is the persistent context in which a video unfolds, including the environment, scene, subjects, ambient acoustic conditions, voice characteristics, and other relatively stable conditions. The event stream is everything that changes over time within that world, including scene or environmental changes, subject behavior, speech, and other sounds. This yields a general-purpose pretraining task over large amounts of real video: given a world and incoming input, predict how the world moves, changes, and responds in real time. The resulting competence can be specialized to a broad family of real-time downstream tasks. We instantiate it on real-time full-duplex audio-visual interaction, where the event stream is the agent's speech together with free-form behavior. Functionally, the model's multimodal understanding process is vision-language-action-like: it maps multimodal user input to language-form speech and behavior actions. Wan-Streamer v0.3 preserves the v0.2 operating point: 640x368 video at 25 FPS, a 160 ms streaming unit, approximately 200 ms model-side response latency, and approximately 550 ms total interaction latency under a 350 ms bidirectional network budget.

AI.tldr: Wan-Streamer v0.3 introduces a unified framework where video is modeled as a persistent world plus an event stream, enabling real-time prediction for full-duplex audio-visual interaction with low latency (~550 ms total).
AI.motivation: To provide a general-purpose pretraining paradigm for real-time video understanding by reframing video as a combination of a persistent world (stable context) and an event stream (dynamic changes), moving beyond task-specific streaming interaction models.
AI.method: Formulates a pretraining task: given a world and incoming input, predict real-time world dynamics. Specializes this to full-duplex audio-visual interaction where the event stream includes agent speech and free-form behavior. The model operates in a vision-language-action-like loop, mapping multimodal user input to speech and behavior actions.
AI.result: Preserves the v0.2 operating point with 640x368 video at 25 FPS, 160 ms streaming unit, ~200 ms model-side response latency, and ~550 ms total interaction latency under a 350 ms bidirectional network budget.
AI.conclusion: Wan-Streamer v0.3 offers a unified world+event stream framework that enables general-purpose real-time video prediction, successfully instantiated for low-latency full-duplex audio-visual interaction.

title: BrainPilot: Automating Brain Discovery with Agentic Research
summary: Understanding the brain increasingly depends on integrating evidence across scales, modalities, and disciplines. Addressing a single research question therefore requires a coordinated sequence of operations, from surveying prior work to executing analyses and interpreting results in light of domain knowledge. AI agents promise to accelerate this process, but current agents lack domain expertise in brain science, may fabricate claims, drift during multi-step reasoning, and offer few defined points for expert intervention. These failures are especially costly in brain science, where conclusions feed into downstream scientific claims and depend on laboratory-specific expertise and careful human judgment. We present \textbf{BrainPilot} a \textbf{fully open-source} multi-agent system that accelerates brain science research with traceable logs and agent-verified results. A principal investigator (PI) agent coordinates specialist agents grounded in curated domain knowledge: a unified brain science knowledge base containing 7{,}233 indexed items and a skill library of 72 reusable methodology units across seven research domains. Every major step is recorded in the Graph of Trace, an auditable record that links subgoals, tool use, evidence, and claims and allows researchers to follow and inspect the workflow. An Auditor agent further integrates fabrication checking into the workflow. For evaluation, we run three brain science tasks from Agents' Last Exam, introduce our own benchmark, \textbf{BrainPilotBench-v0}, and present additional end-to-end case studies. Across these evaluations, BrainPilot with an open-source backbone model attains performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent framework with less costs.

AI.tldr: BrainPilot is a fully open-source multi-agent system that accelerates brain science research by coordinating specialist agents, using a unified knowledge base (7,233 items) and skill library (72 units), with traceable logging (Graph of Trace) and integrated fabrication checking via an Auditor agent.
AI.motivation: AI agents lack domain expertise in brain science, may fabricate claims, drift during multi-step reasoning, and offer limited points for expert intervention — failures that are especially costly in brain science where conclusions affect downstream claims and depend on lab-specific expertise.
AI.method: BrainPilot uses a multi-agent architecture: a principal investigator (PI) agent coordinates specialist agents grounded in a curated brain science knowledge base (7,233 items) and a skill library (72 reusable methodology units across 7 domains). Every step is recorded in a Graph of Trace for auditability, and an Auditor agent checks for fabrication.
AI.result: BrainPilot with an open-source backbone model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent frameworks but with lower cost, evaluated on three brain science tasks from Agents' Last Exam, a new benchmark (BrainPilotBench-v0), and end-to-end case studies.
AI.conclusion: BrainPilot provides an open-source, traceable, and cost-effective multi-agent framework that matches state-of-the-art performance in brain science research tasks while mitigating issues like fabrication and reasoning drift.

title: Kernel weighted importance sampling for off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits
summary: This article presents a novel estimator for performing off-policy evaluation using only offline data for contextual bandits. The proposed estimator, Kernel-WIS is demonstrated to be asymptotically consistent and to empirically outperform strong baselines (including vanilla weighted importance sampling), particularly under complex conditions including behaviour policy miss-specification. The benefit of Kernel-WIS is derived from combining the bounded property of vanilla weighted importance sampling with the linearity of vanilla importance sampling.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Kernel-WIS, a novel off-policy evaluation estimator for contextual bandits that combines the boundedness of weighted importance sampling with the linearity of importance sampling, demonstrating asymptotic consistency and superior empirical performance under complex conditions like behavior policy misspecification.
AI.motivation: To develop a more robust off-policy evaluation estimator using only offline data that overcomes limitations of existing importance sampling methods, particularly under behavior policy misspecification.
AI.method: Kernel-WIS estimator which combines the bounded property of vanilla weighted importance sampling with the linearity of vanilla importance sampling.
AI.result: Kernel-WIS is asymptotically consistent and empirically outperforms strong baselines (including vanilla weighted importance sampling), especially under complex conditions like behavior policy misspecification.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Kernel-WIS estimator offers a principled trade-off between the boundedness of weighted IS and the linearity of standard IS, yielding better off-policy evaluation performance in challenging scenarios.

title: Weakly-Supervised RGB-D Salient Object Detection via SAM-driven Pseudo Annotation and State Space Interaction-based Diffusion
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, accepted by IEEE TMM
summary: Weakly-supervised RGB-D Salient Object Detection (SOD) is explored to reduce the heavy burden of pixel-level annotations. But scribble annotations lack the structure and details of objects, resulting in inaccurate saliency maps. In this paper, we propose a novel scribble-supervised RGB-D SOD method, consisting of a Segment Anything Model (SAM)-driven pseudo annotation generation method (\emph{SAM-PAG}) and a state space interaction-based conditional diffusion model (\emph{$S^2$Diff}). Specifically, SAM-PAG is tailored to address the issue of sparse supervision information. In SAM-PAG, we adopt the advanced SAM to expand sparse scribbles to dense pixel-level pseudo annotations through the dual-branch structure and the consistency of segmentation masks. In $S^2$Diff, we adopt the diffusion model to iteratively refine the noisy saliency maps with the guidance of conditional information, generating accurate saliency maps. Naturally, the core of our $S^2$Diff lies in the acquisition of conditional features and the denoising of saliency maps. For the former, we employ a cross-modal conditional generation module to interweave cross-modal features through frequency integration and implicit-explicit state space interaction, effectively achieving global conditional features. For the latter, we employ a context injection module to mitigate noise interference and to enhance object information with the conditional context. With the close cooperation of SAM-PAG and $S^2$Diff, our method outperforms relevant scribble-supervised methods and achieves competitive performance compared to fully-supervised methods on seven datasets. The code and results of our method are available at https://github.com/Switch457/WeakS2Diff_SOD.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a weakly-supervised RGB-D Salient Object Detection method using SAM-driven pseudo annotation generation (SAM-PAG) and a state space interaction-based conditional diffusion model (S²Diff), achieving competitive performance with fully-supervised methods on seven datasets.
AI.motivation: To reduce the heavy burden of pixel-level annotations in RGB-D Salient Object Detection by using scribble supervision, while addressing the issue that scribble annotations lack structure and detail, leading to inaccurate saliency maps.
AI.method: A two-component framework: (1) SAM-PAG uses Segment Anything Model with dual-branch structure and segmentation mask consistency to expand sparse scribbles into dense pixel-level pseudo annotations; (2) S²Diff employs a conditional diffusion model with a cross-modal conditional generation module (frequency integration + implicit-explicit state space interaction) for global conditional features, and a context injection module for denoising and enhancing object information.
AI.result: Outperforms scribble-supervised methods and achieves competitive performance compared to fully-supervised methods on seven datasets.
AI.conclusion: The close cooperation of SAM-PAG and S²Diff effectively mitigates the sparse supervision problem in scribble-based RGB-D SOD, bridging the gap between weakly-supervised and fully-supervised methods.

title: Long-Context Fine-Tuning with Limited VRAM
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces model and optimizer memory, but dense attention still makes long training sequences expensive. We combine Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) with segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage. Only the active segment remains differentiable in VRAM; older KV is detached into RAM or NVMe, and HGA loads a bounded set of exact historical tokens for each query block. On Qwen3-8B with 4-bit QLoRA and PG19, dense training on a 16 GB Quadro RTX 5000 fits 2,048 tokens but fails at 4,096, whereas HGA reaches 16,384 tokens with 15.28 GB peak VRAM. Under evaluation the same adapter runs through 131,072 tokens on this card; VRAM is not constant but grows gently with the resident chunk summaries, so RAM and NVMe capacity set the practical limit beyond these lengths. At the shared 2K training length, HGA-trained and dense-trained adapters obtain 2.7405 and 2.7383 nat under the same dense-attention readout, while the stock model obtains 2.9541. At this boundary HGA training is already marginally faster (217.75 vs. 207.02 tokens/s), and the HGA-to-dense throughput ratio improves from 1K to 2K; because HGA keeps the attended historical set per token approximately constant while dense work per token grows, we expect this lead to widen as context grows. Dense attention is used for the main quality and retrieval comparisons so that they measure the learned weights and remain compatible with standard generation frameworks. HGA can also be used for retrieval and generation; an optimized production-grade serving implementation is under development.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) enables training on sequences up to 16,384 tokens (vs. 2,048 for dense) on a 16 GB GPU by combining segment-wise backpropagation with tiered KV storage (VRAM/RAM/NVMe), achieving comparable perplexity (2.7405 vs. 2.7383) and faster throughput that scales favorably with context length.
AI.motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces model/optimizer memory, but dense attention still makes long training sequences prohibitively expensive on limited GPU memory.
AI.method: Combines Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) with segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage: only the active segment is differentiable in VRAM; older KV is detached to RAM or NVMe; HGA loads a bounded set of exact historical tokens per query block.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B with 4-bit QLoRA and PG19, dense training fails at 4,096 tokens while HGA reaches 16,384 tokens with 15.28 GB peak VRAM; evaluation extends to 131,072 tokens; HGA-trained adapters achieve comparable quality (2.7405 vs. 2.7383 nats) to dense-trained adapters; HGA training is marginally faster at 2K (217.75 vs. 207.02 tokens/s) with a growing throughput advantage as context increases.
AI.conclusion: HGA effectively enables long-context training on memory-limited GPUs with minimal quality loss and favorable throughput scaling, with a production-grade serving implementation under development.

title: An Introduction to Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics for Engineering Applications
summary: Many engineering problems involve phenomena whose governing equations are poorly characterized or only partially known. Surrogate modeling techniques such as neural networks can capture the behavior of these systems, but they typically demand large training datasets that are difficult to obtain in engineering contexts and yield models with limited physical interpretability. The Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method addresses both limitations by performing sparse regression over libraries of candidate nonlinear terms, recovering interpretable governing equations from comparatively small datasets. Although SINDy has been demonstrated extensively on canonical benchmark systems, its application to practical engineering problems is less widely documented. This tutorial introduces the SINDy method and progressively builds toward its main extensions, from noise-robust weak-form and ensembling-based variants to constrained and parametrizable formulations. The paper and the accompanying tutorial (available at https://github.com/paullililili/SINDy4Engineers) is organized in three parts: the first introduces the standard SINDy algorithm and progressively extends it, inviting readers without prior knowledge to follow each step and adapt the methods to their own problems; the remaining two parts present detailed case studies on (1) the system identification of an unmanned aerial vehicle and (2) a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger. Through these examples, we aim to demonstrate that SINDy is simple to implement yet flexible enough to serve as a valuable identification tool for advanced engineering applications.

AI.tldr: This tutorial introduces SINDy (Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics) for engineering system identification, progressively covering standard to advanced variants (weak-form, ensembling, constrained, parametrizable), with case studies on UAV dynamics and chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger.
AI.motivation: Engineering problems often involve poorly characterized governing equations; neural network surrogates require large datasets and lack interpretability. SINDy addresses both limitations via sparse regression over nonlinear candidate libraries, but its application to practical engineering is under-documented.
AI.method: Standard SINDy algorithm with extensions: noise-robust weak-form, ensembling-based, constrained, and parametrizable formulations. Tutorial structured in three parts: (1) algorithm introduction and progressive extensions, (2) UAV system identification case study, (3) chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger case study.
AI.result: Demonstrates that SINDy is simple to implement yet flexible for advanced engineering applications, validated through two complex real-world case studies (UAV and chaotic heat exchanger).
AI.conclusion: SINDy serves as a valuable interpretable identification tool for engineering problems, requiring smaller datasets than neural networks while maintaining flexibility via multiple extensions.

title: Parameter-efficient Prompt Tuning of Vision Foundation Model With Adaptive Focal Loss for Interpretable MCI Screening
summary: Mild Cognitive Impairment is a critical early stage of cognitive decline that frequently precedes Alzheimer's disease, yet its automated detection from neuropsychological drawing tests remains fundamentally constrained by data scarcity, class imbalance, and diagnostic ambiguity near clinical boundaries. Existing methodologies attempt to bypass these constraints using computationally expensive, fully fine-tuned hybrid architectures that relegate spatial explainability to a post-hoc approximation rather than an intrinsic model property. We propose a parameter-efficient framework utilizing frozen DINOv2-Small model adapted via three modality-specific learnable prompt tokens while Operating with 1.19 million trainable parameters, each token serves as a query in a shared cross-attention layer over the source image patch tokens. Crucially, spatial explainability is achieved directly through these attention maps; as a structural consequence of the architecture. Then task-conditioned embeddings fused via an attention module to quantify modality-level importance per subject. To handle boundary ambiguity, a MoCA-adapted focal loss introduced that integrates continuous cognitive scores into the training target, loss modulation, and adaptive sample weighting, strictly generalizing standard soft-label approaches. Under stratified five-fold cross-validation, the proposed architecture yields an MCI-class F1 of 0.641 and an AUC of 0.795, outperforming the computationally heavier ResViT baseline by 0.110 in MCI-class F1.

AI.tldr: A parameter-efficient framework using frozen DINOv2-Small with modality-specific learnable prompt tokens and cross-attention achieves MCI detection (F1=0.641, AUC=0.795) from neuropsychological drawing tests, outperforming heavier ResViT baselines while providing intrinsic spatial explainability via attention maps.
AI.motivation: Automated MCI detection from neuropsychological drawing tests is constrained by data scarcity, class imbalance, and diagnostic ambiguity near clinical boundaries; existing hybrid architectures are computationally expensive and relegate spatial explainability to post-hoc approximation rather than intrinsic model property.
AI.method: Frozen DINOv2-Small adapted via three modality-specific learnable prompt tokens (1.19M trainable params); each token serves as query in shared cross-attention over source image patch tokens; spatial explainability achieved directly via attention maps; task-conditioned embeddings fused via attention module; MoCA-adapted focal loss integrating continuous cognitive scores into training target with loss modulation and adaptive sample weighting.
AI.result: Under stratified five-fold cross-validation: MCI-class F1=0.641, AUC=0.795; outperforms ResViT baseline by 0.110 in MCI-class F1 despite being computationally lighter.
AI.conclusion: The proposed parameter-efficient framework with prompt-based adaptation and intrinsic explainability effectively addresses MCI detection challenges, outperforming heavier baselines while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization for World Models in Atari Pong
summary:
World models are usually evaluated as components of model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) systems, while the world models themselves are rarely studied in isolation.
  We examine five representative visual world-model agents in Atari Pong: DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, and STORM. After reproducing their training pipelines and matching the reported agent performance, we freeze the learned world models and evaluate them with a closed-loop rollout diagnostic: a policy trained separately from the corresponding MBRL agent interacts with each frozen model, and the generated video trajectories are inspected for visual and dynamical errors. Across all five models, the rollouts contain clear failures, including ball disappearance, incorrect ball motion, and invalid ball-paddle interactions.
  Beyond visual trajectories, we further evaluate them with pixel-space zero-shot MBRL, where a new policy is trained entirely inside a frozen world model and then evaluated in the real environment. Across all five models, the resulting policies substantially underperform those produced by the corresponding original MBRL training pipelines. The gap is particularly large for DreamerV3, whose mean return drops from -5.5 to -20.9, near the minimum Pong return of -21.
  We hypothesize that insufficient modeling of task-critical concepts, such as the ball in Pong, may contribute to these failures. We therefore propose Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg), an auxiliary pixel reconstruction loss applied to segmented concept regions. Experiments show that CGSReg improves both closed-loop rollouts and pixel-space zero-shot MBRL in DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER. Its effects vary across the remaining models and evaluation metrics, indicating that CGSReg alone does not address all world-model bottlenecks.

AI.tldr: Five visual world models (DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, STORM) are evaluated in isolation on Atari Pong, revealing systematic failures in rollouts and zero-shot MBRL. A proposed auxiliary loss (CGSReg) mitigates some issues but does not fully resolve them.
AI.motivation: World models are typically evaluated as components of MBRL systems, not studied in isolation. The authors aim to isolate and diagnose the learned world models themselves to understand their standalone quality and failure modes.
AI.method: Reproduce five world-model agents on Atari Pong, freeze learned models, then evaluate via (1) closed-loop rollout diagnostic with a separately trained policy and (2) pixel-space zero-shot MBRL (training a new policy entirely inside the frozen model). Propose Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg), an auxiliary pixel reconstruction loss applied to segmented concept regions (e.g., ball in Pong).
AI.result: All five models exhibit clear rollout failures (ball disappearance, incorrect motion, invalid interactions). Zero-shot MBRL policies substantially underperform original MBRL pipelines; DreamerV3 drops from -5.5 to -20.9 (near minimum). CGSReg improves closed-loop rollouts and zero-shot MBRL for DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER, but effects vary across models and metrics.
AI.conclusion: World models have significant isolated failures even when they perform adequately within full MBRL systems. Insufficient modeling of task-critical concepts (e.g., ball) is a key bottleneck. CGSReg helps but does not fully solve world-model limitations.

title: Evaluating covariate balance for long time horizon Markov decision processes
summary: This article explores the application of covariate balance diagnostics for detecting the presence of hidden confounding/model miss-specification in studies applying offline reinforcement learning (RL) to deriving optimal treatment recommendations. The results demonstrate that, either there is a high risk of bias within existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations or, existing covariate balance metrics are not sufficient to assess such studies. Regardless, existing offline RL studies cannot be concluded as being statistically robust. The conclusions propose future research directions for obtaining more methodologically robust applications of offline RL to treatment recommendation problems.

AI.tldr: This paper examines covariate balance diagnostics for detecting hidden confounding in offline RL studies for treatment recommendations, finding that existing studies either have high bias risk or insufficient diagnostic metrics, concluding current results aren't statistically robust.
AI.motivation: To assess whether covariate balance diagnostics can detect hidden confounding/model misspecification in offline RL studies for optimal treatment recommendations, and to evaluate the statistical robustness of existing work in this area.
AI.method: Application and analysis of covariate balance diagnostics to detect hidden confounding and model misspecification in offline reinforcement learning studies for treatment recommendation problems.
AI.result: Existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations either have high bias risk or current covariate balance metrics are insufficient; thus, existing studies cannot be considered statistically robust.
AI.conclusion: Future research directions are needed to develop more methodologically robust applications of offline RL to treatment recommendation problems.

title: RoGS: Adaptive Meshgrid Gaussian for Large-Scale Road Surface Mapping
summary: Road surface mapping plays a crucial role in autonomous driving, supporting high-definition map generation, lane-level perception, and automatic road annotation. Recent mesh-based road surface reconstruction methods have shown promising results, but they still suffer from limited reconstruction quality and high optimization cost, especially in large-scale driving scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose ROADGS-T, a robust and efficient large-scale road surface mapping framework based on adaptive meshgrid Gaussian representation. Specifically, we model the road surface by placing 2D Gaussian surfels on a meshgrid, where each surfel explicitly stores color, semantic, and geometric information. Compared with conventional mesh-based representations and 3D Gaussian primitives, the proposed meshgrid Gaussian representation better matches the thin-surface property of roads while significantly reducing redundant primitives and overlap during optimization. To further improve representation efficiency and structural fidelity, we introduce a road-structure-aware adaptive meshgrid strategy, which allocates denser Gaussian surfels to geometrically or semantically complex regions, such as lane markings, road boundaries, and height discontinuities, while maintaining a compact representation in flat road areas. Moreover, instead of relying on a single nearest vehicle pose, we design a trajectory-consistency-guided pose-robust refinement strategy, which estimates local surface priors from multiple neighboring poses and adaptively weights pose-guided height regularization according to their geometric consistency.

AI.tldr: ROADGS-T is a robust, efficient large-scale road surface mapping framework using adaptive meshgrid Gaussian representation with 2D Gaussian surfels, road-structure-aware adaptive refinement, and trajectory-consistency-guided pose-robust optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing mesh-based road surface reconstruction methods suffer from limited reconstruction quality and high optimization cost, especially in large-scale driving scenarios.
AI.method: (1) Models road surfaces using 2D Gaussian surfels placed on a meshgrid, storing color, semantic, and geometric information. (2) Introduces road-structure-aware adaptive meshgrid strategy for denser Gaussians in complex regions (lane markings, boundaries, discontinuities) and compact representation in flat areas. (3) Designs trajectory-consistency-guided pose-robust refinement using multiple neighboring poses with adaptive weighting of pose-guided height regularization.
AI.result: Better matches thin-surface road properties, reduces redundant primitives and overlap during optimization, and improves representation efficiency and structural fidelity compared to mesh-based and 3D Gaussian primitives.
AI.conclusion: ROADGS-T achieves robust and efficient large-scale road surface mapping, addressing key limitations of prior methods in reconstruction quality and optimization cost.

title: The Industrialization of Research ; On AI-Driven Science and Its Consequences
summary: Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research - not merely as a more powerful instrument, but as an autonomous participant in the research cycle itself. This transition constitutes, in the most precise sense of the term, the industrialization of research: a shift from a craft model, in which knowledge, method, and judgment are embedded in the researcher, to a pipeline model, in which these steps are decomposed, automated, and supervised. The US Department of Energy's Genesis Mission is the most ambitious current instantiation of this shift, but the fundamental questions it raises extend far beyond any single program. This essay examines seven such questions: the erosion of the intergenerational transmission of scientific competence; the growing opacity of AI-generated theories; the collapse of peer evaluation under a flood of machine-generated output; the unproven capacity of AI for paradigm-shifting discovery; the capture of the scientific agenda by political and industrial actors; the compounding of systematic errors in closed-loop pipelines; and the structural bifurcation of the global research community into incommensurable tiers. These concerns do not constitute an argument against AI-driven science - whose demonstrated potential is real and significant. They constitute the conditions under which that potential can be responsibly pursued.

AI.tldr: This essay examines seven critical concerns about AI's transformation of scientific research from a craft model to an industrialized pipeline, arguing these are conditions for responsible pursuit rather than counterarguments against AI-driven science.
AI.motivation: To identify and articulate the fundamental risks and structural challenges posed by AI's transition from a tool to an autonomous participant in the research cycle, using the DOE's Genesis Mission as a case study.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis and critical examination of seven specific challenges arising from the industrialization of research through AI.
AI.result: Identifies seven key concerns: erosion of scientific competence transmission, opacity of AI theories, collapse of peer review under machine output, unproven paradigm-shifting capacity, agenda capture by political/industrial actors, compounded systematic errors in closed-loop pipelines, and structural bifurcation of the global research community.
AI.conclusion: These concerns should be treated as boundary conditions for responsibly pursuing AI's demonstrated potential in science, not as arguments against its use.

title: Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches
summary: This paper develops a categorical framework -- Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches (LINCS) -- as the repair of non-compositionality: failures of diagrams to factor through quotient sketches lifted to the tangent category setting. Machine learning problems are specified as sketches: graphs with commutativity conditions $\mathcal D$, limit cones $\mathcal L$, and colimit cocones $\mathcal K$, generalizing the usual scalarization of loss functions or vector space assumptions. Non-compositionality is defined purely as failure of a universal factorization problem, not as arithmetic error between the desired and actual predictions. Given a learning sketch $\mathbb S=(S,\mathcal D,\mathcal L,\mathcal K)$, whose underlying graph is $S$, and a model $D:J \rightarrow C$, the base defect is the obstruction to factorization $\mbox{Obs}(\mbox{Fact}_{\mathbb S}(D))$. The tangent lift applies the tangent functor $T$ to obtain $TD:J \rightarrow C$, and LINCS is defined as the obstruction $\mbox{Obs}(\mbox{Fact}_{\mathbb S}(TD))$ -- asking whether infinitesimal perturbations preserve the compositionality constraints.The paper also introduces Tangent Learning Sketches, which are sketches equipped with Cockett-Cruttwell tangent structure. The paper defines the INC endofunctor, which iterates the tangent lift, producing a tower $D,TD,T^2D, \cdots$ of factorization problems. ML is thereby formulated as the search for a coalgebraic fixed point where successive tangent unfoldings stabilize ($νT_{\mbox{INC}}$). Using the Aczel--Mendler theorem, we prove existence of a final INC coalgebra whenever $T_{\mbox{INC}}$ admits a set-based class realization that creates its final carrier. A detailed experimental evaluation of LINCS is underway in a number of concrete ML settings, including deep learning, large language models, and reinforcement learning, and is described in companion papers.

AI.tldr: LINCS is a categorical framework that repairs non-compositionality in machine learning by using tangent category theory and sketches (graphs with commutativity, limit, and colimit conditions). It defines learning problems as factorization problems, introduces tangent lifts to check if infinitesimal perturbations preserve compositionality, and iterates this via the INC endofunctor to find stable coalgebraic fixed points using the Aczel-Mendler theorem.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous categorical foundation for repairing non-compositionality (failures of diagrams to factor through quotient sketches) in machine learning, moving beyond arithmetic error definitions to universal factorization problems, and generalizing beyond scalar loss functions or vector space assumptions.
AI.method: The paper defines learning problems as sketches (graphs with commutativity conditions D, limit cones L, colimit cocones K). Non-compositionality is the obstruction to factorization Obs(Fact_S(D)). The tangent functor T lifts to TD, and LINCS is the obstruction Obs(Fact_S(TD)). The INC endofunctor iterates tangent lifts, producing a tower D, TD, T^2D, ... ML is formulated as searching for a coalgebraic fixed point (νT_INC). Existence is proven via the Aczel-Mendler theorem under set-based class realization conditions.
AI.result: A categorical framework LINCS for repairing non-compositionality in ML via tangent category theory. Introduction of Tangent Learning Sketches with Cockett-Cruttwell tangent structure. Definition of the INC endofunctor for iterated tangent lifts. Proof of existence of a final INC coalgebra via the Aczel-Mendler theorem. Experimental evaluation is described as underway in companion papers for deep learning, LLMs, and reinforcement learning.
AI.conclusion: LINCS provides a principled categorical approach to non-compositionality in ML by leveraging tangent category structure and coalgebraic fixed points, with theoretical guarantees for final coalgebra existence and empirical validation planned across multiple ML domains.

title: Beyond Single Expert: Harmonizing Diverse Visual Priors in MLLMs for Spatial Understanding
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated substantial promise in spatial understanding. Existing works typically incorporate prior knowledge extracted from a pre-trained foundation model to further enhance the spatial awareness of MLLMs. In this paper, we first reveal that when integrating diverse foundation models into MLLMs, different models provide complementary spatial priors that benefit different tasks. Motivated by this, we propose $\textbf{ViPS}$, a novel multi-model prior framework designed to fully unleash the potential of incorporating multiple $\textbf{Vi}$sual $\textbf{P}$riors from diverse models into MLLMs for $\textbf{S}$patial understanding. Specifically, ViPS introduces an Efficient Prior Proxy to generate multiple foundational priors with minimal inference overhead, and a Dynamic Prior Fusion mechanism to achieve harmonious and context-aware prior fusion and injection from the prior proxies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ViPS successfully harmonizes diverse visual priors, establishing new state-of-the-art performance across multiple complex spatial reasoning and 3D spatial understanding benchmarks. Project page: https://visual-ai.github.io/vips

AI.tldr: ViPS is a framework that integrates multiple complementary visual priors from diverse foundation models into MLLMs via an Efficient Prior Proxy and Dynamic Prior Fusion, achieving SOTA on spatial reasoning and 3D understanding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs for spatial understanding typically incorporate prior knowledge from a single pre-trained foundation model. The authors first reveal that different foundation models provide complementary spatial priors beneficial for different tasks, motivating the need for a framework that can effectively integrate multiple priors.
AI.method: ViPS introduces two key components: (1) an Efficient Prior Proxy that generates multiple foundational priors with minimal inference overhead, and (2) a Dynamic Prior Fusion mechanism that achieves harmonious, context-aware fusion and injection of these priors into MLLMs.
AI.result: ViPS successfully harmonizes diverse visual priors and establishes new state-of-the-art performance across multiple complex spatial reasoning and 3D spatial understanding benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging complementary priors from multiple foundation models, rather than a single one, significantly enhances MLLMs' spatial understanding capabilities. ViPS provides an effective and efficient solution for multi-prior integration.

title: MedFailBench: A Clinician-Built Open-Source Benchmark for Medical AI Safety Boundary Inspection
comment: 6 pages; clinician-reviewed synthetic benchmark; no patient data
summary: Most medical AI benchmarks measure whether a model knows the correct answer. MedFailBench asks a different question: which safety boundary failed? We present a clinician-built synthetic benchmark and failure atlas that labels medical AI errors by severity (1--5) and safety gate type (missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing, unsafe discharge reassurance, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, source support gap). The current public release (v0.2.1) contains 44 clinician-reviewed synthetic cases with severity annotations, a live HuggingFace leaderboard preview, a safety gate taxonomy, a clinical severity rubric, and an automated pipeline for archiving model-response screening runs. No patient data, clinical validation claims, or model rankings are included. MedFailBench is released under Apache-2.0 and CC-BY-4.0 and carries the Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21205535.

AI.tldr: MedFailBench is a clinician-built synthetic benchmark and failure atlas that labels medical AI errors by severity (1–5) and safety gate type (e.g., missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing), releasing v0.2.1 with 44 clinician-reviewed synthetic cases, a safety taxonomy, a severity rubric, and an automated screening pipeline, under Apache-2.0/CC-BY-4.0.
AI.motivation: Existing medical AI benchmarks evaluate whether models know the correct answer, but fail to systematically analyze which safety boundaries were broken. MedFailBench addresses this gap by introducing a failure-centric evaluation framework.
AI.method: A synthetic benchmark built by clinicians, labeling errors by severity (1–5) and safety gate type (missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing, unsafe discharge reassurance, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, source support gap). Includes 44 clinician-reviewed synthetic cases, a failure atlas, safety gate taxonomy, clinical severity rubric, and an automated pipeline for archiving model-response screening runs.
AI.result: Public release v0.2.1 with 44 annotated synthetic cases, a live HuggingFace leaderboard preview, safety gate taxonomy, severity rubric, and automated pipeline. No patient data, clinical validation claims, or model rankings are included.
AI.conclusion: MedFailBench shifts evaluation from "does the model know the answer?" to "which safety boundary failed?", providing a structured taxonomy and pipeline for diagnosing medical AI safety failures.

title: On-Policy Delta Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation is an alternative post-training method in reinforcement learning that alleviates the constraints imposed by reward models by providing token-level supervision from a teacher model. Although on-policy distillation has been studied and applied across various settings, its fundamental design remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a new distillation reward, termed the delta signal, instead of directly imitating the teacher's output distribution. The delta signal is defined as the difference between the teacher model and its base model prior to instruction tuning for reasoning capability. It therefore captures the changes induced by reasoning tuning and provides a more direct signal for transferring reasoning capabilities. Using extensive empirical evidence, we show that the delta signal substantially improves on-policy distillation and refer to the new distillation method as On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD$^2$). Experiments across mathematics, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that OPD$^2$ consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation, enabling reasoning LLMs to achieve strong performance with only a short post-training period. Code will be available at https://github.com/naver-ai/opd2

AI.tldr: On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD²) improves on-policy distillation for reasoning LLMs by using a delta signal (difference between teacher and base model) instead of directly imitating the teacher's output distribution, achieving better performance on math, science, and code benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy distillation methods directly imitate the teacher's output distribution, which may be suboptimal for transferring reasoning capabilities. The authors propose a more targeted signal by leveraging the gap between the teacher model and its pre-reasoning-tuning base model.
AI.method: The delta signal is defined as the difference between the teacher model's output distribution and that of its base model (before instruction tuning for reasoning). This captures reasoning-specific changes induced by tuning. The method, OPD², uses this delta signal as a distillation reward in an on-policy reinforcement learning framework.
AI.result: OPD² consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation across mathematics, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks, achieving strong performance with only a short post-training period.
AI.conclusion: The delta signal provides a more direct and effective supervision signal for transferring reasoning capabilities, enabling efficient and high-performing on-policy distillation for reasoning LLMs.

title: SUFLECA: Scaling Up Feature Learning for CAD-to-image Alignment
summary: CAD-to-image alignment aims to estimate an object's 9D pose (rotation, translation, and anisotropic scale) from a single RGB image, enabling applications in robotics and augmented reality. Recent zero-shot methods use visual foundation models to match image regions to CAD models, yet typically their correspondences are appearance-driven and degrade under occlusion or sim-to-real domain shift. To address these limitations, we introduce SUFLECA (Scaling Up Feature LEarning for CAD Alignment), a weakly-supervised framework for zero-shot CAD alignment with two key contributions. First, SUFLECA scales up geometry-grounded feature learning from pretrained visual representations through Normalized Object Coordinates (NOCs) supervision on 674K images spanning 12 real and synthetic datasets, learning compact geometry-aware features that generalize across domains. Second, we propose a geometrically consistent matching algorithm that establishes reliable one-to-one CAD-to-image correspondences. Together, these contributions enable accurate, sub-second alignment per object instance without iterative pose refinement. On ScanNet25k, SUFLECA achieves 33.4%/42.3% category/instance accuracy, outperforming, with a smaller computational footprint, the strongest zero-shot baseline by 10.3/12.2 percentage points and, for the first time on this benchmark, even surpassing fully supervised methods. Code is available at: https://github.com/snt-arg/SUFLECA

AI.tldr: SUFLECA is a weakly-supervised framework for zero-shot CAD-to-image alignment that scales geometry-grounded feature learning via NOC supervision on 674K images and uses a geometrically consistent matching algorithm, achieving state-of-the-art results on ScanNet25k (33.4%/42.3% category/instance accuracy) that surpass both zero-shot and fully supervised methods.
AI.motivation: Existing zero-shot CAD-to-image alignment methods rely on appearance-driven correspondences from visual foundation models, which degrade under occlusion or sim-to-real domain shift. The authors aim to overcome these limitations by learning geometry-aware features that generalize across domains.
AI.method: SUFLECA uses a weakly-supervised approach with two key components: (1) scaling up geometry-grounded feature learning from pretrained visual representations using Normalized Object Coordinates (NOCs) supervision on 674K images from 12 real and synthetic datasets, and (2) a geometrically consistent matching algorithm that establishes reliable one-to-one CAD-to-image correspondences.
AI.result: On ScanNet25k, SUFLECA achieves 33.4% category accuracy and 42.3% instance accuracy, outperforming the strongest zero-shot baseline by 10.3/12.2 percentage points with a smaller computational footprint, and for the first time on this benchmark, surpassing fully supervised methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed contributions (scaled geometry-grounded feature learning and geometrically consistent matching) enable accurate, sub-second alignment per object instance without iterative pose refinement, achieving new state-of-the-art results that exceed even fully supervised approaches.

title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Scientific Visualization Literacy
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to interpret visualizations, yet current evaluations remain largely chart-centric and provide limited evidence of understanding of scientific visualization (SciVis). We benchmark six MLLMs on the scientific visualization literacy assessment test, a standardized SciVis literacy assessment comprising 49 items based on 18 scientific visualizations and illustrations, spanning 8 techniques and 11 task types. We evaluate three closed-source and three open-source models under a closed-world protocol and compare their performance using data from 485 human participants. Results show that current MLLMs do not exhibit uniform SciVis literacy. Gemini is the strongest model overall, exceeding the human mean across the evaluated subsets, whereas the open-source models remain below the human baseline. Performance is highly uneven across techniques and tasks: models perform best on scientific illustration, search, and spatial understanding, but struggle on texture-based and integration-based visualizations and on quantitative estimation. Error analysis reveals recurring failures in fine-grained quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation, and grounded encoding interpretation. These findings position SciVis literacy as a necessary benchmark dimension for evaluating multimodal AI systems. Our code and model outputs are publicly available at https://github.com/patdmp/mllm-scivis-lit-benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks six multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on a scientific visualization literacy assessment with 49 items across 18 visualizations and 11 task types, comparing them against 485 human participants. Results show Gemini exceeds human mean overall, while open-source models lag behind; models excel at scientific illustration, search, and spatial understanding but struggle with texture-based/integration-based visualizations and quantitative estimation.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of MLLMs on visualization understanding remain largely chart-centric and provide limited evidence of comprehension of scientific visualization (SciVis), motivating the need for a standardized SciVis literacy benchmark.
AI.method: Benchmarked six MLLMs (three closed-source, three open-source) on the scientific visualization literacy assessment test, a standardized 49-item test based on 18 scientific visualizations covering 8 techniques and 11 task types, under a closed-world protocol, and compared performance against data from 485 human participants.
AI.result: Gemini is the strongest model overall, exceeding human mean; open-source models remain below human baseline. Performance is uneven across techniques/tasks: best on scientific illustration, search, and spatial understanding; struggles on texture-based and integration-based visualizations and quantitative estimation. Error analysis reveals recurring failures in fine-grained quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation, and grounded encoding interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs do not exhibit uniform SciVis literacy, and SciVis literacy should be positioned as a necessary benchmark dimension for evaluating multimodal AI systems.

title: RTS Smoother-Guided Learning of Physics-Based Neural Differential Models
summary: Ordinary differential equations (ODEs) are widely used to model dynamical systems in physics, biology, neuroscience, and physiology, but in many applications some equations of the dynamics are unknown and only a subset of the state variables are measured. We propose a hybrid neural--physics framework in which the known components of the ODE are kept explicit and the missing components are represented by a neural network. The proposed method consists of two stages where we alternate between state and parameter estimation and iterate until a predetermined criterion is met. Specifically, in the first step, we treat the model parameters as being known and we infer the latent states from the available measurements using a Rauch--Tung--Striebel (RTS) smoother. In the second stage, we treat the smoothed trajectories as being known and use them to estimate the neural networks' parameters through backpropagation. We evaluate the method on benchmark systems spanning linear, nonlinear, and stiff dynamics under partial state observation. Across these settings, the proposed method learns missing ODE components from incomplete measurements while exploiting and retaining interpretable mechanistic structure and improving latent-state reconstruction and long-horizon prediction.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hybrid neural-physics framework that keeps known ODE components explicit and uses neural networks to represent missing dynamics, alternating between state estimation (RTS smoother) and parameter learning (backpropagation) for systems with partial observations.
AI.motivation: Many dynamical systems have unknown ODE components and only partial state measurements are available, limiting the applicability of purely mechanistic or purely data-driven approaches.
AI.method: Two-stage iterative approach: (1) treat model parameters as known, infer latent states via RTS smoother; (2) treat smoothed trajectories as known, estimate neural network parameters via backpropagation. Repeat until convergence criterion is met.
AI.result: Evaluated on benchmark systems with linear, nonlinear, and stiff dynamics under partial state observation. The method learns missing ODE components, improves latent-state reconstruction, and enables better long-horizon prediction.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid framework effectively combines mechanistic interpretability with neural network flexibility, learning missing dynamics from incomplete measurements while retaining the known interpretable structure.

title: Towards Hierarchical Structure Understanding of Newspaper Images
comment: Accepted at ICDAR 2026 Workshop on Historical Document Imaging and Processing (HIP)
summary: Understanding newspaper images remains a challenging task due to their complex, nested hierarchical structures and dense, heterogeneous layouts. In this paper, we explore two complementary approaches for newspaper structure understanding. First, we present a modular bottom-up pipeline that combines state-of-the-art open-source models: YOLO for layout detection, LayoutReader for reading order prediction, and a custom algorithm for article segmentation. This approach leverages existing robust components while maintaining flexibility and interpretability. Second, we introduce Tiramisu (Tiered Transformers for Hierarchical Structure Understanding), a novel end-to-end transformer-based architecture that explicitly models document hierarchy through an iterative tiered process. Tiramisu performs section and article separation, block localization, semantic categorization, and reading order prediction using highly parallelized attention mechanisms. Finally, we release Finlam La Liberté, a new dataset designed specifically for evaluating hierarchical information retrieval in historical newspapers. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of both approaches in reconstructing complex newspaper hierarchies, with comparative analysis highlighting their respective strengths for scalable document digitization. The Tiramisu training code, including the synthetic newspaper generator, is available at https://git.litislab.fr/tiramisu/tiramisu-newspaper-articles-extractor.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes two approaches for understanding hierarchical newspaper structures: a modular bottom-up pipeline (YOLO + LayoutReader + custom algorithm) and a novel end-to-end transformer (Tiramisu), evaluated on a new dataset (Finlam La Liberté), with code released.
AI.motivation: Newspaper images are challenging due to their complex nested hierarchies and dense heterogeneous layouts, motivating the need for effective structure understanding solutions.
AI.method: Two approaches: (1) a modular bottom-up pipeline combining YOLO for layout detection, LayoutReader for reading order, and a custom article segmentation algorithm; (2) Tiramisu, an end-to-end transformer with iterative tiered attention mechanisms for hierarchical structure modeling (section/article separation, block localization, semantic categorization, reading order).
AI.result: Both approaches effectively reconstruct complex newspaper hierarchies; comparative analysis reveals respective strengths for scalable document digitization.
AI.conclusion: The two complementary approaches are both effective for newspaper hierarchy reconstruction, with Tiramisu offering end-to-end advantages and the modular pipeline maintaining flexibility and interpretability.

title: Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?
summary: AI benchmarks increasingly leverage item-level statistical models, particularly item response theory (IRT), to estimate model capabilities, rank systems, select informative examples, and diagnose benchmark quality. However, AI benchmark data often departs from the data regime of human testing, for which standard IRT estimation tools were originally developed: benchmarks typically involve fewer evaluated models, far more items, and capability distributions that may be skewed, clustered, or multimodal. We examine how these regime mismatches challenge the reliability of IRT modeling for AI evaluation. Using item parameters and capability distributions derived from six widely used LLM benchmarks, we simulate response matrices under three common IRT models and compare four estimation tools used in recent benchmark studies: marginal maximum likelihood, Markov chain Monte Carlo, variational inference, and a neural pseudo-Siamese estimator. Across 18,000 simulation conditions, we systematically evaluate computational feasibility, scalability, and the reliability of IRT inferences about model rankings, predicted performance, and item characteristics. Results show that classical estimators can become infeasible in large benchmark settings, whereas scalable estimators can produce unreliable item-level and ranking inferences with small or nonnormally distributed model sets. This study identifies when latent trait models reliably support or risk distorting AI benchmarking claims, and what sample sizes and diagnostics are needed for trustworthy use.

AI.tldr: This paper examines how Item Response Theory (IRT) modeling, borrowed from human testing, faces reliability challenges when applied to AI benchmarks due to regime mismatches (fewer models, more items, non-normal capability distributions). Through 18,000 simulations across six LLM benchmarks and four estimators, the study finds classical estimators become infeasible at scale while scalable estimators yield unreliable inferences with small/non-normal model sets.
AI.motivation: AI benchmarks increasingly use IRT but the data regimes differ substantially from human testing (fewer models, more items, skewed/multimodal capability distributions), potentially compromising the reliability of IRT-based inferences for AI evaluation.
AI.method: Using item parameters and capability distributions from six LLM benchmarks, the authors simulate response matrices under three IRT models and compare four estimation tools (MML, MCMC, variational inference, neural pseudo-Siamese estimator) across 18,000 simulation conditions, evaluating feasibility, scalability, and reliability of rankings, predicted performance, and item characteristics.
AI.result: Classical estimators (MML, MCMC) become computationally infeasible at large benchmark scales, while scalable estimators (VI, neural) produce unreliable item-level and ranking inferences when model sets are small or non-normally distributed.
AI.conclusion: Latent trait models can reliably support or distort AI benchmarking claims depending on regime conditions; the study identifies required sample sizes and diagnostics for trustworthy use of IRT in AI evaluation.

title: BadWAM: When World-Action Models Dream Right but Act Wrong
summary: World-action models (WAMs) are emerging as a promising foundation for embodied control: rather than predicting actions alone, they learn representations that couple action generation with future world prediction. This coupling is often viewed as a source of robustness, interpretability, and safety, as a robot's action can in principle be checked against its imagined future. In this paper, we show that this assumption is fragile. We introduce BadWAM, a unified framework for modeling and evaluating World-Action Drift Attacks: a new class of WAM-specific adversarial attacks that use small visual perturbations to break the alignment between what a WAM imagines and what it executes. BadWAM characterizes this attack surface along two natural criteria: attack strength and stealthiness. When the adversary prioritizes disruption, BadWAM instantiates an action-only adversarial attack, which directly drives the model toward task-failing actions. When the adversary additionally prioritizes stealth, BadWAM instantiates an imagination-preserving adversarial attack, which seeks to induce harmful action shifts while keeping the model's predicted future close to its clean imagination. Together, these two attacks capture a spectrum of WAM-specific failures: from overt action hijacking to stealthier cases where the model appears to imagine a plausible future but executes a desynchronized action. We evaluate BadWAM across different variants of WAMs. Results show that our attacks substantially reduce task success rates under closed-loop execution. For example, our action-only attack reduces the model performance from 96.5% to 43.1% success. The results of our imagination-preserving attack further exposes a WAM-specific vulnerability: moderate future-preserving regularization can maintain strong attack performance while reducing future imagination drift.

AI.tldr: BadWAM introduces a unified framework for World-Action Drift Attacks that exploit vulnerabilities in World-Action Models by using visual perturbations to break the alignment between imagined futures and executed actions, achieving significant performance degradation (e.g., 96.5%→43.1% success) with both overt and stealthy variants.
AI.motivation: World-Action Models (WAMs) are assumed to be robust, interpretable, and safe because their action generation is coupled with future world prediction, allowing action verification against imagined futures. The paper challenges this assumption by exploring whether this coupling can be adversarially broken.
AI.method: BadWAM defines two attack variants along strength-stealthiness criteria: (1) action-only adversarial attack that directly drives task-failing actions, and (2) imagination-preserving adversarial attack that induces harmful action shifts while keeping predicted future close to clean imagination. Both use small visual perturbations against WAMs.
AI.result: Action-only attack reduces task success from 96.5% to 43.1% under closed-loop execution. Imagination-preserving attack reveals that moderate future-preserving regularization maintains strong attack performance while reducing future imagination drift, exposing a WAM-specific vulnerability.
AI.conclusion: The assumed robustness of WAMs' action-future coupling is fragile; adversarial visual perturbations can desynchronize imagined futures from executed actions, creating a new attack surface specific to WAM architectures.

title: Quantifying Training Membership Information in the Hyperspherical Embedding Geometry of Face Recognition Models
summary: Face recognition models represent each face as an embedding vector on the unit hypersphere by clustering embeddings of the same identity while pushing different identities apart through angular-margin losses. Because these losses act only on training identities, non-member identities may form clusters with different geometric properties. In this paper, we quantify the magnitude of this difference and what training-time factors control it. We compute four statistics based on cluster geometry across 180 face recognition models in a factorial design over IResNet backbone size, loss head, training duration, and the number of training identities, and evaluate each configuration on nine benchmarks. Our results indicate that the number of training identities has the largest effect on member/non-member separability, while backbone and loss head contribute far less, and that, on a same-domain held-out reference, the geometric membership signal decreases monotonically as more identities are added to training. We provide an analysis of cross-domain (pose, age, quality, ethnicity) non-member benchmarks and report that these inflate the apparent membership signal. Finally, we fuse all four statistics with a learned classifier to reveal additional membership information beyond the best individual statistic.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how face recognition models create geometrically different embedding clusters for member vs. non-member identities, finds that the number of training identities is the dominant factor controlling separability, and shows that cross-domain benchmarks inflate membership signal while a fused multi-statistic classifier reveals more information.
AI.motivation: To quantify the geometric differences between member and non-member identity clusters in face recognition embeddings, and to understand which training-time factors control this separability.
AI.method: Computed four cluster-geometry statistics across 180 face recognition models in a factorial design over IResNet backbone size, loss head, training duration, and number of training identities; evaluated on nine benchmarks; learned classifier to fuse statistics.
AI.result: Number of training identities has the largest effect on member/non-member separability; backbone and loss head contribute much less; membership signal decreases monotonically with more training identities on same-domain held-out reference; cross-domain benchmarks inflate apparent membership signal; fused statistics reveal more membership information than any single statistic.
AI.conclusion: The geometric membership signal in face recognition embeddings is primarily controlled by the number of training identities, not model architecture or loss function, and cross-domain evaluations overestimate membership separability.

title: Plover: Steering GUI Agents through Plan-Centric Interaction
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) automation remains challenging in real-world environments, where dynamic layouts, unexpected dialogs, and evolving interface states can cause autonomous agents to drift from user intent. Recent vision-based multimodal agents improve flexibility by operating directly over screenshots and natural language instructions, but planning and adaptation often remain internal, limiting users' ability to inspect, supervise, or correct system behavior. We present Plover, a plan-centric vision-based GUI automation system that externalizes task plans and replanning as persistent, inspectable, and revisable artifacts. Through a planner--executor architecture, Plover supports explicit supervision of evolving execution, localized correction through editable plans, natural-language guidance, and screenshot-grounded interventions, while preserving prior progress during repair. A formative study with six participants informed the interaction design. We then evaluate Plover through benchmark failure-case repair and scenario-based workflow analyses. Our results show that many autonomous GUI-agent failures are structurally repairable when plans remain visible and interventions are localized, and that explicit replanning helps make GUI automation more transparent, controllable, and adaptable.

AI.tldr: Plover is a plan-centric GUI automation system that externalizes task plans as inspectable and revisable artifacts, using a planner-executor architecture to support supervision, localized correction, and intervention while preserving prior progress.
AI.motivation: GUI automation agents often struggle with dynamic layouts and unexpected states, and their planning/adaptation remains internal, limiting users' ability to inspect, supervise, or correct system behavior.
AI.method: Plover uses a planner-executor architecture with externalized task plans as persistent, inspectable, and revisable artifacts, supporting editable plans, natural-language guidance, and screenshot-grounded interventions.
AI.result: Many autonomous GUI-agent failures are structurally repairable when plans remain visible and interventions are localized; explicit replanning improves transparency, controllability, and adaptability.
AI.conclusion: Making GUI automation plans visible and editable enables more transparent, controllable, and adaptable systems, with many failures being repairable through localized interventions.

title: Data Driven Block Replacement Scheduling
summary: We develop data-driven algorithms for maintaining $N$ independent identical machines under a \textit{block replacement policy}, in which each machine is replaced upon failure and all machines are jointly replaced at regular intervals of length $k$. The goal is to learn the cost-minimizing interval $k^*$ from operational data when the lifetime distribution is unknown. At each decision epoch, the operator selects $k \in \{1, 2, \ldots, K\}$, observes the resulting failure history (a mixture of complete and right-censored lifetimes) and incurs a per-unit-time cost governed by the renewal function. We formulate this as a stochastic multi-armed bandit and propose Hoeffding- and Bernstein-based lower-confidence-bound algorithms achieving $O(K \log T)$ regret, matching the Lai--Robbins lower bound. Exploiting a nested observation property unique to block replacement, correlated variants attain $O((K-k^*)\log T)$ regret and require only $O(1)$ direct pulls of suboptimal arms $k < k^*$. A complementary Kaplan--Meier renewal algorithm estimates the lifetime distribution nonparametrically from censored data, achieving almost-sure policy consistency and empirically near-zero incremental regret at long horizons. We additionally analyze two average-cost MDPs: a time-elapsed formulation establishing that block replacement is optimal within its policy class for any lifetime distribution, and an age-vector formulation proving a monotone threshold structure under increasing failure rate distributions and providing a gold-standard cost benchmark. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical ordering and reveal structural cost gaps between optimal block and age-dependent replacement.

AI.tldr: This paper develops bandit algorithms and MDP formulations for learning the optimal block replacement interval \(k^*\) for \(N\) identical machines under a block replacement policy, achieving \(O(K \log T)\) regret and proving optimality properties of block replacement.
AI.motivation: To learn the cost-minimizing replacement interval \(k^*\) when the lifetime distribution is unknown, using operational data that includes both complete and right-censored lifetimes.
AI.method: Formulates the problem as a stochastic multi-armed bandit with block replacement; proposes Hoeffding- and Bernstein-based LCB algorithms; exploits a nested observation property for correlated variants; develops a Kaplan–Meier renewal algorithm for nonparametric distribution estimation; also analyzes two average-cost MDP formulations (time-elapsed and age-vector).
AI.result: Hoeffding/Bernstein LCB algorithms achieve \(O(K \log T)\) regret matching the Lai–Robbins lower bound; correlated variants achieve \(O((K-k^*)\log T)\) regret with only \(O(1)\) direct pulls of suboptimal arms \(k < k^*\); Kaplan–Meier renewal algorithm achieves almost-sure consistency and near-zero incremental regret; MDP analysis proves block replacement is optimal within its class and reveals monotone threshold structure under IFR distributions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithms are provably efficient and consistent for learning optimal block replacement under unknown lifetime distributions, and the MDP analyses provide theoretical justification and benchmarks for block replacement policies.

title: AlphaWiSE: Adaptive Weight Interpolation for Continual Multimodal Representation Learning
summary: Multimodal models such as CLIP learn a shared embedding space for cross-modal retrieval, but continual adaptation to sequentially arriving data can disrupt the cross-modal alignment acquired from earlier phases. Conventional continual-learning methods return a single checkpoint, which commits every retrieval direction to the same stability-plasticity trade-off. We propose AlphaWiSE, a post-hoc weight-space interpolation method that composes two frozen source checkpoints. For each aligned parameter tensor identified by its checkpoint key, AlphaWiSE fits one scalar interpolation coefficient shared by all tensor entries. The coefficients are fitted on a smaller exemplar memory and used to materialize one interpolated checkpoint. The deployed model has the same architecture and parameter count as either source checkpoint, which does not require additional inference time. Extensive experiments on audio-image-text retrieval show consistent improvements over strong continual-learning baselines across multiple retrieval directions and evaluation metrics.

AI.tldr: AlphaWiSE is a post-hoc weight-space interpolation method that composes two frozen source checkpoints to improve continual cross-modal retrieval without extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: Multimodal models like CLIP lose cross-modal alignment when continually adapted to sequential data, and existing continual learning methods force all retrieval directions into a single stability-plasticity trade-off.
AI.method: AlphaWiSE performs post-hoc weight-space interpolation by fitting a scalar interpolation coefficient per aligned parameter tensor (keyed by checkpoint) using a small exemplar memory, then materializing a single interpolated checkpoint with identical architecture and inference cost.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over strong continual learning baselines across multiple retrieval directions and evaluation metrics on audio-image-text retrieval tasks.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc weight interpolation is an effective, architecture-preserving strategy for continual multimodal retrieval that avoids committing to a single stability-plasticity trade-off.

title: Mutable Low-Rank Sketches for Retrain-Free Recommendation
summary: A common bottleneck in two-stage recommendation is embedding staleness: when a user rates a new item, their embedding remains fixed until the next retrain cycle. We propose mutable sketches, which store each user's preferences in a KP-tree (a sparse segment tree with sum aggregation), fit a low-rank projection once, and recompute embeddings on-the-fly as ratings arrive. We prove that each new observation monotonically tightens the prediction error envelope (Theorem 1), a guarantee that FunkSVD and eALS lack. On KuaiRec, the mutable sketch achieves 0.810 RMSE at 1.8% data read vs. ALS 0.822 at 100%, with 8x faster per-batch updates. A new user receives personalized recommendations in <1 ms after their first rating, with no model retraining required. A comparison of sampling strategies across density regimes shows that the KP-tree's norm-proportional sampling provides 40-130% better item coverage on sparse data (<1% density), while uniform sampling suffices on dense matrices.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes mutable sketches using KP-trees to address embedding staleness in two-stage recommendation systems, enabling real-time embedding updates with provable error guarantees. It achieves 0.810 RMSE on KuaiRec (vs. ALS 0.822) with only 1.8% data read, 8x faster updates, and sub-millisecond personalization for new users.
AI.motivation: Embedding staleness in two-stage recommendation systems causes delayed personalization; user embeddings remain fixed until the next retrain cycle even when new ratings arrive. This limits the system's ability to quickly adapt to user feedback.
AI.method: Mutable sketches store user preferences in a KP-tree (sparse segment tree with sum aggregation), fit a low-rank projection once, and recompute embeddings on-the-fly as new ratings arrive. The method includes norm-proportional sampling via KP-tree for improved item coverage on sparse data.
AI.result: 0.810 RMSE on KuaiRec at 1.8% data read vs. ALS 0.822 at 100%; 8x faster per-batch updates; <1 ms personalization for new users; 40-130% better item coverage on sparse data (<1% density) with norm-proportional sampling.
AI.conclusion: Mutable sketches with KP-trees effectively eliminate embedding staleness, provide provable error convergence guarantees, and achieve strong performance with drastically reduced data and computation requirements, especially beneficial for sparse recommendation scenarios.

title: QuReC: All-in-One Image Restoration with Query-Specific Guidance and Local-Global Response Calibration
summary: All-in-one image restoration aims to recover clean images degraded by multiple corruption types using a single unified model. Existing methods typically rely on image-level prompts or shared guidance to handle diverse degradations.
