However, such a paradigm becomes inadequate when degradations are spatially heterogeneous or even coexist in mixed forms within a single image. Yet spatially adaptive guidance alone is not sufficient, since accurate restoration also requires each spatial query to reliably aggregate complementary information from local neighborhoods and global contexts. To this end, we propose QuReC, a unified framework for all-in-one image restoration. QuReC consists of a Degradation-Guided Query Reconstruction Module (DQRM) and a Local-Global Response Calibration Module (LGRCM). Specifically, DQRM matches each spatial query against a degradation prototype space to reconstruct a query-specific degradation-aware representation, thereby providing fine-grained spatially adaptive restoration guidance. To further stabilize this query-wise matching process, we introduce a weakly supervised prototype matching learning strategy to improve optimization stability and degradation semantic consistency. Meanwhile, LGRCM performs local-global dual-branch aggregation and calibrates the aggregated responses with learnable priors, improving the reliability of feature aggregation and the coordination between local detail modeling and global context modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that QuReC achieves superior performance on multiple all-in-one image restoration benchmarks. The code is released at https://github.com/zhoushen1/QuReC.

AI.tldr: QuReC is a unified framework for all-in-one image restoration that uses a Degradation-Guided Query Reconstruction Module (DQRM) with weakly supervised prototype matching and a Local-Global Response Calibration Module (LGRCM) to achieve spatially adaptive restoration for heterogeneous and mixed degradations, outperforming existing methods on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing all-in-one image restoration methods rely on image-level prompts or shared guidance, which fail when degradations are spatially heterogeneous or coexist in mixed forms within a single image. Moreover, spatially adaptive guidance alone is insufficient because accurate restoration requires each spatial query to reliably aggregate complementary information from both local neighborhoods and global contexts.
AI.method: QuReC introduces two key components: (1) Degradation-Guided Query Reconstruction Module (DQRM) that matches each spatial query against a degradation prototype space to reconstruct query-specific degradation-aware representations, trained with a weakly supervised prototype matching learning strategy for stability; and (2) Local-Global Response Calibration Module (LGRCM) that performs dual-branch aggregation with learnable priors to calibrate local and global responses for reliable feature coordination.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that QuReC achieves superior performance on multiple all-in-one image restoration benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed fine-grained spatially adaptive guidance coupled with calibrated local-global feature aggregation effectively addresses heterogeneous and mixed degradations in all-in-one image restoration, setting new state-of-the-art results.

title: When Words Are Safe But Actions Kill: Probing Physical Danger Beyond Text Safety in Hidden-State Risk Space
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as high-level planners for embodied agents, where linguistically benign instructions can become unsafe once grounded in the physical world. We study whether this physically grounded danger is the same safety problem as ordinary text-level content danger. Through hidden-state direction analysis and random-split null tests, we show that content danger (CD) and physical danger (PD) form separable signals in LLM representations across Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B/32B, Phi-3.5 and SmolLM2. Building on the CD/PD separability, we propose PRISM, a single-layer L2-regularized logistic probe over full hidden states. PRISM achieves 86.2--87.7\% accuracy on SafeAgentBench with 11.7--13.7\% FPR, while same-scale LLM judges over-block safe tasks at 24.7--39.0\% FPR. We further introduce PhysicalSafetyBench-1K (PSB-1K), a contrastive benchmark of 1{,}000 physical-risk pairs without direct harm keywords, to test whether methods detect physically grounded danger rather than explicit unsafe wording. On PSB-1K, PRISM reaches 99.6\% accuracy and 0.7\% FPR, whereas a Qwen2.5-3B judge rejects 67.8\% of safe tasks. PRISM also replicates on SafeText and EARBench, supporting hidden-state probing as a representation-level method for physical safety beyond text moderation.

AI.tldr: LLMs' physically grounded danger (PD) is separable from content danger (CD) in representations. PRISM, a single-layer logistic probe, detects PD with high accuracy (86-88% on SafeAgentBench, 99.6% on PSB-1K) and low false positive rate, significantly outperforming same-scale LLM judges.
AI.motivation: Linguistically benign instructions can become unsafe when grounded in physical environments (physical danger, PD). It is unclear whether PD is the same safety problem as ordinary text-level content danger (CD) and whether existing text moderation methods suffice.
AI.method: (1) Hidden-state direction analysis and random-split null tests across Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B/32B, Phi-3.5, SmolLM2 to show CD/PD separability. (2) PRISM: a single-layer L2-regularized logistic probe over full hidden states. (3) PhysicalSafetyBench-1K (PSB-1K): a contrastive benchmark of 1,000 physical-risk pairs without direct harm keywords.
AI.result: PRISM achieves 86.2-87.7% accuracy on SafeAgentBench with 11.7-13.7% FPR vs. 24.7-39.0% FPR for LLM judges. On PSB-1K, PRISM reaches 99.6% accuracy and 0.7% FPR, while Qwen2.5-3B judge rejects 67.8% of safe tasks. Results replicate on SafeText and EARBench.
AI.conclusion: Physical danger is a representation-level safety problem separable from content danger. Hidden-state probing (PRISM) is an effective method for physical safety beyond traditional text moderation.

title: Decoding Market Emotion from Blockchain Activity: A Data-Driven Sentiment Classifier
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for presentation at the IEEE International Symposium on Computers and Communications (ISCC 2026)
summary: The growing use of Bitcoin as a decentralized digital asset and investment tool has sparked strong interest in understanding its market behavior. This study presents a new approach to analyze Bitcoin market sentiment by combining on-chain and financial data with social media posts. Unlike models that aim to predict prices, this work focuses on explaining market sentiment using blockchain transactions, historical price data of Bitcoin, and daily Twitter sentiment classifications. The method merges sentiment trends with on-chain and financial metrics, normalized into a dataset for detailed market analysis. Multiple machine learning models were tested using cross-validation, with Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) emerging as the most reliable model for classifying sentiment, achieving an average F1-score of about 0.84. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), a game theory-based method for model interpretability, was used to quantify the contribution of on-chain features to the model's predictions, improving transparency. The results indicate that this data combination yields meaningful predictive signals and insights, supporting data-driven cryptocurrency analysis and future improvements with deep learning.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes Bitcoin market sentiment by combining on-chain data, financial metrics, and Twitter sentiment classifications. Using XGBoost with SHAP interpretability, it achieves an F1-score of ~0.84 for sentiment classification, focusing on explanation rather than price prediction.
AI.motivation: Growing interest in Bitcoin as a decentralized asset and investment tool creates a need to better understand its market behavior and sentiment drivers.
AI.method: Combines on-chain transactions, historical price data, and daily Twitter sentiment classifications, normalized into a unified dataset. Tests multiple ML models via cross-validation; uses XGBoost for classification and SHAP for feature contribution analysis.
AI.result: XGBoost achieved an average F1-score of approximately 0.84 for sentiment classification; SHAP analysis quantified on-chain feature contributions, improving model transparency.
AI.conclusion: The data combination produces meaningful predictive signals and insights for sentiment analysis, supporting data-driven cryptocurrency analysis and potential improvements with deep learning.

title: DAPGNet: Dynamic Adaptive Physics-Guided Graph Diffusion Network for Hyperspectral Image Classification
comment: 9 figures and 9 tables. Pengkun Wang and Weijia Cao contributed equally to this work
summary: Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification requires reliable pixel-relation modeling under spectral variability, mixed pixels, and heterogeneous boundaries. Existing graph-based HSI classifiers usually construct graph topology from spatial proximity, superpixel connectivity, or learned feature affinity. However, the spectral physical prior carried by contiguous bands has limited influence on topology estimation and message propagation. This paper presents DAPGNet, a dynamic adaptive physics-guided graph diffusion network that injects a structure-constrained physical prior into relation-level graph learning. DAPGNet first encodes contiguous spectral responses into node-wise multiscale physical-prior representations. A two-stage graph constructor then combines spectral-spatial affinity, physical-prior consistency, and spatial distance to form a physical-prior-aware sparse topology. During graph diffusion, learned edge weights are transformed into additive attention biases, while a physical gate performs node-wise and feature-wise interpolation between graph-aggregated features and projected physical-prior features. Cross-scale fusion integrates node states from different diffusion depths, and the network is optimized with main classification, auxiliary supervision, and second-order spectral smoothness regularization. Experiments on Indian Pines, WHU-Hi-LongKou, Houston2013, and Houston2018 show that DAPGNet achieves the best OA, AA, and Kappa among representative CNN-, Transformer-, Mamba-, and graph-based baselines. It improves AA over the strongest competing method by 3.64 to 7.31 percentage points across the four datasets. Ablation and sensitivity analyses further support the complementary effects of physical-prior extraction, prior-aware topology construction, physics-gated propagation, and spectral smoothness regularization.

AI.tldr: DAPGNet is a dynamic adaptive physics-guided graph diffusion network for HSI classification that injects spectral physical priors (from contiguous bands) into graph topology construction and message propagation, achieving state-of-the-art OA, AA, and Kappa on four benchmark datasets with 3.64–7.31 percentage points AA improvement over the best competitor.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based HSI classifiers rely on spatial proximity, superpixel connectivity, or learned feature affinity but largely ignore the spectral physical prior carried by contiguous bands, limiting topology estimation and message propagation quality.
AI.method: DAPGNet encodes multiscale physical-prior representations from contiguous spectral responses; constructs a physical-prior-aware sparse topology via a two-stage graph constructor combining spectral-spatial affinity, physical-prior consistency, and spatial distance; transforms learned edge weights into additive attention biases during graph diffusion; applies a physical gate for node-wise and feature-wise interpolation between graph-aggregated and projected physical-prior features; performs cross-scale fusion across diffusion depths; and optimizes with classification, auxiliary supervision, and second-order spectral smoothness regularization.
AI.result: DAPGNet achieves the highest OA, AA, and Kappa on Indian Pines, WHU-Hi-LongKou, Houston2013, and Houston2018, surpassing CNN-, Transformer-, Mamba-, and graph-based baselines. AA improvements over the strongest competitor range from 3.64 to 7.31 percentage points across datasets.
AI.conclusion: Injecting spectral physical priors into graph topology and diffusion significantly enhances HSI classification, with ablation studies confirming the complementary benefits of physical-prior extraction, prior-aware topology, physics-gated propagation, and spectral smoothness regularization.

title: AutoSynthesis: An agentic system for automated meta-analysis
summary: Evidence synthesis is crucial for turning primary research into reliable knowledge for science, medicine, education, and policy. Yet, quantitative evidence synthesis remains largely manual and difficult to scale. Here, we introduce AutoSynthesis, an end-to-end multi-agent system for automated meta-analysis. Given a research question in natural language, AutoSynthesis formulates a search strategy, retrieves scientific literature, screens candidate studies, assesses full-text eligibility, extracts quantitative statistics, computes standardized effect sizes, and finally performs random-effects meta-analysis. AutoSynthesis further supports heterogeneity analysis to examine how effect sizes vary across moderators, as well as risk-of-bias assessment. As output, AutoSynthesis produces a transparent report aligned with PRISMA guidelines. In our application, AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates produced by AutoSynthesis are similar to Hedges' $g$ of expert-conducted meta-analyses, indicating close agreement with manual evidence synthesis. Together, these results show that AutoSynthesis can make quantitative evidence synthesis more scalable, thereby supporting evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.

AI.tldr: AutoSynthesis is an end-to-end multi-agent system that automates quantitative evidence synthesis (meta-analysis), from formulating search strategies to producing PRISMA-aligned reports, achieving results comparable to expert-conducted meta-analyses.
AI.motivation: Quantitative evidence synthesis is crucial for evidence-based decision-making but remains largely manual, labor-intensive, and difficult to scale across disciplines.
AI.method: AutoSynthesis is a multi-agent system that: (1) formulates search strategy from a natural language question, (2) retrieves and screens literature, (3) assesses full-text eligibility, (4) extracts quantitative statistics, (5) computes standardized effect sizes, and (6) performs random-effects meta-analysis with heterogeneity analysis and risk-of-bias assessment, outputting a PRISMA-compliant report.
AI.result: Applied to over 28 studies with more than 20 extracted quantitative claims, AutoSynthesis produced pooled effect estimates closely matching Hedges' g from expert-conducted meta-analyses, demonstrating strong agreement with manual synthesis.
AI.conclusion: AutoSynthesis can make quantitative evidence synthesis more scalable, supporting evidence-based decision-making across scientific, medical, educational, and policy domains.

title: Ray-based phase error correction for miniaturized DOE projector-based FPP under single-directional hyperbolic projection
summary: Fringe Projection Profilometry (FPP) systems using miniaturized DOE pro-jectors often suffer from severe phase artifacts due to nonlinear projection characteristics and limited pattern controllability. We propose a ray-based phase error correction framework that models phase artifacts along projection rays from the projector pinhole, incorporating projector geometry without re-lying on image-domain processing or neighboring pixels. A projector pinhole estimation method based on a single-directional hyperbolic fringe pattern is introduced, through which projector geometry can be recovered without stereo calibration. In addition, a data-efficient strategy constructs the re-finement model from a single calibration pose. Experiments on miniaturized DOE projector-based FPP systems demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy under nonlinear projection conditions, confirming the robustness and physical consistency of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: A ray-based phase error correction framework for miniaturized DOE projector-based Fringe Projection Profilometry that models phase artifacts along projection rays, uses a single-directional hyperbolic fringe pattern for projector pinhole estimation without stereo calibration, and constructs a refinement model from a single calibration pose to improve reconstruction accuracy under nonlinear projection conditions.
AI.motivation: Miniaturized DOE projector-based FPP systems suffer from severe phase artifacts caused by nonlinear projection characteristics and limited pattern controllability, degrading reconstruction accuracy.
AI.method: (1) A ray-based phase error correction framework that models phase artifacts along projection rays from the projector pinhole, incorporating projector geometry. (2) A projector pinhole estimation method using a single-directional hyperbolic fringe pattern to recover projector geometry without stereo calibration. (3) A data-efficient strategy to construct the refinement model from a single calibration pose.
AI.result: Significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy under nonlinear projection conditions on miniaturized DOE projector-based FPP systems, demonstrating robustness and physical consistency of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: The ray-based correction framework effectively addresses phase artifacts in miniaturized DOE projector FPP systems by leveraging projector geometry and a data-efficient calibration strategy, achieving robust and physically consistent 3D reconstruction.

title: teLLMe Why (Ain't Nothing but a Jam): Exploratory Causal Analysis of Urban Driving Data
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on UrbanAI. 6 pages
summary: Traffic agencies now have access to large volumes of video-derived data for studying safety and congestion. Most of these data are observational and collected without interventions, which makes causal questions such as "How would rain change traffic density?" difficult to answer. We present teLLMe, a system for exploratory causal analysis of urban driving datasets. The system starts from a structured event table built from dashcam annotations and combines causal structure learning with the PC algorithm, bootstrap-based stability checks, and query-specific effect estimation using linear regression and DoWhy. Natural-language questions are mapped to structured causal queries through a schema-aware LLM, enabling users to specify treatments, outcomes, and subpopulations. teLLMe returns a "Causal Card" that summarizes effect estimates, adjustment sets, DAG support, and assumptions, followed by a short natural-language explanation. Case studies on BDD-derived traffic events show that the system can surface plausible relationships involving weather, peak hours, and traffic density, while making uncertainty and modeling choices explicit. The system is designed as a tool for hypothesis generation and expert reasoning rather than a source of definitive causal claims.

AI.tldr: teLLMe is a system for exploratory causal analysis of urban driving data that combines causal structure learning, bootstrap stability checks, and LLM-based query mapping to estimate causal effects from observational dashcam video data, returning a "Causal Card" with effect estimates and assumptions for hypothesis generation.
AI.motivation: Traffic agencies have large volumes of observational video-derived data but cannot easily answer causal questions (e.g., "How would rain change traffic density?") because most data are collected without interventions, making causal inference challenging.
AI.method: teLLMe combines causal structure learning with the PC algorithm, bootstrap-based stability checks, and query-specific effect estimation using linear regression and DoWhy. Natural-language questions are mapped to structured causal queries through a schema-aware LLM, and results are summarized in a "Causal Card" with DAG support, adjustment sets, and assumptions.
AI.result: Case studies on BDD-derived traffic events show teLLMe can surface plausible relationships involving weather, peak hours, and traffic density while making uncertainty and modeling choices explicit.
AI.conclusion: teLLMe is designed as a tool for hypothesis generation and expert reasoning rather than a source of definitive causal claims, enabling exploratory causal analysis from observational driving data.

title: MAGiSt3R: Multi-Agent Feed-forward 3D Reconstruction from Monocular RGB Videos
summary: This paper presents MAGiSt3R, a multi-agent 3D reconstruction framework performing reconstruction and camera tracking for monocular RGB videos at almost 10 FPS. MAGiSt3R relies on a feed-forward model from the 3R family to process RGB videos and regress local point maps, and on a merging model, MAGMA, that combines local maps at both intra-agent and inter-agent levels to obtain the final global point map. Furthermore, MAGiSt3R performs pose graph optimization to mitigate cumulative camera drift occurring along the feed-forward pipeline. We evaluate MAGiSt3R on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior reconstruction and camera tracking accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: MAGiSt3R is a multi-agent 3D reconstruction framework that performs real-time (10 FPS) monocular RGB video reconstruction and camera tracking by combining feed-forward 3R-family models with a merging module (MAGMA) and pose graph optimization to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy.
AI.motivation: To achieve fast (near real-time) 3D reconstruction and camera tracking from monocular RGB videos while maintaining high accuracy.
AI.method: Uses a feed-forward model from the 3R family to regress local point maps from RGB videos, a merging model (MAGMA) to combine local maps at intra-agent and inter-agent levels into a global point map, and pose graph optimization to reduce cumulative camera drift.
AI.result: Achieves superior reconstruction and camera tracking accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches on both synthetic and real-world datasets, operating at nearly 10 FPS.
AI.conclusion: MAGiSt3R enables fast, accurate monocular 3D reconstruction and tracking via a multi-agent framework with effective local-to-global map merging and drift mitigation.

title: SearchOS-V1: Towards Robust Open-Domain Information-Seeking Agent Collaboration
summary: Recent advances in Tool-Integrated Large Language Models have made web search a core capability of information-seeking agents. However, as interaction histories grow, agents increasingly struggle to track task progress. When search attempts fail to yield useful evidence, current single- and multi-agent systems can become trapped in repetitive loops, wasting search budgets and ultimately compromising the quality and completeness of the final output. We introduce SearchOS, a system-level multi-agent framework that turns fragile, implicit search progress into explicit, persistent, and shared state. First, we formulate open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations, where agents discover entities, populate attributes across linked tables, and anchor each value to source evidence. Then we design Search-Oriented Context Management (SOCM), which externalizes the evolving state into Frontier Task, an Evidence Graph, a Coverage Map, and Failure Memory. Built on SOCM, SearchOS applies a pipeline-parallel scheduling mechanism that overlaps the execution of sub-agents and continuously refills freed slots with tasks targeting unresolved coverage gaps to improve utilization and throughput. To schedule and control the execution of search agents, SearchOS introduces a Search Tool Middleware Harness that intercepts model and tool interactions to record grounded evidence and react to stalls or budget exhaustion, and provides a reusable hierarchical skill system comprising strategy and access skills to augment the agents' search process and avoid repeating failed search patterns across runs. On WideSearch and GISA, SearchOS leads all metrics among the evaluated single- and multi-agent baselines, paving the way toward robust information-seeking collaboration.

AI.tldr: SearchOS is a multi-agent framework that externalizes search progress into explicit shared state (Frontier Task, Evidence Graph, Coverage Map, Failure Memory) to prevent repetitive loops, using pipeline-parallel scheduling and a Search Tool Middleware Harness, achieving state-of-the-art results on WideSearch and GISA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current Tool-Integrated LLMs struggle to track task progress as interaction histories grow, leading to repetitive search loops that waste budgets and compromise output quality.
AI.method: (1) Formulates open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations. (2) Designs Search-Oriented Context Management (SOCM) with Frontier Task, Evidence Graph, Coverage Map, and Failure Memory. (3) Applies pipeline-parallel scheduling overlapping sub-agent execution. (4) Introduces Search Tool Middleware Harness for monitoring and a hierarchical skill system to avoid repeating failed patterns.
AI.result: On WideSearch and GISA, SearchOS outperforms all evaluated single- and multi-agent baselines across all metrics.
AI.conclusion: SearchOS demonstrates that externalizing fragile search progress into persistent, shared state enables robust information-seeking collaboration and paves the way for more effective multi-agent search systems.

title: Symbal: Detecting Systematic Misalignments in Model-Generated Captions
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often introduce errors when generating image captions, resulting in misaligned image-text pairs. Our work focuses on a class of captioning errors that we refer to as systematic misalignments, where a recurring error in MLLM-generated captions is closely associated with the presence of a specific visual feature in the paired image. Given a vision-language dataset with MLLM-generated captions, our aim in this work is to detect such errors, a task we refer to as systematic misalignment detection. As our first key contribution, we present Symbal, which utilizes a structured, dual-stage setup with off-the-shelf foundation models to identify systematic misalignments and summarize results in natural language. As our second key contribution, we introduce SymbalBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate automated methods on our proposed task. SymbalBench consists of 1.7 million image-text pairs from two domains (natural and medical images), organized into 420 vision-language datasets with annotated systematic misalignments. Symbal exhibits strong performance on this benchmark, correctly identifying systematic misalignments in 63.8% of datasets, a nearly 4x improvement over the closest baseline. We supplement our evaluations on SymbalBench with real-world evaluations, showing that (1) Symbal can accurately surface systematic misalignments in captions generated by four MLLMs and (2) Symbal is a powerful tool for auditing off-the-shelf image-caption datasets. Ultimately, our novel task, method, and benchmark can aid users with auditing MLLM-generated captions and identifying critical errors, without requiring access to the underlying MLLM. Code is available at https://github.com/Stanford-AIMI/Symbal.

AI.tldr: Symbal is a dual-stage framework using off-the-shelf foundation models to detect systematic misalignments (recurring captioning errors tied to specific visual features) in MLLM-generated image captions. The authors also introduce SymbalBench, a benchmark of 1.7M image-text pairs across 420 datasets from natural and medical domains. Symbal achieves 63.8% accuracy in identifying systematic misalignments, a ~4x improvement over baselines, and proves effective for auditing MLLM-generated captions without requiring access to the underlying model.
AI.motivation: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) frequently generate erroneous image captions, leading to misaligned image-text pairs. The authors aim to detect a specific class of errors called systematic misalignments—recurring captioning errors strongly associated with a particular visual feature—in vision-language datasets, without needing access to the underlying MLLM.
AI.method: The authors propose Symbal, a structured dual-stage setup that leverages off-the-shelf foundation models to first identify candidate systematic misalignments and then summarize findings in natural language. They also create SymbalBench, a benchmark with 1.7M image-text pairs from natural and medical domains, organized into 420 datasets with annotated systematic misalignments.
AI.result: Symbal correctly identifies systematic misalignments in 63.8% of datasets on SymbalBench, achieving nearly a 4x improvement over the closest baseline. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that Symbal can surface systematic misalignments in captions generated by four different MLLMs and effectively audit off-the-shelf image-caption datasets.
AI.conclusion: Symbal provides a novel task, method, and benchmark for detecting systematic misalignments in MLLM-generated captions, enabling users to audit caption quality and identify critical errors without requiring access to the underlying MLLM. The approach demonstrates strong performance and practical utility across both natural and medical image domains.

title: Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda
summary: Poisoning pretraining data can introduce harmful behaviors to LMs that are difficult to detect and mitigate. Prior work on poisoning pretraining data has largely exploited established data sources such as Wikipedia, which do not represent the large scale and heterogeneity typical of pretraining corpora, and has ignored the interaction between poisoned data and data curation pipelines. We demonstrate that poisoning attacks on pretraining data are feasible beyond this limited setting through an existing web-scale content injection mechanism: public discussion interfaces. Additionally, to measure whether malicious content is included after web crawling and data curation, we introduce HalfLife, a novel analysis for estimating adversarial content inclusion in web-crawl based LM training data. We use HalfLife to explore the feasibility of poisoning pretraining corpora at web scale through open discussion interfaces. Our analysis demonstrates the importance of estimating whether poison injections are included in pretraining data, and establishes third-party webpage content as a possible vector for attacking language model pretraining.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that poisoning attacks on LM pretraining data are feasible beyond controlled settings via public discussion interfaces, and introduces HalfLife—a novel analysis method for estimating adversarial content inclusion in web-crawl based training data.
AI.motivation: Prior work on poisoning pretraining data has been limited to established data sources like Wikipedia, failing to address the large scale and heterogeneity of real pretraining corpora, and ignoring interactions between poisoned data and data curation pipelines.
AI.method: Introduces HalfLife, a novel analysis for estimating adversarial content inclusion in web-crawl based LM training data, and demonstrates poisoning attacks via an existing web-scale content injection mechanism: public discussion interfaces.
AI.result: Demonstrates that poisoning attacks on pretraining data are feasible beyond limited settings, and that public discussion interfaces serve as a viable vector for injecting malicious content into web-scale pretraining corpora.
AI.conclusion: Estimating poison injection inclusion in pretraining data is important, and third-party webpage content represents a possible vector for attacking language model pretraining.

title: Structural-Semantic Reciprocal Learning for Unsupervised Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification
summary: Unsupervised visible-infrared person re-identification (USVI-ReID) is challenging due to the large modality gap and the lack of cross-modal identity annotations. Progressive association paradigms have been proposed to gradually bridge the gap, but they suffer from two critical bottlenecks: reliance on ambiguous global representations and unchecked propagation of pseudo-label noise in an open-loop manner. To address these issues, we propose Structural-Semantic Reciprocal Learning (SSRL), a framework that transforms open-loop association into a self-correcting closed-loop system. Structurally, we introduce Fine-grained Structural Decoupling (FSD) to extract discriminative body-part primitives as reliable spatial anchors, complementing ambiguous holistic silhouettes with spatially consistent structural details. Semantically, we design a Closed-loop Semantic Calibration (CSC) mechanism that reconstructs shared semantic prototypes at each epoch and feeds them back into the training loop, effectively filtering pseudo-label noise before the next clustering cycle. Through the reciprocal interaction between structural and semantic learning, SSRL achieves robust cross-modal representation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the competitive performance of SSRL against state-of-the-art USVI-ReID methods on both SYSU-MM01 and RegDB, notably surpassing several supervised counterparts on RegDB.

AI.tldr: SSRL introduces a closed-loop framework with Fine-grained Structural Decoupling (FSD) and Closed-loop Semantic Calibration (CSC) to address ambiguous global representations and pseudo-label noise propagation in unsupervised visible-infrared person re-identification.
AI.motivation: USVI-ReID suffers from reliance on ambiguous global representations and unchecked open-loop propagation of pseudo-label noise under large modality gaps without cross-modal identity annotations.
AI.method: Proposes Structural-Semantic Reciprocal Learning (SSRL) with two components: (1) Fine-grained Structural Decoupling (FSD) extracts body-part primitives as spatial anchors, and (2) Closed-loop Semantic Calibration (CSC) reconstructs shared semantic prototypes at each epoch to filter noise before the next clustering cycle, forming a self-correcting closed-loop system.
AI.result: Competitive performance against state-of-the-art USVI-ReID methods on SYSU-MM01 and RegDB, surpassing several supervised counterparts on RegDB.
AI.conclusion: Reciprocal interaction between structural and semantic learning enables robust cross-modal representations, effectively transforming open-loop association into a self-correcting closed-loop system.

title: Falsifiable Release Gates for Self-Improving Systems
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures. Software, gate suite, run artifacts, and TLA+ specification are open source
summary: Safety claims on self-improving agent runtimes are almost always self-graded: a policy file, a guardrail, or a README commitment. We describe falsifiable release gates, and a methodology to build and validate such systems, such that every new capability must pass a pre-specified, machine-verifiable acceptance suite before it ships, and a fixed set of standing invariants is preserved at each gate. A purposely broken model gives the shortest counterexample, so the checker has teeth, is apparent. The self-enhancement loop is positively Constrained: the entire write surface is policy rules, tightening changes. may auto-apply loosening changes always require a human merge and a proposal autoclosed is one that mispredicts its own effect; We publish the acceptance measured results for all the seven gates, define precisely the scope of each claim (a bounded of the coordination skeleton (not the learned components) and free the runtime, either command line tools and the gate suite, so the results reproduce, and gates can run against other agent frameworks. Reviewers may repeat the single command central non-bypass in seconds.

AI.tldr: The paper presents falsifiable release gates for self-improving agent runtimes, where every new capability must pass a machine-verifiable acceptance suite. Applied in Antahkarana, an open runtime, the method uses seven gates with a control ring that mints safety-critical tokens, exhaustively checked over 1M reachable states. The self-enhancement loop is constrained: tightening changes auto-apply, loosening requires human merge. Results are published and reproducible.
AI.motivation: Current safety claims on self-improving agent runtimes are self-graded (policy files, guardrails, README commitments) and lack formal, machine-verifiable verification. There is no falsifiable methodology to ensure new capabilities preserve safety invariants before shipping.
AI.method: Define falsifiable release gates with pre-specified, machine-verifiable acceptance suites. Apply via seven gates in Antahkarana runtime: from basic observability to a self-governing loop. A control ring mints capability tokens; exhaustively machine-check over 1M reachable state space (bounded model) and re-check against execution traces. Self-enhancement loop constrained: tightening changes auto-apply, loosening requires human merge; proposals mispredicting own effects auto-close.
AI.result: Published acceptance measured results for all seven gates. Scope precisely defined (bounded coordination skeleton, not learned components). Runtime and gate suite released as open-source command line tools. Single-command central non-bypass verification completes in seconds. Purposely broken model yields shortest counterexample, demonstrating checker effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Falsifiable release gates provide a rigorous, reproducible methodology for safety verification in self-improving agent runtimes. Antahkarana demonstrates feasibility with seven gates, bounded model checking over 1M states, and constrained self-enhancement loops. The approach is generalizable to other agent frameworks.

title: Divergent Gaze Patterns in Artistic Viewing: Spatial and Temporal Signatures of Attention Across Autistic Individuals, Artists, and Neurotypical Observers
summary: How different populations visually explore artworks bears on cognitive science and on accessibility design, yet most eye-tracking work in autism has used social scenes rather than art, and has analysed where the eyes land while ignoring when and in what order. We present a comparative free-viewing study across three groups, autistic adults (ASD), trained artists, and neurotypical observers, who each viewed 30 paintings for 15s. We introduce a directed, metric-grounded framework that compares groups along two complementary axes: a spatial axis, in which one group's fixation-density map predicts another's fixations under six saliency metrics (AUC-Judd, NSS, CC, SIM, KL, Information Gain); and a temporal axis, in which individual scanpaths are compared with MultiMatch, ScanMatch, a foveal-disc IoU score (FDISS), and dynamic time warping (DTW). Fixations are extracted uniformly for all groups with a dispersion-threshold algorithm. Three results converge. (i)Artists and neurotypicals are almost indistinguishable in both space (density-map correlation CC=0.96) and time (they form the most alignable scanpath pair), whereas ASD gaze diverges from both. (ii)ASD attention is dissociated: it matches artists' wide spatial exploration (dispersion, explored area) but carries a distinct temporal signature, shorter fixations, less dwell, and the most idiosyncratic (least self-consistent) scanpaths of any group. (iii)ASD gaze is not selectively artist-like on any metric; if anything it is marginally closer to neurotypical. Together these findings indicate that autistic viewing of art is a distinct, group-specific attentional profile in both space and time, and they motivate population-conditioned models of aesthetic attention. We release all analysis code and per-stimulus results.

AI.tldr: This study compares how autistic adults, trained artists, and neurotypical observers visually explore artworks using both spatial (fixation-density maps) and temporal (scanpath) analyses, finding that autistic viewing is a distinct attentional profile in both dimensions, while artists and neurotypicals are nearly indistinguishable.
AI.motivation: Prior eye-tracking work in autism focused on social scenes rather than art, and analyzed spatial fixation locations while ignoring temporal dynamics (when and in what order fixations occur). The study aims to fill this gap by characterizing autistic visual exploration of art in both space and time.
AI.method: Three groups (ASD adults, trained artists, neurotypical observers) viewed 30 paintings for 15s each. Spatial analysis used 6 saliency metrics (AUC-Judd, NSS, CC, SIM, KL, Information Gain) comparing fixation-density maps. Temporal analysis used MultiMatch, ScanMatch, foveal-disc IoU (FDISS), and dynamic time warping (DTW) comparing scanpaths. Fixations were extracted via dispersion-threshold algorithm.
AI.result: (i) Artists and neurotypicals are nearly indistinguishable spatially (CC=0.96) and temporally. (ii) ASD gaze shows dissociation: matches artists' wide spatial exploration but has distinct temporal signature (shorter fixations, less dwell, most idiosyncratic scanpaths). (iii) ASD gaze is not selectively artist-like; marginally closer to neurotypical overall.
AI.conclusion: Autistic viewing of art is a distinct, group-specific attentional profile in both space and time, motivating population-conditioned models of aesthetic attention.

title: CRISP: Constrained Refinement via Iterative Squeezing Process for Robust Medical Image Segmentation under Domain Shift
comment: X pages, 3 figures, 3 tables; submitted to AAAI 2027
summary: Distribution shift in medical imaging remains a central bottleneck for the clinical translation of medical AI. Failure to address it can lead to severe performance degradation in unseen environments and exacerbate health inequities. Existing methods for domain adaptation are inherently limited by exhausting predefined possibilities through simulated shifts or pseudo-supervision. Such strategies struggle in the open-ended and unpredictable real world, where distribution shifts are effectively infinite. To address this challenge, we adopt the "Rank Stability of Positive Regions" as a working assumption under distribution shift, and use it to derive robust spatial hints for source-only segmentation. Guided by this assumption, we propose CRISP, a model-agnostic framework that, unlike deployment-time adaptation, requires no test-time parameter updates and no target-domain data--a target-free, plug-in refinement framework that segments with frozen weights. Rather than using ranking to directly output masks, CRISP exploits the stability of probability rankings under distribution shift to derive robust spatial priors. Via latent feature perturbation, perturbation-invariant high-grade regions define a high-precision (HP) core, while voxels that remain potentially foreground under at least one perturbation define a high-recall (HR) support; these dual priors are then recursively refined under perturbation. We then design an iterative training framework that progressively squeezes HP and HR toward the final segmentation. Extensive evaluations on multi-center cardiac MRI and CT-based lung vessel segmentation demonstrate CRISP's superior robustness, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods with striking HD95 reductions of up to 0.14 (7.0% improvement), 1.90 (13.1% improvement), and 8.39 (38.9% improvement) pixels across multi-center, demographic, and modality shifts, respectively.

AI.tldr: CRISP is a target-free, plug-in refinement framework that improves segmentation robustness under distribution shifts by exploiting the stability of probability rankings, requiring no test-time adaptation or target-domain data. It significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multi-center cardiac MRI and CT lung vessel segmentation tasks.
AI.motivation: Distribution shift in medical imaging causes severe performance degradation and health inequities in clinical AI. Existing domain adaptation methods are limited by relying on predefined simulated shifts or pseudo-supervision, which fail in the open-ended real world where shifts are effectively infinite.
AI.method: CRISP adopts "Rank Stability of Positive Regions" as a working assumption. It uses latent feature perturbation to derive two robust spatial priors: a high-precision (HP) core (perturbation-invariant high-grade regions) and a high-recall (HR) support (voxels potentially foreground under at least one perturbation). These dual priors are recursively refined under perturbation within an iterative training framework that progressively squeezes HP and HR toward the final segmentation.
AI.result: On multi-center cardiac MRI and CT lung vessel segmentation, CRISP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving striking HD95 reductions of up to 0.14 (7.0% improvement), 1.90 (13.1% improvement), and 8.39 (38.9% improvement) pixels across multi-center, demographic, and modality shifts, respectively.
AI.conclusion: CRISP provides a robust, model-agnostic solution for segmentation under open-ended distribution shifts without requiring test-time parameter updates or target-domain data, offering a promising direction for clinical translation of medical AI.

title: ARMOR++: Agentic Orchestration of a Multi-Domain Primitive Set for Transferable Attacks on Deepfake Detectors
summary: The reliability of deepfake detectors frequently degrades under black-box adversarial transfer, as these models often rely on fragile, architecture-dependent forensic cues. Existing transfer attacks often lack semantic awareness and struggle to maintain effectiveness under strict no-query constraints, particularly when perturbations are transferred from convolutional surrogates to transformer-based targets. To address these limitations, this paper introduces ARMOR++, a robust multi-agent framework designed for high-transferability deepfake evasion. The framework leverages the Qwen2.5-VL Vision-Language Model (VLM) to supply spatial semantic priors, while the Qwen3 Large Language Model (LLM) orchestrates primitive selection, adaptive hyperparameter reparameterization, and entropy-regularized perturbation mixing. By integrating five complementary primitives, spanning dense optimization, saliency-based methods, spatial transformations, frequency-domain perturbations, and block-structured modifications, ARMOR++ effectively targets heterogeneous inductive biases. Rigorous evaluation on the AADD-2025 benchmark demonstrates that ARMOR++ significantly outperforms existing agentic and non-agentic baselines across both low- and high-quality image regimes. Statistical analysis confirms a substantial gain in blind-target Attack Success Rate (ASR) over the state-of-the-art agentic baseline, with further performance advantages evidenced against non-agentic benchmarks and under robust defensive configurations. These findings highlight a significant residual reliability gap in current deepfake detector deployments and demonstrate the efficacy of agentic orchestration in identifying latent vulnerabilities.

AI.tldr: ARMOR++ is a multi-agent framework using Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3 LLMs to orchestrate five complementary perturbation primitives for high-transferability black-box adversarial attacks against deepfake detectors, significantly outperforming existing baselines on the AADD-2025 benchmark.
AI.motivation: Deepfake detectors suffer from reliability degradation under black-box adversarial transfer due to reliance on fragile, architecture-dependent forensic cues, and existing transfer attacks lack semantic awareness and struggle under strict no-query constraints, especially when transferring from convolutional to transformer-based architectures.
AI.method: ARMOR++ employs Qwen2.5-VL VLM for spatial semantic priors and Qwen3 LLM for orchestrating primitive selection, adaptive hyperparameter reparameterization, and entropy-regularized perturbation mixing across five complementary primitives: dense optimization, saliency-based methods, spatial transformations, frequency-domain perturbations, and block-structured modifications.
AI.result: On the AADD-2025 benchmark, ARMOR++ significantly outperforms existing agentic and non-agentic baselines across low- and high-quality image regimes, with substantial gains in blind-target Attack Success Rate (ASR) over state-of-the-art agentic baselines and further advantages against non-agentic benchmarks and robust defensive configurations.
AI.conclusion: There is a significant residual reliability gap in current deepfake detector deployments, and agentic orchestration is effective in identifying latent vulnerabilities.

title: HoloGeo: Mitigating Landmark Bias in Geo-localization via Evidence-Driven Reasoning
summary: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have significantly improved image geo-localization, yet existing models remain susceptible to landmark bias, causing them to overlook geographical cues or form spurious correlations, ultimately resulting in inaccurate localization. To systematically investigate this issue, we first design two quantitative metrics, Bias Intensity (BI) and Bias Harmfulness (BH), to characterize the impact of landmarks exerted on model reasoning, and establish a comprehensive benchmark, LandmarkBias-3K. To mitigate landmark bias, we further propose an evidence-driven reasoning framework, HoloGeo, to improve the reliability of geo-localization. HoloGeo is supported by a high-quality dataset, BF-30k, annotated with structured multi-evidence bias-free reasoning chains. By incorporating multi-dimensional rewards, HoloGeo explicitly encourages balanced attention over diverse visual cues and achieves evidence-driven joint reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HoloGeo not only maintains excellent performance on IM2GPS3K and YFCC4k but also significantly outperforms existing open-source VLMs on LandmarkBias-3K, validating its effectiveness for robust geospatial reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and addresses landmark bias in Vision-Language Models for geo-localization by introducing metrics (BI, BH), a benchmark (LandmarkBias-3K), a bias-free dataset (BF-30k), and a evidence-driven reasoning framework (HoloGeo) that achieves robust geospatial reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing VLMs for image geo-localization suffer from landmark bias, either overlooking geographical cues or forming spurious correlations, leading to inaccurate localization. The authors aim to systematically investigate and mitigate this issue.
AI.method: The authors design two metrics (Bias Intensity and Bias Harmfulness) and a benchmark (LandmarkBias-3K) to quantify landmark bias. They propose HoloGeo, an evidence-driven reasoning framework supported by a high-quality dataset (BF-30k) with structured multi-evidence bias-free reasoning chains. HoloGeo uses multi-dimensional rewards to encourage balanced attention over diverse visual cues and achieve evidence-driven joint reasoning.
AI.result: HoloGeo maintains excellent performance on IM2GPS3K and YFCC4k, and significantly outperforms existing open-source VLMs on LandmarkBias-3K, validating its effectiveness for robust geospatial reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed metrics, benchmark, and HoloGeo framework effectively address landmark bias in VLMs for geo-localization, improving reliability and robustness of geospatial reasoning.

title: Motion-Conditioned Multi-View Fusion for Myocardial Infarction Localization from Echocardiography
summary: Myocardial infarction (MI) remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Echocardiography (Echo) is a widely available modality for MI assessment, where regional wall motion abnormality is a key indicator. Prior learning based methods for myocardial motion analysis often use handcrafted descriptors or densely supervised estimation, but the need for extensive annotation limits applicability. Foundation models have recently improved vision-based Echo analysis; however, most methods operate on single views and segment-level localization remains unreliable under view-dependent ambiguity, especially in apical views. To address this, we propose MCF-Net, a novel motion-guided multi-view fusion framework that fuses myocardial motion cues with foundation model representations to localize infarction. Visual features are extracted using EchoPrime, a pretrained Echo foundation model shared across dual views. Cardiac motion is modeled with extremely sparse supervision: a single annotated template frame is transferred across videos to initialize point tracking, avoiding dense labels. Motion-derived segment-aware soft masks provide coarse spatial priors that selectively enhance features for challenging myocardial segments. A motion-conditioned fusion mechanism then integrates motion and vision across views, refining predictions without overriding strong appearance cues. On segment-level MI localization, MCF-Net achieves 72.4\% F1 and 84.9\% accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art motion-only, vision-only, and fusion baselines.

AI.tldr: MCF-Net is a motion-guided multi-view fusion framework that combines myocardial motion cues with foundation model representations (EchoPrime) to localize myocardial infarction from echocardiography, using extremely sparse supervision (single annotated template frame) and achieving 72.4% F1 and 84.9% accuracy on segment-level MI localization, outperforming prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing myocardial motion analysis methods rely on handcrafted descriptors or densely supervised estimation requiring extensive annotation. Foundation models improve Echo analysis but operate on single views and suffer from unreliable segment-level localization under view-dependent ambiguity, especially in apical views.
AI.method: (1) Visual features extracted via EchoPrime (pretrained Echo foundation model) shared across dual views. (2) Cardiac motion modeled with extremely sparse supervision: single annotated template frame transferred across videos to initialize point tracking. (3) Motion-derived segment-aware soft masks provide coarse spatial priors to selectively enhance features for challenging segments. (4) Motion-conditioned fusion mechanism integrates motion and vision across views, refining without overriding strong appearance cues.
AI.result: MCF-Net achieves 72.4% F1 and 84.9% accuracy on segment-level MI localization, outperforming state-of-the-art motion-only, vision-only, and fusion baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed motion-guided multi-view fusion with sparse supervision addresses view-dependent ambiguity in echocardiography, enabling more reliable infarction localization without dense annotation requirements.

title: Online Neural Space Time Memory for Dynamic Novel View Synthesis
comment: 15 pages. Preprint. Project page with demos and video results: https://nst-mem.github.io
summary: Online novel view synthesis from multi-view streaming videos faces a fundamental trade-off: maintaining a persistent, long-horizon memory to reconstruct temporarily occluded regions while operating under strict real-time constraints. While Test-Time Training (TTT) offers a powerful memory mechanism, standard models mandate gradient-based memory updates at every frame to adapt to the changing motion in dynamic scenes. The computational cost of heavy memory updates precludes real-time application and can lead to instability over long contexts. Given that memory updates are more demanding than memory application and video content is largely redundant, we propose to decouple the frequencies of these two processes. Our approach performs periodic memory updates while applying the memory on a per-frame basis, using cross-view attention to manage deformations between the prior memory state and the current frame. To lock in the historical context, we introduce two critical mechanisms: an auxiliary Memory Loss that forces persistent internalization of the scene, and a Memory Caching strategy that regularizes active weights against catastrophic drift. Our method demonstrates real-time, state-of-the-art performance on scenes with dynamic human motion as well as minute-scale online memorization.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes decoupling memory update frequency from memory application frequency in online novel view synthesis, using periodic updates and per-frame application with cross-view attention, plus Memory Loss and Memory Caching to achieve real-time, state-of-the-art performance on dynamic scenes.
AI.motivation: Online novel view synthesis from multi-view streaming videos faces a trade-off between maintaining long-horizon memory for occluded regions and strict real-time constraints. Standard TTT models require gradient-based memory updates at every frame, which is computationally prohibitive for real-time application and causes instability over long contexts.
AI.method: The method decouples memory update frequency from memory application frequency: periodic memory updates are performed while per-frame memory application is maintained. Cross-view attention handles deformations between prior memory and current frame. Two key mechanisms are introduced: an auxiliary Memory Loss for scene internalization and a Memory Caching strategy to prevent catastrophic drift of active weights.
AI.result: The method achieves real-time, state-of-the-art performance on scenes with dynamic human motion and demonstrates minute-scale online memorization capabilities.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling update and application frequencies, the proposed approach enables real-time novel view synthesis with persistent long-horizon memory, overcoming the computational bottleneck of per-frame gradient updates while maintaining stability over long video streams.

title: MeanFlowNFT: Bringing Forward-Process RL to Average-Velocity Generators
comment: Project Page: https://harahan.github.io/meanflownft-project-page/, GitHub: https://github.com/Harahan/MeanFlowNFT, Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/Harahan/MeanFlowNFT
summary: MeanFlow generators achieve fast few-step sampling by predicting average velocities over time intervals, making them attractive for efficient generation. Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a powerful way to align diffusion and flow models with human preferences and task-specific objectives. In particular, DiffusionNFT offers an efficient forward-process RL framework that does not require reverse-process trajectories or likelihood estimation. However, applying such RL methods to MeanFlow remains underexplored. DiffusionNFT optimizes instantaneous velocities, whereas MeanFlow samples with average velocities. To bridge this gap, we introduce MeanFlowNFT. Inspired by the MeanFlow identity, which bridges average and instantaneous velocities, we construct an induced instantaneous-velocity predictor. We apply the DiffusionNFT objective to this predictor, making reward optimization well-defined for MeanFlow. Sampling remains based on the average velocity, preserving MeanFlow's fast few-step generation. We further prove that MeanFlowNFT inherits DiffusionNFT's strict policy-improvement guarantee. Experiments on image and video generation show that MeanFlowNFT consistently improves baselines. Moreover, it outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL-tuned few-step generators on most metrics ($6$ of $8$ on SD3.5-M), and can even surpass multi-step RL-tuned diffusion while using only a few sampling steps. For instance, on Wan 2.1, $4$-step MeanFlowNFT reaches a VBench score of $84.33$, surpassing $50$-step LongCat-Video RL ($82.57$).

AI.tldr: MeanFlowNFT extends Reinforcement Learning (DiffusionNFT) to MeanFlow generators by bridging average and instantaneous velocities via the MeanFlow identity, enabling fast few-step sampling with strict policy improvement guarantees and achieving state-of-the-art results in image and video generation.
AI.motivation: Applying RL-based alignment methods (like DiffusionNFT) to MeanFlow generators is underexplored because DiffusionNFT optimizes instantaneous velocities while MeanFlow uses average velocities for sampling, creating a fundamental gap.
AI.method: Leveraging the MeanFlow identity, the authors construct an induced instantaneous-velocity predictor from the average velocity, apply the DiffusionNFT objective to it, while keeping sampling based on the original average velocity to preserve fast few-step generation.
AI.result: MeanFlowNFT consistently improves baselines on image and video generation; outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL-tuned few-step generators on 6/8 metrics on SD3.5-M; and on Wan 2.1, 4-step MeanFlowNFT achieves VBench 84.33, surpassing 50-step LongCat-Video RL (82.57).
AI.conclusion: MeanFlowNFT successfully bridges RL fine-tuning with MeanFlow, inherits strict policy-improvement guarantees, and demonstrates that few-step RL-tuned MeanFlow can surpass multi-step RL-tuned diffusion models.

title: Hierarchical Denoising For Multi-Step Visual Reasoning
summary: Video models are evolving into vision foundation models, yet they still lack human-like multi-step reasoning. Streaming autoregressive diffusion models are efficient but limited in reasoning, while bidirectional diffusion enables global revision with high inference costs due to dense frame-level denoising. Both paradigms struggle to achieve logical consistency and low-latency streaming for complex reasoning tasks. We propose HDR (Hierarchical Denoising for Visual Reasoning), a unified framework that integrates hierarchical latents into causal video generation for multi-step reasoning. HDR organizes video latents into a tree-structured hierarchy, enabling coarse-to-fine reasoning before streaming output. Coarse denoising layers preserve uncertain hypotheses for global planning, while finer layers progressively refine them into concrete visual states. A sparse hierarchical attention pattern (SHAP) further reduces temporal attention costs. We introduce a level-stratified multi-step video reasoning benchmark with out-of-distribution cases, covering six tasks: maze navigation, Tower of Hanoi, one-line drawing, sliding puzzle, Sokoban, and water pouring. Compared with streaming autoregressive diffusion baselines, HDR improves success from 34.22 to 60.29 (76.2% relative gain) and increases average progress from 76.00 to 89.56, demonstrating more consistent reasoning trajectories. HDR maintains low-latency streaming at 0.70 seconds per latent, achieving 54.2 times faster inference than bidirectional diffusion. It also retains 82.9% of full-data performance with only 2% training data, compared with 52.0% for bidirectional diffusion. Real-world robot experiments further demonstrate HDR's potential for physical interaction and world modeling. Project demo: https://hierarchical-diffusion-reasoning.github.io/.

AI.tldr: HDR is a hierarchical denoising framework that integrates tree-structured video latents into causal video generation, enabling coarse-to-fine multi-step reasoning with low-latency streaming. It achieves 76.2% relative gain over autoregressive diffusion baselines and 54.2x faster inference than bidirectional diffusion.
AI.motivation: Existing video models (streaming autoregressive diffusion and bidirectional diffusion) lack human-like multi-step reasoning—either limited in reasoning capability or incurring high inference costs. Neither achieves logical consistency and low-latency streaming for complex reasoning tasks.
AI.method: HDR organizes video latents into a tree-structured hierarchy for coarse-to-fine reasoning: coarse denoising layers preserve uncertain hypotheses for global planning, finer layers refine them into concrete visual states. A sparse hierarchical attention pattern (SHAP) reduces temporal attention costs. A level-stratified multi-step video reasoning benchmark with six out-of-distribution tasks is introduced.
AI.result: HDR improves success from 34.22 to 60.29 (76.2% relative gain) and average progress from 76.00 to 89.56 over autoregressive baselines. It achieves 0.70s per latent (54.2x faster than bidirectional diffusion) and retains 82.9% of full-data performance with only 2% training data (vs. 52.0% for bidirectional diffusion). Real-world robot experiments show potential.
AI.conclusion: HDR effectively bridges the gap between reasoning capability and streaming efficiency in video generative models, demonstrating strong out-of-distribution generalization and real-world applicability for physical interaction and world modeling.
